title: Post-pandemic strategic evaluation of food supply chains using hybrid decision models
source: Pamukkale University Journal of Engineering Sciences
summary: The increasing complexity and disruptions in global food supply chains (FSCs), particularly after COVID-19, have emphasized the need for resilient and adaptive strategies. This study conducts a comparative analysis of various FSC structures
content: The increasing complexity and disruptions in global food supply chains (FSCs), particularly after COVID-19, have emphasized the need for resilient and adaptive strategies. This study conducts a comparative analysis of various FSC structures, such as Centralized, Decentralized, Digitalized, Localized, and Hybrid models. The comparison was carried out by applying two integrated multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) methods: Entropy-based MOORA and Entropy-based MARCOS. Objective weights for the eight criteria (cost, flexibility, resilience, lead time, sustainability, service level, innovation capability, and risk management) were assigned through the Entropy method that was used to reduce the subjective bias. In general, both methods identified the Digitalized and Hybrid supply chain models as the two highest-ranked alternatives, while the Centralized model ranked last. To make the findings even more robust, we carried out a sensitivity analysis where we changed the criterion weights in different scenarios. Moreover, an Entropy-based COPRAS method was employed for the robustness analysis, and the findings supported the stability and consistency of the rankings across different methodological approaches. By comparing two MCDM methods in a post-pandemic context, the study contributes to the literature while offering practical guidance for stakeholders on investing in digital infrastructure, adopting hybrid supply chain models, and integrating sustainability objectives into supply chain planning. The findings provide practical guidance for policymakers and executives seeking to enhance the resilience and environmental sustainability of FSCs amid global uncertainty.

title: Addressing emerging authenticity issues using novel data-driven analytics
summary: As globalization continues to grow, trade structures are becoming increasingly complex, which creates numerous challenges for businesses. One of these is ensuring the authenticity of high-priced products. Recent developments have made it cl
content: As globalization continues to grow, trade structures are becoming increasingly complex, which creates numerous challenges for businesses. One of these is ensuring the authenticity of high-priced products. Recent developments have made it clear that established control mechanisms are often inadequate for ensuring protection against fraud or mislabeling, so the need for new analytical solutions is growing rapidly. In its individual studies, this dissertation examines the application of modern data-driven approaches for the authentication of various goods of agricultural and non-agricultural origin. At the heart of all investigations is a software that was developed specifically for this research project but, thanks to its modular design, has great potential for future applications in diverse fields. It enables the automated processing, modeling, and evaluation of spectroscopic and spectrometric data. To date, there has been no solution that enables streamlined analysis of data from, for example, isotope ratio mass spectrometry (IRMS), nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy (NMR), near-infrared spectroscopy (NIR), and the associated metadata in a fully reproducible and transparent manner. One area of investigation focused on the authentication of spring barley with respect to the harvest year. Grain samples were taken directly from active trade flows and then analyzed to ensure that they reflected realistic conditions in the supply chain, in contrast to numerous studies that relied on samples from strictly controlled experimental fields and are therefore hardly transferable to real-world conditions. The aim was to develop a novel analytical approach that allows differentiation of the two harvest years 2017 and the extremely dry 2018 for spring barley samples by means of multiple modern analytical techniques and to link the observed metabolic differences to the physiological responses of plants to drought stress. Samples from the 2018 harvest year showed significantly less negative δ¹³C values than those from 2017, likely reflecting reduced stomatal conductance and altered carbon assimilation during the grain-filling stage. These findings were supported by NIR, which showed lower protein, starch, and moisture content and an increase in lipid content for 2018. NMR analysis revealed elevated concentrations of the osmolyte betaine, a well-known biochemical marker for abiotic stress adaptation. By merging the isotope and NIR datasets and applying multivariate statistical analysis, a classification model was built that achieved 100% separation accuracy between the two investigated years. Although not directly linked to authenticity, differences in variety-specific stress responses were also observed, demonstrating the broader applicability of the approach for selecting stress-resilient varieties in the future. Subsequently, the established chemometric framework for authenticity testing was adapted and transferred to a fundamentally different sample matri

title: Adventitious Root Formation and its Utilization for Sustainable Plant Propagation
summary: Adventitious roots arise from non-root organs such as stems, leaves, or floral tissues, thereby enhancing plant growth, development, and survival. Their formation represents an important adaptive response that is triggered by mechanical inj
content: Adventitious roots arise from non-root organs such as stems, leaves, or floral tissues, thereby enhancing plant growth, development, and survival. Their formation represents an important adaptive response that is triggered by mechanical injury, environmental stress, or other external stimuli. Consequently, adventitious rooting is closely associated with improved plant establishment, stress tolerance, and crop productivity under adverse environmental conditions, including drought, soil salinity, and waterlogging, which are common in arid and semi-arid regions. The initiation and development of adventitious roots are regulated by a complex interplay of phytohormones, particularly auxins, cytokinins, and ethylene, together with transcription factors, signalling pathways, and epigenetic mechanisms. Recent advances in molecular biology have identified several key genes involved in auxin signalling and transcriptional regulation that govern adventitious root formation. This review synthesizes current knowledge on the physiological, hormonal, molecular, and genetic mechanisms underlying adventitious root development and highlights their applications in plant propagation, crop improvement, and sustainable agricultural production. These insights provide a valuable foundation for enhancing plant resilience and productivity, particularly under environmentally challenging conditions.

title: Necessity or Indulgence: Reconsidering Space Exploration
summary: Taking the debate over whether space exploration constitutes a necessity or a mere indulgence as its starting point, this essay adopts a philosophical and interdisciplinary perspective to re-examine the value of human space activities inspi
content: Taking the debate over whether space exploration constitutes a necessity or a mere indulgence as its starting point, this essay adopts a philosophical and interdisciplinary perspective to re-examine the value of human space activities inspired by the Pale Blue Dot photograph. The study breaks down the binary opposition between necessity and indulgence, arguing that this distinction is not purely economic but hinges on definitions of resource purposes and human civilisational goals. Three core dimensions are adopted for analysis: the failure of private markets to fund long-horizon innovative investment, unique planetary-scale challenges that can only be addressed via space infrastructure, and the intrinsic moral and philosophical meaning of exploration beyond utilitarian calculation. The analysis demonstrates that public investment in space programmes yields sustained economic spillover effects, delivers irreplaceable capabilities in climate monitoring, planetary defence and microgravity scientific research. Further, drawing on the concept of the overview effect, the paper distinguishes space exploration from historical colonial expansion, framing it as a secular pilgrimage oriented toward human self-transformation. This research concludes that dismissing space exploration as an indulgence relies on narrow short-term utilitarian standards; undertaking space exploration represents a civilisational choice concerning humanity's self-identity and shared responsibility for Earth.

title: Walking the Talk: Tourism Performance vs. Sustainability Communication in Six European Destinations
source: Journal of Strategic Innovation and Sustainability
summary: Tourism destinations increasingly promote sustainability, yet a persistent gap often separates measurable performance from communicated brand narratives. This study examines how six European destinations—Germany, Spain, Turkey, Italy, Greec
content: Tourism destinations increasingly promote sustainability, yet a persistent gap often separates measurable performance from communicated brand narratives. This study examines how six European destinations—Germany, Spain, Turkey, Italy, Greece, and Portugal—with differing World Economic Forum Travel & Tourism Development Index (TTDI) 2024 scores deploy sustainability themes. TTDI data are complemented by the Tourism Potential Creation Index (TPCI), capturing tourism efficiency relative to population, and by content analysis of official tourism websites, campaigns, and social media materials. The analysis extends Kiraz's Sustainability-Oriented City Branding Index to national contexts across three dimensions: Environmental Communication, Adaptive Branding, and Communication Authenticity. Findings reveal a strong negative correlation (r = -0.913, p < 0.01) between environmental performance and communication intensity, indicating that lower-performing destinations compensate through intensified messaging. Four patterns emerge: aligned leaders, silent performers, aspirational communicators, and moderate aligners. Sustainability communication appears to function as a defensive strategy to avoid negative perceptions rather than a proactive differentiator, carrying both opportunities and credibility risks for destination marketing.

title: Screening and identification of significant media components using Plackett–Burman design for enhanced extracellular protease production by Bacillus sp. MTCC 511 under mutagenic stress conditions
summary: Abstract Background Statistical screening of media components is essential for identifying the key variables that govern protease yield from Bacillus species. We used a 12-run Plackett–Burman Design (PBD) to screen ten independent variables
content: Abstract Background Statistical screening of media components is essential for identifying the key variables that govern protease yield from Bacillus species. We used a 12-run Plackett–Burman Design (PBD) to screen ten independent variables—dipotassium phosphate, monopotassium phosphate, ammonium sulphate, sodium nitrate, magnesium sulphate heptahydrate, calcium chloride, carbon source, nitrogen source, agitation speed, and pH—for their effects on extracellular protease production by Bacillus sp. MTCC 511 under four mutagenic stress conditions: thermal treatment at 70 °C and 80 °C (10 min each) and UV irradiation (2 and 3 min). Results Enzyme activity was quantified by Folin–Ciocalteu assay against a tyrosine standard (R2 = 0.998). The highest protease activity, 8.66 U/mL, was recorded under 3-min UV irradiation in a medium containing starch (1%), yeast extract (0.1%), K 2 HPO 4 (0.05 M), KH 2 PO 4 (0.05 M), (NH 4 ) 2 SO 4 (0.05 M), NaNO 3 (0.1 M), MgSO 4 ·7H 2 O (0.002 M), and CaCl 2 (0.002 M) at pH 9 and 120 rpm, representing a 20.6-fold improvement over the unsupplemented basal medium. ANOVA showed R2 > 97% for the 70 °C, 80 °C, and UV-3 min models; the UV-2 min model was statistically inadequate (R2 = 56.52%). Pareto analysis pointed to agitation speed, NaNO 3 , MgSO 4 ·7H 2 O, and carbon source as the most influential factors. Pearson correlation between thermal and UV-3 min responses (r = 0.72–0.83) is consistent with previously described σ B -dependent stress–response pathways. Conclusions The PBD screening efficiently identified significant factors whose effects are consistent with established regulatory mechanisms including nitrogen catabolite repression, carbon catabolite repression, and dissolved oxygen-dependent secretion. Follow-up response surface optimization is warranted to characterize factor interactions and identify the global optimum.

title: Effects of Farmer-participatory Natural Farming Practices on Soil Properties, Pest Incidence, and Economic Performance of Tomato in Red-lateritic Soils of Eastern India
source: Journal of Scientific Research and Reports
summary: Aims: To evaluate a complete farmer-managed natural farming (NF) package relative to a recommended-dose-of-fertilizer (RDF)-based comparison treatment in tomato, with an emphasis on short-term soil properties, crop performance, pest and dis
content: Aims: To evaluate a complete farmer-managed natural farming (NF) package relative to a recommended-dose-of-fertilizer (RDF)-based comparison treatment in tomato, with an emphasis on short-term soil properties, crop performance, pest and disease incidence, and farm economics under acidic red-lateritic conditions. Study Design: A randomized paired farmer-field design was used. Ten farmer fields served as blocks, and each field contained one NF plot and one RDF-based comparison plot. Treatment was evaluated within the paired field structure. Place and Duration of Study: The trial was conducted during the 2025 kharif season in Bankura district, West Bengal, India, on acidic red-lateritic soils. Methodology: The NF package comprised beejamrit, jeevamrit, ghanajeevamrit, locally adapted botanical crop-protection formulations, and mulching. The comparison treatment received the recommended N:P2O5:K2O dose, while farmyard manure, irrigation, staking, and sanitation were common to both treatments. Soil properties, crop growth and yield attributes, pest and disease incidence, and economic indicators were recorded. Crop growth and yield were evaluated using the paired farmer-field/block structure; pest and disease percentages and economic indicators are presented descriptively. Results: Within the NF treatment, post-harvest soil pH, soil organic carbon, available nitrogen and available phosphorus were 5.86 ± 0.04, 0.457 ± 0.017%, 221.38 ± 5.69 kg ha-1, and 19.83 ± 0.95 kg ha-1, respectively. Growth and yield attributes did not differ significantly (P > .05) between NF and the RDF-based comparison treatment; plot-wise marketable yields were 42.63 ± 1.21 and 44.18 ± 1.27 t ha-1, respectively. Observed early blight, late blight, and fruit borer incidence values were numerically lower under NF (12.2%, 8.1%, and 8.3%) than under RDF (18.4%, 12.6%, and 15.2%). NF also had a lower recorded cultivation cost (₹84,913.65 ha-1 vs. ₹129,684.25 ha-1), with a higher descriptive net return (₹85,614.75 ha-1 vs. ₹47,050.55 ha-1) and B:C (2.01 vs. 1.36). Conclusion: Under the conditions of this single-season, ten-field study, no statistically significant difference in marketable tomato yield was detected between the integrated NF package and the RDF-based treatment. Within the NF treatment, selected soil indicators showed favourable within-season changes, while pest and disease incidence values were numerically lower and recorded cultivation cost was lower than under the RDF-based treatment. Because pest and disease outcomes and economic comparisons are descriptive, and because the NF treatment was evaluated as an integrated package, the findings should be interpreted as context-specific evidence that warrants multi-season and multi-location validation.

title: Stable isotopes from Earth science to bedside medicine: beyond tracers and toward mechanistic biomarkers in medical oncology
summary: Stable isotopes are non-radioactive variants of the same element whose small mass differences produce predictable effects in chemical and biological systems. While medicine has mainly used the administration of enriched stable isotopes as t
content: Stable isotopes are non-radioactive variants of the same element whose small mass differences produce predictable effects in chemical and biological systems. While medicine has mainly used the administration of enriched stable isotopes as tracers of physiological function, the natural sciences developed stable-isotope ratios into robust measures of source, transformation, and underlying mechanism across Earth and life history. This analytical power - that often goes beyond conventional concentration-based assays - emerged through advances in isotope theory, mass spectrometry, but perhaps most importantly also globally shared reference systematics. Here, we review that trajectory and argue that medicine is positioned for a similar shift, as new computational and analytical tools make isotope analysis increasingly compatible with clinical throughput. In this shift, some natural isotope variation may serve as mechanistic biomarkers of physiology and disease. Integrated with multiomics and machine learning, stable isotopes could support earlier detection, improved risk stratification, and personalized care, particularly in cancer.

title: Scaling Productivity in Harsh Rainfed Ecosystems: The Strategic Role of Frontline Demonstrations (FLDs) in Pali, Rajasthan
summary: Frontline Demonstrations (FLDs) were evaluated to assess the productivity, technological gaps and economic performance of improved crop production technologies under farmers’ field conditions in Pali district, Rajasthan, during 2018-19 to 2
content: Frontline Demonstrations (FLDs) were evaluated to assess the productivity, technological gaps and economic performance of improved crop production technologies under farmers’ field conditions in Pali district, Rajasthan, during 2018-19 to 2022-23. Demonstrations were conducted on six major crops green gram, cluster bean, sesame, wheat, mustard and cumin using improved varieties and recommended agronomic practices, with adjacent farmers’ fields maintained as local checks. FLDs consistently outperformed farmers’ practices, recording yield increases of 43.75-57.35% in green gram, 41.88-64.57% in cluster bean, 55.48-62.83% in sesame, 35.96-50.26% in wheat, 50.12-58.73% in mustard and 42.22-56.57% in cumin. Technology gaps declined across all crops while technology indices decreased progressively, indicating improved realization of yield potential under farmers’ field conditions. The decline was associated with repeated exposure to improved production practices, closer technical supervision, better synchronization of agronomic operations and increasing familiarity with recommended technologies, although seasonal and field-level variability remained important. Although extension gaps remained considerable, they highlighted the substantial scope for increasing productivity through wider dissemination of recommended technologies. Frontline Demonstrations also recorded consistently higher benefit-cost ratios than farmers’ practices, confirming the economic viability of the improved production packages. Overall, the study demonstrated that FLDs are an effective extension approach for enhancing crop productivity and profitability under the semi-arid conditions of western Rajasthan. Further research should include adoption and long-term impact assessments to evaluate the sustainability and wider diffusion of demonstrated technologies.

title: A BIO – POIYMERIC POSACONAZOLE NAIL LAQUER FOR ENHANCED TRANSUNGAL PENETRATION AND ANTIFUNGAL PERFORMANCE
source: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
summary: Onychomycosis is a common fungal infection affecting the nail unit and accounts for nearly 50% of all nail disorders worldwide.It is mainly caused by dermatophytes, non-dermatophyte moulds, and yeasts, leading to nail discoloration, thicken
content: Onychomycosis is a common fungal infection affecting the nail unit and accounts for nearly 50% of all nail disorders worldwide.It is mainly caused by dermatophytes, non-dermatophyte moulds, and yeasts, leading to nail discoloration, thickening, and separation from the nail bed.Conventional therapies include systemic antifungal drugs and topical formulations; however, systemic treatments are often associated with adverse effects and drug interactions.Nail lacquer formulations have emerged as an effective topical delivery system due to their ability to form a film over the nail surface and provide sustained drug release.Recently, bio-polymeric nail lacquer systems containing antifungal agents such as posaconazole have been investigated to enhance transungual penetration and improve therapeutic efficacy.This review discusses the epidemiology, classification, treatment strategies, and recent advancements in nail lacquer-based drug delivery systems for the treatment of onychomycosis Additionally, controlled and sustained drug release from nail lacquers improves therapeutic results and reduces the frequency of application.The use of biodegradable and biocompatible polymers to create safer and more potent antifungal compositions is another area of recent research.As a result, nail lacquer-based delivery methods offer a novel and promising approach to the successful treatment of onychomycosis.

title: Iraq's Climate Negotiation Handbook: Enlil Center's contribution and assessment
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: An Enlil Center brief by Othman Kareem, Director of Research & Policy at Enlil Center, on Climate Negotiation Handbook — Conference of Parties on Climate Change, the 333-page reference prepared for Iraq's COP28 delegation and published by U
content: An Enlil Center brief by Othman Kareem, Director of Research & Policy at Enlil Center, on Climate Negotiation Handbook — Conference of Parties on Climate Change, the 333-page reference prepared for Iraq's COP28 delegation and published by UNDP Iraq and the Ministry of Environment of the Republic of Iraq (2023). Othman Kareem (Enlil Center), working as a consultant to UNDP, drafted three of its sections: the mitigation chapters (NDCs, Article 6 cooperative approaches, carbon markets), the Energy Security policy brief, and Section D, Iraq's Position Paper for COP28. The brief summarises the Handbook, sets out Enlil's contribution and gives Enlil's assessment of why it matters as Iraq's first institutional negotiating memory. It does not reproduce the Handbook, which remains the work and property of its publishers. Web version: https://enlilcenter.org/research/iraq-climate-negotiation-handbook-enlil-contribution

title: Enhancing Farm Productivity and Income through Farmers’ Participatory Livestock Based Farming System in Arid Regions of Rajasthan
summary: The study was conducted by ICAR-Central Arid Zone Research Institute, Jodhpur at Harsolav village in Nagaur district from 2016 to 2018 to increase farm productivity and income through improved crop technologies together with the integration
content: The study was conducted by ICAR-Central Arid Zone Research Institute, Jodhpur at Harsolav village in Nagaur district from 2016 to 2018 to increase farm productivity and income through improved crop technologies together with the integration of crops and livestock in participatory mode. The grass species Cenchrus ciliaris and C. setigerus were selected for pasture development under different land use systems. Intervention related to dual purpose crops viz., pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum), clusterbean (Cyamopsis tetragonoloba), mung bean (Vigna radiata) and barley (Hordeum vulgare); and fodder crops viz., lucerne (Medicago sativa), oat (Avena sativa) and pearl millet (Pennisetum glaucum) were undertaken both under rainfed and irrigated condition. For livestock feed supplementation, low-cost concentrate mixtures containing non-conventional feed resources, multi-nutrient blocks (MNB), and multi-nutrient mixtures (MNM) were provided to the small and large ruminants owned by selected farmers. The results showed that improved cultivation practices for dual-purpose crops increased yield and economic returns by 12 to 18% compared with the farmers’ traditional practices. Improved fodder crop cultivation enhanced green fodder availability, increased milk yield and farmers’ income. The fodder crops like lucerne, oat and pearlmillet provided net returns ranging from Rs. 26652 to Rs. 121924 ha-1. Perennial pasture grasses increased fodder availability and provided benefit to the tune of Rs. 5000 to 6000 ha-1 under rainfed condition. Supplementation of multi-nutrient blocks (MNB) at 250 g animal-¹ day-¹ increased daily milk yield by 9.14% in cattle, with a benefit–cost (B:C) ratio of 1.53, and by 8.32% in buffaloes, with a B:C ratio of 2.22. Similarly, supplementation of multi-nutrient mixture (MNM) at 100 g animal-¹ day-¹ in goats enhanced daily milk yield by 11.38%, with a B:C ratio of 1.12. Feeding a low-cost concentrate mixture fortified with Prosopis juliflora pod powder to cattle increased milk yield by 8.35% and reduced concentrate feed costs by Rs. 2.75 kg- ¹, resulting in a B:C ratio of 2.20. Overall, the adoption of improved livestock management practices enhanced farm income by Rs. 13,998 (12.2%) over the existing farmers’ practices (Rs. 114,293), demonstrating the economic viability of integrated crop–livestock farming systems under arid-zone conditions.

title: Pore-network homogeneity for mechanically reliable powder-compacted solid-electrolyte separators
summary: All-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) with alloy anodes require solid-electrolyte (SE) separators that sustain ion transport while accommodating repeated electrode-derived mechanical loads. However, the mechanical state of powder-compacted sepa
content: All-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) with alloy anodes require solid-electrolyte (SE) separators that sustain ion transport while accommodating repeated electrode-derived mechanical loads. However, the mechanical state of powder-compacted separators is commonly inferred from bulk porosity, averaged mechanical properties, or cell-level stack pressure changes, obscuring spatially heterogeneous local responses. Here, we show that pore-network homogeneity is a key determinant of the mechanical reliability of sulfide solid-electrolyte separators by governing local mechanical heterogeneity and stress localization. FIB-SEM tomography and spatially resolved nanoindentation reveal that a highly densified separator with a broad particle-size distribution (PSD) retains clustered pore-rich and mechanically compliant regions, whereas a narrower-PSD separator exhibits a more homogeneous pore network and local mechanical response. Despite comparable cell-level pressure evolution, the two separators show markedly different cycling stability. Post-cycling microscopy reveals cracking and interfacial delamination in the heterogeneous separator, while microstructure-resolved simulations reveal stronger local stress amplification consistent with these observations. Controlled digital structures with identical D50 and porosity further isolate PSD-dependent changes in pore architecture and stress distribution. These findings establish pore-network homogeneity as a key design criterion for mechanically reliable solid-electrolyte separators beyond ionic conductivity and bulk densification.

title: Functional, next-generation, polymeric materials for targeted and controlled drug delivery applications
summary: Despite their broad clinical use, conventional drug delivery technologies are still limited by inadequate bioavailability, non-specific biodistribution, and uncontrolled drug release, which compromise therapeutic efficacy and safety. With t
content: Despite their broad clinical use, conventional drug delivery technologies are still limited by inadequate bioavailability, non-specific biodistribution, and uncontrolled drug release, which compromise therapeutic efficacy and safety. With their customizable molecular architecture, physicochemical adaptability, and multifunctional, stimuli-responsive design, next-generation polymeric materials overcome these constraints and allow for precise, site-specific, and regulated therapeutic action. In addition to stimuli-responsive platforms and structurally diverse nanocarriers such as nanoparticles, micelles, dendrimers, polymerases, and nanogels, this review critically examines the molecular and physicochemical design principles, nanoengineering and fabrication strategies, such as self-assembly, microfluidics, and emerging 3D/4D printing. Moreover, the passive, active, and organelle-level targeting mechanisms that govern these systems. In addition to clinical translation challenges, existing research gaps, and emerging directions like sustainable polymer chemistry, AI-driven design, adaptive 4D-printed systems, and personalized therapeutics, their disease-specific applications in cancer, neurological, cardiovascular, and infectious diseases, chronic wound healing, and regenerative medicine are critically evaluated. When taken as a whole, next-generation polymeric materials provide a flexible, clinically translatable platform for accurate, effective, and safe therapeutic intervention. However, they also highlight the crucial issues that need to be addressed in order to expedite clinical translation.

title: Agricultural continuity as a non-compensatory test for food-system value in agrivoltaics
summary: Agrivoltaics is often justified by the joint production of food or forage and electricity. Yet co-location does not show that farming can remain viable for the life of a solar asset. Existing standards and policy guidance already refer to p
content: Agrivoltaics is often justified by the joint production of food or forage and electricity. Yet co-location does not show that farming can remain viable for the life of a solar asset. Existing standards and policy guidance already refer to primary agricultural use or continuity. Their thresholds are important, but they do not by themselves provide a cross-context test of whether a functioning farm system is preserved. This Perspective develops agricultural continuity as a non-compensatory decision rule for food-system claims. The test has four conditions: usable agricultural space, a commercially credible production plan, effective decision rights for the agricultural operator, and safe, adaptable operations. All four conditions must be satisfied. Strong electricity output, average yield, or an environmental co-benefit cannot compensate for failure of one condition. The framework links infrastructure design and governance to food availability, access, stability, sustainability, and agency. It can be applied at site selection, design review, contracting, commissioning, and periodic operation reviews. Environmental life cycle assessment, energy performance, and farm economics remain essential parallel assessments; they should not be folded into the continuity threshold. The framework is conceptual and requires validation across farm types, climates, ownership models, and regulatory settings. Its value lies in making agricultural claims testable and in identifying correctable failure points before long-lived infrastructure locks them in.

title: FLEXIBLE UNIVERSITY APPROACHES TO PREPARING PROFESSIONALS FOR THE LABOR MARKET: A CASE STUDY OF A STUDY PROGRAM AT THE UNIVERSITY OF OSTRAVA
summary: This paper analyzes an approach to humanities education through a case study of the Applied Humanities for the Labor Market program (University of Ostrava). In the era of AI and Industry 4.0/5.0, it demonstrates how to bridge academia and m
content: This paper analyzes an approach to humanities education through a case study of the Applied Humanities for the Labor Market program (University of Ostrava). In the era of AI and Industry 4.0/5.0, it demonstrates how to bridge academia and market needs using micro-credentials, internships, and project-based learning. Key findings highlight the efficacy of co-teaching (academics with practitioners) and replacing traditional theses with practical solutions to real organizational challenges.

title: Lunar Helium 3 and the Future of Clean Energy
source: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
summary: Lunar helium-3 offers a possible connection between space resource development and cleaner energy on Earth. Its significance rests on two distinct markets. Small quantities already support cryogenic cooling, neutron detection, and scientifi
content: Lunar helium-3 offers a possible connection between space resource development and cleaner energy on Earth. Its significance rests on two distinct markets. Small quantities already support cryogenic cooling, neutron detection, and scientific research. A much larger future market could emerge if deuterium–helium-3 fusion becomes a reliable and economical source of electricity. These markets require different development strategies and cannot be treated as interchangeable. This paper reviews the established lunar resource evidence, earlier mining and fusion proposals, and current industrial initiatives. It then develops a practical architecture for prospecting, excavation, thermal extraction, isotope separation, autonomous operation, product certification, and return to Earth. Illustrative calculations connect resource concentration to soil throughput, processing heat, and the maximum fuel expenditure an electricity producer could sustain. The proposed five-layer development framework allows specialty-gas commerce to advance independently while reserving power-industry expansion for demonstrated net electricity and competitive fuel delivery. Potential benefits include reduced combustion pollution, a broader supply of firm low-carbon electricity, and lower exposure to selected fossil-fuel supply disruptions. Those benefits depend on actual displacement, lifecycle performance, affordable access, and resilient supply arrangements. Lunar helium-3 warrants disciplined research and staged demonstrations. Its global energy role will depend on evidence from both the mine and the power plant. Independent research and development concept paper. This paper has not undergone formal peer review. It is presented for public dissemination and independent technical critique. Numerical examples are illustrative calculations, not measured reserves or demonstrated plant performance.

title: Data‐Driven Harmonic Measurement, Reliability Enhancement, and Adaptive Power Flow Optimization for Renewable Energy Integrated Smart Microgrids
summary: ABSTRACT The increasing penetration of renewable energy sources in smart microgrids introduces significant challenges related to power quality degradation, harmonic distortion, operational uncertainty, and system reliability. Conventional c
content: ABSTRACT The increasing penetration of renewable energy sources in smart microgrids introduces significant challenges related to power quality degradation, harmonic distortion, operational uncertainty, and system reliability. Conventional centralized control approaches often suffer from communication bottlenecks, limited scalability, and reduced adaptability under dynamic operating conditions. This study presents a data‐driven intelligent framework for harmonic measurement, reliability enhancement, and adaptive power flow optimization in renewable energy‐integrated smart microgrids. The proposed framework combines decentralized multi‐agent control, reinforcement learning‐based energy management, Long Short‐Term Memory (LSTM) networks for harmonic prediction, and adaptive filtering for real‐time harmonic mitigation. Graph‐based interaction modeling is further incorporated to improve coordination among distributed energy resources, storage systems, and loads. The framework enables continuous monitoring of power quality indicators while supporting reliable and resilient microgrid operation under varying renewable generation and load conditions. Performance evaluation is conducted using renewable energy operational datasets and MATLAB/Simulink‐based validation. Results demonstrate significant improvements in renewable energy utilization, reduction of harmonic distortion, enhanced energy balancing, faster dynamic response, and improved system reliability compared with conventional control methods. The proposed approach provides an effective reliability‐oriented solution for intelligent monitoring, adaptive control, and sustainable operation of next‐generation renewable energy microgrids.

title: Metabolomics and Nutritional Profiling of Azolla microphylla: Insights from Amino Acid Quantification and GC-MS Analysis
summary: Azolla microphylla, a free-floating nitrogen-fixing aquatic fern, has emerged as a promising sustainable bioresource owing to its rapid biomass accumulation, high protein content, and rich phytochemical composition. The present study invest
content: Azolla microphylla, a free-floating nitrogen-fixing aquatic fern, has emerged as a promising sustainable bioresource owing to its rapid biomass accumulation, high protein content, and rich phytochemical composition. The present study investigated the seasonal growth dynamics, biomass productivity, nutritional composition, amino acid profile, mineral content, and phytochemical constituents of A. microphylla cultivated under controlled pond conditions across three climatic quarters over one annual cycle. Species authentication through molecular barcoding confirmed 99% homology with Azolla microphylla. Biomass productivity exhibited significant seasonal variation (p<0.05), with maximum wet biomass yield (40,584.25±2,093.37 kg ha⁻¹) and dry matter yield (8,116.85±418.60 kg ha⁻¹) recorded during Q1 (May-August), characterized by elevated temperature, humidity, and rainfall, whereas reduced yields were observed during Q2 (September-December) under comparatively cooler and drier environmental conditions. Despite fluctuations in biomass production, proximate analysis demonstrated substantial nutritional stability throughout the year, with crude protein content consistently maintained at approximately 30%, indicating resilience of nitrogen assimilation and protein biosynthesis under varying climatic conditions. Amino acid profiling revealed significant seasonal modulation (p<0.05), with elevated concentrations of leucine, lysine, glutamic acid, glycine, threonine, and isoleucine during Q2, while arginine and methionine reached maximum levels during Q1. Mineral analysis confirmed the presence of appreciable concentrations of calcium, phosphorus, potassium, magnesium, sodium, and zinc, supporting the nutritional suitability of the biomass for feed applications. GC–MS analysis of the n-hexane extract identified twelve major phytochemical constituents, predominantly fatty acids, phytosterols, and long-chain hydrocarbons, including stigmasterol (42.30%), phytol (23.79%), n-hexadecanoic acid (12.35%), oleic acid, campesterol, and gamma-sitosterol, compounds previously associated with antimicrobial, antioxidant, antiinflammatory, and pharmacological activities. Collectively, the findings indicate that optimum cultivation of A. microphylla is achieved at temperatures ranging from 29 to 33ºC and pH 6.3-6.8, while its stable nutritional quality and diverse bioactive profile establish this species as a sustainable alternative feed resource and a potential reservoir of industrially and pharmacologically valuable metabolites.

title: More than a grain of salt: technological substitution and the instability of critical mineral policy
summary: Abstract Critical mineral policy rests on an underexamined premise: that the importance of specific minerals is stable rather than contingent on evolving technological systems. This paper makes two operational contributions. First, it speci
content: Abstract Critical mineral policy rests on an underexamined premise: that the importance of specific minerals is stable rather than contingent on evolving technological systems. This paper makes two operational contributions. First, it specifies technological substitution as a monitorable seven-stage sequence with observable indicators. Second, it defines the criticality lag: the jurisdiction-specific interval between commercially meaningful market entry of a substituting technology (t₁) and material revision of classifications or policy commitments (t₂). The framework is applied prospectively to sodium-ion batteries, an unfolding development with the potential to reconfigure lithium demand across stationary storage, short-range mobility, and hybrid battery systems. Using a structured, case-oriented evidence synthesis, process tracing, and three bounding scenarios, the analysis distinguishes demonstrated performance from realised deployment, contracted capacity, corporate announcements, and projections. The evidence does not establish that sodium-ion will displace lithium-ion across the battery market: energy density, hard-carbon supply, manufacturing concentration, and uncertain cost parity remain substantial constraints. It does show that sodium-ion has moved beyond a purely theoretical alternative and has entered commercially relevant niches. The consequential policy question is therefore not whether lithium ceases to be critical, but whether criticality frameworks can detect material reordering before classifications and investment commitments become misaligned. The paper concludes that criticality assessment should shift from fixed classification toward time-bounded, technology-conditional monitoring, and specifies the indicators through which this can be operationalised.

title: Decision-making and diffusion dynamics of photovoltaic green roof retrofits: evidence from a tripartite evolutionary game
summary: Purpose This study investigates the diffusion of photovoltaic green roof (GR-PV) retrofits in existing buildings from the perspective of strategic interaction among government, technology suppliers and property owners. It examines how polic
content: Purpose This study investigates the diffusion of photovoltaic green roof (GR-PV) retrofits in existing buildings from the perspective of strategic interaction among government, technology suppliers and property owners. It examines how policy incentives, firm supply decisions and owner investment choices jointly affect GR-PV diffusion, and identifies the conditions under which the market can move from policy-led initiation to self-sustaining development. Design/methodology/approach A tripartite evolutionary game is constructed to model the boundedly rational choices of the three actors. Government chooses between economic and guidance-based incentives, firms choose between supplying GR-PV and conventional photovoltaic roofs, and property owners choose between GR-PV and conventional photovoltaic retrofit options. Replicator dynamics and numerical simulations are used to assess evolutionary stability and trace system trajectories under different initial and policy conditions. Findings GR-PV diffusion proceeds through initiation, development and stabilisation. Direct subsidies are most effective at the outset, differentiated incentives help align firm supply with owner demand during market development, and guidance-based policies become more suitable as the market matures. Owner willingness to invest is the main demand-side driver, while firm supply is shaped by R&D costs and policy support. Excessive incentives may delay market formation, whereas combined subsidies promote convergence more effectively than a single instrument. Originality/value The study develops a co-evolutionary framework linking public intervention, firm response and owner adoption in low-carbon building retrofits. It shows that GR-PV diffusion is shaped by dynamic feedback among multiple actors rather than isolated cost–benefit calculations, and identifies stage-specific mechanisms and threshold conditions for incentive design and market cultivation.

title: CHIRAL DRUGS BIOACCUMULATION IN AQUATIC ENVIRONMENT AND THE OPPORTUNITIES, CHALLENGES IN BIOANALYSIS
source: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
summary: Chiral compounds are asymmetric three-dimensional molecules that have one or more stereogenic centers or asymmetry that is caused by planes or axes and results in two molecules that cannot be superimposed on one another.Chiral separation ha
content: Chiral compounds are asymmetric three-dimensional molecules that have one or more stereogenic centers or asymmetry that is caused by planes or axes and results in two molecules that cannot be superimposed on one another.Chiral separation has become more important in forensic chemistry and has been used in the examination of biological fluids, environmental samples, and the examination of illicit drug mixtures.Most of the molecules at the center of life, including DNA, amino acids (AAs), and sugars, are chiral compounds.The investigated compounds included synthetic psychoactive drugs (stimulants), synthetic opioids, β-blockers, antidepressants, anticoagulants, bronchodilators, and dissociative anesthetics.Racemate use frequently causes stereoselective pharmacological activity and pharmacokinetic effects on absorption, metabolism, and excretion that may raise the risk of death or have major side consequences such as poisoning.Many medications are still delivered as racemates, despite the trend towards making pharmaceuticals as single enantiomers.Chiral analysis in biological fluids can provide details about use and help distinguish between legitimate medications and illicit substances that only contain one enantiomer.Additionally, it has been demonstrated that the presence of these substances in wastewater can be used as a tool for community-level drug consumption monitoring.Pharmaceuticals and illicit drugs may enter the aquatic environment by direct sewage discharge or effluents from WWTPs that are unable to completely remove these micro-pollutants.Studies of the presence of chiral medicines in environmental matrices are motivated by the potential negative effects of enantiomers on aquatic and human life.This study reviewed 90 articles that have been published between 1996 and 2022 based on ScienceDirect and ISI Web of Knowledge databases.In this review discussed about the challenges and opportunities of the application of chiral analysis in biological, environmental samples and their relevance in the forensic field.

title: What Competencies Should I be Teaching in my Introductory Business-to-Business Sales Course in the Age of Artificial Intelligence?
summary: The present study investigates a current question among sales educators: What competencies should I be teaching in my introductory business-to-business (B2B) sales course in the age of artificial intelligence (AI)? Using a mixed-methods app
content: The present study investigates a current question among sales educators: What competencies should I be teaching in my introductory business-to-business (B2B) sales course in the age of artificial intelligence (AI)? Using a mixed-methods approach, data were collected from seven interviews with sales managers and 13 interviews with alumni, along with an online survey of 157 sales professionals. Based on these data, the contribution presents five relevant findings about which competencies to teach. First, the findings highlight the importance of active listening and salesperson authenticity. Second, they emphasize an increased focus on discovery and the need for diagnosis rather than simply closing. Third, the role of AI emerges as one of augmentation, not replacement, of the salesperson’s human judgment. Fourth, participants identified knowing when not to use AI as the most critical AI competency. Fifth, the findings reveal a data privacy paradox: Although 77% of sales professionals avoid using AI when managing confidential data, data privacy ranked lowest among sales curriculum priorities. Together, these findings suggest ways to revise the competencies taught in introductory sales courses, potentially closing the gap between what is taught and what employers expect in the age of AI.

title: Focus on the ‘next generation of water economics’: navigating complexity, interdependence and change
summary: Abstract Water systems worldwide face mounting pressures from climate change, biodiversity loss, growing water demand, pollution, and persistent inequalities in access, allocation, and decision-making. Traditional approaches to water econom
content: Abstract Water systems worldwide face mounting pressures from climate change, biodiversity loss, growing water demand, pollution, and persistent inequalities in access, allocation, and decision-making. Traditional approaches to water economics have made important contributions; however, the complexity and interconnected nature of water challenges require broadening the scope of economic analysis and practice. This editorial summarises contributions received for the Focus Collection on the ‘next generation of water economics’ that engage with the economics of water and sustainability, equity, justice, resilience, governance, and diverse water values. Drawing on these contributions, the editorial highlights four major themes emerging in water economics. The articles in this Collection demonstrate the growing diversity of approaches shaping the field and identify opportunities to advance more inclusive, adaptive, and context-sensitive forms of economic considerations in water governance.

title: Future-ready Industrial systems: A RIDIT approach to evaluating industry 4.0 technological and strategical readiness of MSMEs
summary: Industry 4.0 (I4.0) adoption among micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) in emerging and resource-constrained regions is shaped by heterogeneous technology adoption patterns and varying strategic priorities. The aim of this stud
content: Industry 4.0 (I4.0) adoption among micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) in emerging and resource-constrained regions is shaped by heterogeneous technology adoption patterns and varying strategic priorities. The aim of this study is to empirically examines the adoption stages of selected I4.0 technologies and strategic dimensions among MSMEs in Jammu & Kashmir, India. A quantitative exploratory research design was employed using primary data collected through a structured questionnaire from 220 MSMEs. The seven I4.0 technologies that are used in this study are Big Data (BD), Digital Supply Chain (DSC), Internet of Things (IoT), Cloud Computing (CC), Robotics, 3D Printing and Automated Guided Vehicles (AGV) and six strategic dimensions including Servitization, Supply Chain Integration (SCI), Machinery and Database Integration, Lean Manufacturing (LM), Green Manufacturing (GM) and Design-to-Cost were evaluated using a five-point Likert scale. RIDIT analysis was used to find the ordinal response distributions among the relative strategic priorities selected for this study. The findings reveal heterogeneous technology implementation with DSC recorded the highest quantity of completed implementation (15.24%), while CC showed the highest combined proportion of current and completed implementation (48.17%), followed by IoT (43.30%). AGV exhibited the highest consideration rate (56.10%) but the lowest completed implementation (6.71%). The strategic analysis indicates that GM received the highest mean RIDIT score (0.5863), followed by Design-to-Cost (0.5675) and Machinery and Database Integration (0.5031), whereas LM recorded the lowest relative preference (0.4256). The results reveal that the technological implementation and strategic priority dimensions do not follow the same trajectory due to the multifaceted dependability of the I4.0 transition. It provides empirical evidence from MSMEs in an understudied emerging market and illustrates the applicability of RIDIT as a reliable non-parametric prioritisation method. The results offer managers a framework for selecting I4.0 technologies and strategic dimensions that is supported by evidence. MSMEs should prioritise GM to improve operational efficiency and coordination before gradually investing in Servitization, system integration, design-to-cost, and LM.

title: Tracing lead white sources in central European drawings from the 15th to 19th centuries using lead isotope analysis
summary: This study reports lead isotope ratios of lead white sampled from 26 drawings produced in the German-speaking regions of central Europe, dating from the 15th to the 19th century. The analysis identified four isotopically distinct types of l
content: This study reports lead isotope ratios of lead white sampled from 26 drawings produced in the German-speaking regions of central Europe, dating from the 15th to the 19th century. The analysis identified four isotopically distinct types of lead white. Two correspond to well-documented production types, namely Dutch and Venetian lead white, while two additional types are newly recognised. Both newly identified types occur along the Antwerp–Cologne–Nuremberg–Augsburg–Venice trade corridor. One shows isotopic affinities with sources in the Massif Central in France or the Achselalpe region in Austria, while the other is linked to the Nordwesteifel deposits in Germany. Although both types appear in the same cities, one is found predominantly in later drawings, indicating a chronological shift in lead supply along this route. The study of lead isotope ratio data, together with the provenance of the lead ore and the location of use of these two types of lead white, suggests that they may have been produced in or supplied through Venice and traded across Europe. The results presented in this study provide new insight into the trade and distribution of lead white in Europe, and show how this information can be linked to infer the time and place of production of unknown works of art.

title: Promotion of land-based carbon sequestration: state of research, knowledge gaps and strategy in India
summary: Land-based Carbon sequestration is projected to play a critical role in India’s long-term low-carbon development strategy. This study aims to (i) identify the data, monitoring and modeling needs for Carbon sequestration programs in forestry
content: Land-based Carbon sequestration is projected to play a critical role in India’s long-term low-carbon development strategy. This study aims to (i) identify the data, monitoring and modeling needs for Carbon sequestration programs in forestry and agroforestry systems, (ii) review the research funding agencies and programs, (iii) identify the research priorities and (iv) suggest a strategy to promote research on Carbon sequestration in India. The methodology for the study adopted includes review and assessments of research institutions, programs and projects on Carbon sequestration in India. Carbon trading mechanisms, Carbon sequestration programs, projects, and inventory estimations require Carbon sequestration data and modeling. A number of government departments fund research programs, and there are large research organizations involved, along with many think tanks in Carbon sequestration research. Despite these efforts, there are limitations with respect to the lack of data on land availability, its suitability, and Carbon sequestration rates for the forestry and agroforestry systems for land-based Carbon sequestration projects. Additionally, there is an absence of models and frameworks for mitigation potential assessment. Research priorities identified include: creation of databases and access to the existing datasets, development of region-specific forestry and agroforestry models for the assessment of mitigation potential and the reduction of uncertainties. The strategies include enhanced funding and networking to create accessible databases and the establishment of dedicated programs to develop forestry and agroforestry systems, along with Carbon sequestration rates and institutional arrangements for long-term research, modeling and uncertainty reduction. This could lead to the promotion of robust large-scale Carbon sequestration programs in India.

title: ESG measurement, innovation pathways, and sustainable firm value creation: A systematic review of metrics, mechanisms, and contexts
summary: Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance is increasingly linked to firm value through innovation, yet evidence remains fragmented across measurement systems, mechanisms, and contexts (Li & Sutunyarak, 2024; Widyantoro et al.,
content: Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance is increasingly linked to firm value through innovation, yet evidence remains fragmented across measurement systems, mechanisms, and contexts (Li & Sutunyarak, 2024; Widyantoro et al., 2025). This study systematically reviews how ESG is measured, which innovation pathways connect ESG to value creation, and which contextual conditions shape these relationships. Following PRISMA 2020, 60 Scopus- and Web of Science-indexed studies published between 2022 and 2026 were analyzed. The findings show that ESG ratings, composite scores, and disclosure-based indicators dominate measurement, while green innovation, technological innovation, digital transformation, research and development (R&D) intensity, and innovation capability constitute the main transmission pathways. Firm value is most frequently assessed through return on assets (ROA), return on equity (ROE), Tobin’s Q, profitability, enterprise value, and broader performance indicators. Overall, ESG is associated with favorable firm-level outcomes, but these effects depend on credible measurement, active innovation mechanisms, and supportive organizational and institutional conditions. For industry, the findings support integrating ESG with innovation capabilities; for research and academia, they highlight the need for more comparable ESG measures and context-sensitive models of sustainable value creation.

title: Planning Concerts with AI: An Integrated Decision-Support Framework for Demand, Sustainability, and Economic Feasibility
source: Student Journal of Business and Economics
summary: Concert organizers must balance financial success, operational efficiency, and environmental sustainability, yet these factors are often evaluated separately. Artificial intelligence and workflow automation offer opportunities for integrati
content: Concert organizers must balance financial success, operational efficiency, and environmental sustainability, yet these factors are often evaluated separately. Artificial intelligence and workflow automation offer opportunities for integration, but integrated decision-support systems remain limited in concert planning. This study develops an AI-assisted concert-planning decision-support system implemented in n8n. It combines user-defined event parameters with external artist-popularity metrics and currency exchange services to estimate audience demand, environmental indicators, and financial feasibility, and generate structured planning recommendations within one workflow. A case study based on Coldplay’s Music of the Spheres World Tour concert at Olympiastadion Berlin demonstrates the framework’s functionality. The system predicted attendance of 72,306 spectators, approximately 97% of stated venue capacity, and generated planning estimates for energy consumption, carbon emissions, waste, transportation, ticket revenue, costs, and profitability. Because complete verified concert-specific data were unavailable, these outputs demonstrate system functionality and plausibility rather than validate predictive accuracy or reconstruct actual concert performance. The framework illustrates how integrated AI and workflow automation can support efficiency, transparency, and consistency in pre-event decision-making. It also shows how environmental sustainability and economic viability can be assessed together rather than as independent objectives. Intended to support early-stage feasibility assessment, the system does not replace detailed operational analyses or comprehensive life-cycle assessments. It provides a practical approach to more sustainable, transparent, and data-driven planning in the live event industry.

title: Green acceleration, uneven sectoral change: Green industrial policy mixes and China's transition to electric mobility (2000−2022)
summary: Green industrial policy has become increasingly important for understanding how the state shapes low-carbon industrial transitions, yet there remains limited explanation of how evolving policy configurations reshape sectoral systems over ti
content: Green industrial policy has become increasingly important for understanding how the state shapes low-carbon industrial transitions, yet there remains limited explanation of how evolving policy configurations reshape sectoral systems over time, especially under latecomer conditions. Existing studies often focus on discrete outcomes such as innovation, diffusion or firm entry, rather than on how interacting policy instruments redirect the system of production and consumption. To address this gap, the study develops an analytical framework centred on green industrial policy, combining the policy mix lens with the sectoral system of innovation and production framework. The framework is applied to China's electric mobility transition between 2000 and 2022. Based on a longitudinal single-case study, the analysis combines qualitative content analysis and process tracing, drawing on 83 elite and expert interviews, six factory visits, and diverse secondary data. The study traces how China's green industrial policy mix cumulatively reconfigured the sectoral system through interacting supply-side, demand-side and coordination-oriented instruments. The analysis suggests that policy effects were mediated by sectoral structures, path-dependent dynamics and feedback loops. The “pure electric drive” strategy and complementary instrument mixes accelerated electric vehicle diffusion and supported the emergence of an indigenous power battery sector. However, this also generated uneven changes across technological trajectories, vehicle segments and sectoral capabilities, revealing tensions between the speed and scope of transitions. The study thus shows how systemic green industrial policy can accelerate low-carbon transitions under latecomer conditions while reshaping sectoral structures in ways that generate uneven patterns of technological change and sectoral competitiveness.

title: The cost of regulatory delay: quantifying how permitting timelines affect offshore wind energy costs
summary: Abstract Rapid deployment of offshore renewable energy and transmission infrastructure can be a major contributor to energy system decarbonization. However, regulatory obligations frequently impose deployment delays that are typically not q
content: Abstract Rapid deployment of offshore renewable energy and transmission infrastructure can be a major contributor to energy system decarbonization. However, regulatory obligations frequently impose deployment delays that are typically not quantified in cost terms. The costs of such delays should be incorporated in project and technology assessments. Here, a framework is developed that treats the development lag between project inception and operation as a temporal proxy for regulatory and related obligations, and propagates it through a levelized-cost-of-energy calculation to quantify the cost of delay. This framework is used to compare, on a common basis, conventional high-voltage cable transmission with offshore power-to-hydrogen (PtH) alternatives. The framework is applied to three strategies to move energy to shore from offshore wind facilities. The results show that for an example, one gigawatt plant, deploying one year sooner can save €110 million—a relevant metric to gauge the cost of policy designed to expedite deployment. In scenarios where the PtH can be deployed faster than high-voltage cables, the results suggest a limited decision space in which PtH transmission is cheaper, indicating that it will need to realize other benefits to compete with high-voltage cable transmission on cost. Profitability between electricity-based and hydrogen-based transmission is then compared, considering differences in deployment time. There are existing conditions of hydrogen and electricity prices that indicate PtH pathways may be more profitable when a difference in deployment lag is applied. In the example considered here, a lag difference can result in a greater number of exploratory price scenarios where PtH is more profitable. This framework is useful to quantify the implications of regulatory obligations and tune policies to accelerate low-carbon energy deployment.

title: The predictive power of liquidity measures and ohlson model variables for corporate valuation of major quoted companies in Nigeria
summary: This study investigates the relative influence of liquidity measures and traditional accounting variables used in the Ohlson model of equity valuation (earnings and book equity per share) on corporate valuation in the Nigerian capital marke
content: This study investigates the relative influence of liquidity measures and traditional accounting variables used in the Ohlson model of equity valuation (earnings and book equity per share) on corporate valuation in the Nigerian capital market. To conduct the investigation, the study collected data for 38 listed Nigerian companies from 2014 to 2024, using FGLS for baseline regression, with the BC-MM and PCSE estimators for robustness and sensitivity analyses. The empirical results show that dynamic liquidity measures have a more consistent effect on corporate valuation than static measures. In the combined models, liquidity measures, earnings, and equity book value significantly affect corporate valuation, both in aggregate and in some individual sectors. However, earnings are more consistent at explaining variation in corporate valuation across sectors. Also, where liquidity measures are significant, they have a stronger effect on corporate valuation. In conclusion, liquidity measures exhibit strong value-relevance properties depending on the indicators used and the sector. Furthermore, empirical results validate and sustain the Ohlson model variables in equity valuation, but liquidity measures will enhance the equity valuation model. Therefore, regulators should strengthen disclosure requirements for liquidity measures. Management should pursue optimal business growth, liquidity management, and financing strategies to create shareholder value.

title: Legacy effects of land use land cover change on species distribution dynamics: evidence from a landscape of diverse biogeographic crossroads
summary: Abstract Context Land use and land cover (LULC) change is a key driver of biodiversity distribution, yet species responses vary among taxa, habitats, and regions. Because species responses are context-dependent, understanding how ecological
content: Abstract Context Land use and land cover (LULC) change is a key driver of biodiversity distribution, yet species responses vary among taxa, habitats, and regions. Because species responses are context-dependent, understanding how ecological characteristics and landscape history influence biodiversity distribution is essential for conservation planning. Objectives We evaluated how nearly two centuries of LULC change have influenced vertebrate distribution dynamics across Texas, USA, a landscape of biogeographic crossroads. We tested whether habitat specialization, taxonomic identity, conservation status, and ecoregional context better explain range expansion, contraction, and redistribution than landscape change metrics alone. Methods We compared historical and contemporary distributions of 100 native vertebrate species (mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians). Multi-temporal LULC datasets (1850–2023) were integrated with species occurrences, habitat associations, and ecoregional data to identify drivers of distribution range change. Results LULC change was spatially heterogeneous, driven by agricultural expansion, cropland abandonment, shrubland encroachment, and urbanization. Most species shifted ranges, with responses varying by habitat, taxon, and ecoregion. Habitat specialists, reptiles, and amphibians showed the greatest contractions, whereas birds were comparably stable or expanding, with responses differing among ecoregions. Habitat affinity, vertebrate class, and ecoregional identity were stronger predictors of range change than landscape transformation metrics alone. Conclusions LULC legacies set the environmental template and influence species distributions indirectly through ecological filtering, species-specific traits, and regional context rather than change magnitude alone. By linking historical landscape trajectories with contemporary biodiversity patterns, this study provides a useful template for understanding land use legacies, species redistribution, and community reassembly in diverse landscapes, emphasizing adaptive capacity and connectivity for conservation planning.

title: A tongue-controlled FES-robotic exoskeleton restores hand function in users with cervical spinal cord injury
summary: Abstract Hand exoskeletons and functional electrical stimulation (FES) have shown promise in restoring hand function after stroke or cervical spinal cord injury. However, major challenges remain in providing reliable user command input in i
content: Abstract Hand exoskeletons and functional electrical stimulation (FES) have shown promise in restoring hand function after stroke or cervical spinal cord injury. However, major challenges remain in providing reliable user command input in individuals with severe paralysis and in enabling safe and effective control of hand closing and opening. Here, we present a non-invasive tongue-based control strategy for a hybrid soft hand exoskeleton system combining tongue-controlled independent tendon-driven flexion of five fingers with tongue-triggered FES-induced finger extension. This user-intent-driven hybrid approach supports multiple activities of daily living, such as grasping a bottle or toothbrush, and enables hand opening while mitigating muscle fatigue and reducing system complexity. The system was evaluated in five users with cervical spinal cord injury, demonstrating high task success rates in daily living tasks and user preference due to its wearability and ease of use, as well as consistently low reported levels of discomfort, pain, and fatigue. These findings show that the proposed hybrid system can restore activities of daily living in individuals with cervical tetraplegia, including those with long-term injuries.

title: From Densification to High-Rise Development
source: Transactions of the Association of European Schools of Planning
summary: Oslo has long pursued an ambitious anti-sprawl agenda, with densification at the core of its urban development strategy. Compact growth, efficient land use, and climate-oriented planning have shaped the city’s approach to sustainability. Ho
content: Oslo has long pursued an ambitious anti-sprawl agenda, with densification at the core of its urban development strategy. Compact growth, efficient land use, and climate-oriented planning have shaped the city’s approach to sustainability. However, as densification intensifies, concerns about its social, spatial, climate, and ecological consequences have increasingly emerged; challenging the assumption that compact urbanism is inherently equitable and sustainable.This paper presents a meta-analysis of a decade of research on the relationship between densification strategies and socio-spatial justice in Oslo. Drawing on studies of neighbourhoods, planning documents, and governance processes, we examine how densification is implemented and justified, and what inequalities it may reinforce.We analyse how climate goals and planning frameworks have established compact development as Oslo’s dominant paradigm, explore environmental trade-offs with ecological protection, and assess socio-spatial impacts such as rising housing costs and unequal access to amenities. We also consider how the city’s emerging high-rise strategy may intensify these tensions.

title: Climate Harm, Managerial Capability, and the Corporate Environmental Action Gap: Evidence From 24 Economies
source: Corporate Social Responsibility and Environmental Management
summary: ABSTRACT Why do some firms that experience climate‐related damage also take environmental action while others do not? Using the World Bank's B‐READY enterprise surveys, covering 36,401 firms across 24 economies surveyed with a harmonized in
content: ABSTRACT Why do some firms that experience climate‐related damage also take environmental action while others do not? Using the World Bank's B‐READY enterprise surveys, covering 36,401 firms across 24 economies surveyed with a harmonized instrument, this study estimates linear probability models with country and sector fixed effects, drawing on the capabilities view of the firm and the institution‐based view of strategy. Experienced climate harm is associated with energy‐management measures but not with CO 2 monitoring, and the association is observable only among smaller establishments, although the size contrast is not itself statistically significant. Managerial capability is robustly associated with both practices within countries, and does not reliably moderate the harm–action relationship. Capability and institutions operate at different levels: capability distinguishes acting from inactive firms within countries, whereas the cross‐country gap aligns more closely with institutional and developmental conditions than with average capability stock. The action gap is therefore more closely associated with organizational capability and institutional context than with risk exposure alone. All estimates are associational.

content: In a digital economy customers expect individualized interactions businesses in e-commerce banking healthcare streaming and retail are increasingly competing on experience rather than product a key component of this change is artificial intelligence ai today s consumers depend firms to be familiar with them they dont want to see the same emails offers and website as everyone else ai lets a company with millions of customers treat each one individually.
