summary: Over the past two decades, significant population recoveries of tigers and leopards have driven a substantial rise in human-carnivore conflict across South Asia. Sustaining the long-term conservation of both species demands effective, adapt
content: Over the past two decades, significant population recoveries of tigers and leopards have driven a substantial rise in human-carnivore conflict across South Asia. Sustaining the long-term conservation of both species demands effective, adaptive conflict management. However, existing research is largely confined to isolated landscapes or protected areas, hindering the identification of spatial conflict drivers across broader, heterogeneous regions. To address this gap, this study compiled 4,457 human leopard conflict (HLC) and 2,563 human tiger conflict (HTC) records spanning 2000 to 2024 across Bangladesh, Bhutan, India, and Nepal. We evaluated conflict locations against 33 landscape, anthropogenic, climatic, topographic, and hydrological predictors across three spatial scales using binomial generalized linear regression models and three alternative background sampling methods. Model performance peaked at the largest spatial scale for both species and remained consistent across sampling strategies. HTC correlated positively with forest fragmentation and proximity to human settlements, but decreased with higher overall anthropogenic disturbance. Conversely, HLC concentrated in highly productive, high-precipitation, human-modified landscapes. These contrasting spatial patterns highlight distinct ecological responses to habitat modification and carry unique conservation implications. Ultimately, this study underscores the need to integrate carnivore abundance, wild prey densities, and socioeconomic factors to achieve a holistic understanding of conflict dynamics.

title: Drivers governing the seasonality of new particle formation in the Arctic
summary: Abstract. New particle formation (NPF) is the phenomenon wherein gaseous precursors form critical clusters of barely a few nanometres in diameter, after which, under favourable conditions these particles can grow to climate-relevant sizes.
content: Abstract. New particle formation (NPF) is the phenomenon wherein gaseous precursors form critical clusters of barely a few nanometres in diameter, after which, under favourable conditions these particles can grow to climate-relevant sizes. Here we present measurements from 2022 to 2024 of particle and ion number size distributions from the Zeppelin Observatory (ZEP), an Arctic research station situated on the western edge of Svalbard. NPF events begin in April and continue occurring into November. The events at the start of the NPF season (i.e. April/May) are considerably stronger (i.e. a larger production of nucleation mode particles). The peaks in NPF strength coincide with peaks in the solar insolation experienced by arriving air masses. During the summer period NPF events occur on 20–40 % of days each month, however, there is a consistent decline in June. We show that the combined influence of solar radiation and the surface area of pre-existing aerosols (i.e. condensation sink, CS) are strong predictors for the likelihood of NPF. We develop a simplified predictive model which matches the frequency of NPF events identified via the classification schemes used in this study. We show that NPF events occur during the polar night (i.e. when the Sun does not pass above horizon), and speculate that these events are linked to high altitude air masses. Furthermore, we detail the likely geographic origins of nucleation within the Arctic, as measured at ZEP. We show that NPF events are considerably more likely to originate from the marine regions towards the west of Svalbard, particularly the Greenland Sea which presented the greatest likelihood that arriving air masses from this marine region would be linked to an NPF day. We also remark on the proportion of the Aitken mode particles within the Arctic that could originate from NPF; we show that NPF events lead to an increase in the number of Aitken mode particles. We measure over 50 NPF events where the nucleation mode particles grew beyond 25 nm, a diameter representing the minimum activation diameter for particles to act as cloud condensation nuclei. Overall, we present a concise picture of the lifecycle of nucleation mode particles in the Arctic, including the effect wet scavenging has in reducing the condensation sink, which in turn encourages NPF events to occur.

title: Tree-ring chronologies reveal unexpected geographic patterns of drought vulnerability in western Canadian forests
summary: Adaptive reforestation under climate warming will increasingly involve northward or upslope movement of tree species and seed sources. However, in western Canadian boreal and sub-boreal forests, release from cold constraints may be offset b
content: Adaptive reforestation under climate warming will increasingly involve northward or upslope movement of tree species and seed sources. However, in western Canadian boreal and sub-boreal forests, release from cold constraints may be offset by emerging drought limitations, where low evapotranspiration has historically supported tree growth despite modest precipitation. We used 392 tree-ring chronologies from western Canada to compare drought resistance, recovery, and resilience among seven common conifer tree species across regional climatic gradients. Drought vulnerability metrics were not strongest at the southern forest-grassland transition, as might be expected from current moisture deficits alone. Instead, drought impacts were most pronounced further north in dry boreal mixedwood regions. Specifically, white spruce and jack pine showed lower post-drought resilience in northern boreal regions than in their southern boreal populations. We interpret this pattern as consistent with limited historical selection for drought tolerance in northern populations, where cold temperatures have historically moderated moisture stress. Similarly, interior Douglas-fir showed particularly low resilience in its sub-boreal distribution, near its northern range limit. These results suggest practical limits to northward planting of interior Douglas-fir, while southern boreal populations of white spruce and jack pine may be useful seed sources for improving drought resilience in central and northern boreal forests. More broadly, these results suggest that drought vulnerability in western Canadian forests is not confined to the southern boreal fringe, but also affects northern boreal and sub-boreal populations, where adaptive reforestation may be needed to maintain forest resilience under continued warming.

title: Grassland soil bulk density decreases under grazing exclusion and responds asymmetrically to altered precipitation
summary: Soil structure is a key determinant of grassland health and functioning, with bulk density serving as a widely used proxy. Grazing exclusion is a common restoration practice that often reduces soil bulk density in grasslands by restoring pl
content: Soil structure is a key determinant of grassland health and functioning, with bulk density serving as a widely used proxy. Grazing exclusion is a common restoration practice that often reduces soil bulk density in grasslands by restoring plant productivity and removing livestock trampling. Plant productivity is strongly influenced by precipitation, but the interactive effects of precipitation and grazing exclusion on grassland soil bulk density remain unclear. We presented a synthesis based on 671 paired observations from 111 field studies to investigate the responses of soil bulk density in grasslands to grazing exclusion and altered precipitation, and the key drivers. Overall, grazing exclusion decreased soil bulk density by 7.88% compared to grazing, with the strongest effect occurring in tropical grasslands and in surface soils. This decrease was more strongly controlled by standardized precipitation evapotranspiration index (SPEI) than by soil factors, declining with increasing wetness and becoming negligible in severely wet regions. Under altered precipitation, increased precipitation reduced bulk density by 9.06% relative to ambient precipitation, whereas decreased precipitation increased it by 17.10%, showing an asymmetric response. In extreme events, the response per unit precipitation change was stronger for decreased than for increased precipitation. The asymmetric response was directly and negatively related to SPEI, soil organic carbon content, and the magnitude of precipitation change. Publication bias and sensitivity analysis confirmed that the results were reliable. These results quantitatively demonstrate the global-scale decrease in grassland soil bulk density under grazing exclusion and its asymmetric response to altered precipitation. The results suggest that the efficacy of grazing exclusion in reducing soil bulk density is probably modulated by precipitation regimes, particularly extreme events.

title: Analyzing hobby-gardeners' purchase intentions for peat-reduced potting soils in Germany, UK and USA – An extended theory of planned behavior approach
summary: Peat is an important raw material for high-quality potting soils in horticulture. Since this use is associated with the release of greenhouse gases, governments, especially in Europe, are striving to reduce the proportion of peat in potting
content: Peat is an important raw material for high-quality potting soils in horticulture. Since this use is associated with the release of greenhouse gases, governments, especially in Europe, are striving to reduce the proportion of peat in potting soils. As consumer reactions are hardly analyzed in this field, we investigate the purchase intention for peat-reduced potting soils in Germany, the UK, and the US using an extended framework of the theory of planned behavior (TPB). The results show a limited power of the classical TPB model parameters in explaining the differences between the three analyzed countries. Concerning the extended framework, variables related to the situation at the point of sale show the strongest influence on the purchase intention. Based on these results, we derive recommendations for marketing activities for peat-reduced potting soils to increase gardeners’ interest in such products.

title: Measurements and Analysis of Light Non‐Methane Hydrocarbon Mole Fractions in 1982–1987 at Six Remote Sites Along the Pacific Rim
summary: Abstract Atmospheric non‐methane hydrocarbons (NMHCs) are important trace species with anthropogenic and natural sources including fugitive emissions from fossil fuel mining and distribution, biomass burning, biofuel combustion, and biogeni
content: Abstract Atmospheric non‐methane hydrocarbons (NMHCs) are important trace species with anthropogenic and natural sources including fugitive emissions from fossil fuel mining and distribution, biomass burning, biofuel combustion, and biogenic emissions from microbes and plants. We present previously unpublished whole air sample measurements of NMHCs collected at approximately weekly intervals from 1982 to 1987 at six stations spanning the Northern and Southern hemispheres, which sampled primarily Pacific Basin air masses as determined by back‐trajectory analysis. The four alkanes in this data set, ethane, propane, i‐ and n‐butane had a mean measured mole fraction of 712 22 ppt, 245 13 ppt, 55.2 4.4 ppt, and 87.6 8.7 ppt, respectively. When compared with measurements at comparable sites two decades later, the global ethane mole fraction decreased by 21% between the mid‐1980s and 2009–2010 with larger decreases in propane and butanes, corroborating a multi‐decadal decline in NMHCs over this period. No discernible Pacific Basin secular trend for the NMHCs was found over the 5‐year period 1982–1987, but significant trends at some individual sites including short‐term increases in the Northern Hemisphere and decreases in the Southern Hemisphere. A large multi‐year enrichment anomaly that is likely associated with the strong El Niño of 1982–83 occurs at all sites and influences trends observed in the Southern Hemisphere. Using the GEOS‐Chem chemical transport model, we estimated global emissions of ethane during this period were 13.4 0.4 Tg/yr based on the globally‐averaged measured mole fractions.

title: Leaf economic strategy and stand structural complexity are associated with net woody productivity in a subtropical mixed forest
summary: The associations of net woody productivity with biodiversity, functional composition, and stand structure remain poorly resolved in subtropical mixed evergreen–deciduous broad-leaved forests. We used the 2016 and 2021 censuses of 150 contig
content: The associations of net woody productivity with biodiversity, functional composition, and stand structure remain poorly resolved in subtropical mixed evergreen–deciduous broad-leaved forests. We used the 2016 and 2021 censuses of 150 contiguous 20 × 20 m subplots in a 6-ha permanent plot at Jinzi Mountain, central China. Net woody productivity was calculated as the annualized net change in live woody biomass. Univariate and multiple linear regressions, random forests, and piecewise structural equation modeling were used to examine relationships with community attributes measured in 2016. Live woody biomass increased from 144.78 to 167.86 t·ha -1 , corresponding to a mean net woody productivity of 4.62 t·ha -1 ·yr -1 . Net gains were concentrated in the tree stratum and larger diameter and height classes; classes with a diameter at breast height ≥29 cm accounted for 78.53% of community net woody productivity. In univariate regressions, productivity was positively associated with community-weighted mean (CWM) leaf thickness and negatively associated with CWM specific leaf area and leaf area. Multiple regression also identified species relative-abundance structure and stand structural heterogeneity as significant correlates. In the piecewise structural equation model, species diversity and structural diversity had significant positive direct associations with productivity. A principal component representing higher CWM specific leaf area and leaf area but lower CWM leaf thickness had a significant negative direct association. Functional and phylogenetic diversity had nonsignificant direct paths, although Rao’s quadratic entropy was negatively associated with productivity in the multiple regression. These relationships may partly reflect differences in baseline biomass stocks, which were not included as predictors. Retention of healthy large canopy trees, woody-species diversity, and heterogeneous stand structure warrants consideration in close-to-nature forest management, but its consequences for productivity require further testing.

title: Miniaturized solid-liquid extraction with low-temperature partitioning for determining thiamethoxam residues in soil, bean leaves, and grains
summary: Monitoring pesticide residues in complex agricultural matrices requires analytical methods that combine robustness, sensitivity, and operational simplicity. This study proposes solid-liquid extraction with low-temperature partitioning (SLE-
content: Monitoring pesticide residues in complex agricultural matrices requires analytical methods that combine robustness, sensitivity, and operational simplicity. This study proposes solid-liquid extraction with low-temperature partitioning (SLE-LTP) as a unified strategy for determining thiamethoxam residues in soil, bean leaves, and bean grains, followed by HPLC-DAD analysis. The methods were optimized using sample masses of 1000 mg for soil, 100 mg for leaves, and 500 mg for grains, with 4 mL of extraction solvent for all matrices. Under optimized conditions, recoveries ranged from 82.6 to 98.6%, with limits of quantification of 1 μg kg −1 for soil, 10 μg kg −1 for leaves, and 2 μg kg −1 for grains. The LOQ for bean grains was below the maximum residue limits established by the European Union (10 μg kg −1 ) and Brazilian regulations (20 μg kg −1 ). Precision (RSD < 10%), low expanded uncertainties (< 17%), and high robustness confirmed the reliability of the proposed methods according to international validation guidelines. The validated methods were subsequently applied to samples from a controlled bean cultivation experiment. Thiamethoxam residues were detected in soil only during the first 30 days and in leaves only after foliar application, with no thiamethoxam residues above the method LOQ detected in bean grains. These results demonstrate the applicability of SLE-LTP for thiamethoxam monitoring in soil and bean tissues under the cultivation conditions studied, while requiring low sample and solvent amounts and no additional extract cleanup steps.

title: A global consistent database of plankton and detritus from in situ imaging by the Underwater Vision Profiler 5
summary: Abstract. Plankton and detritus are essential components of the Earth’s oceans influencing biogeochemical cycles and carbon sequestration. Climate change impacts their composition and marine ecosystems as a whole. To improve our understandi
content: Abstract. Plankton and detritus are essential components of the Earth’s oceans influencing biogeochemical cycles and carbon sequestration. Climate change impacts their composition and marine ecosystems as a whole. To improve our understanding of these changes, standardized observation methods and integrated global datasets are needed to enhance the accuracy of ecological and climate models. Here, we present a global dataset for plankton and detritus obtained by two versions of the Underwater Vision Profiler 5 (UVP5). This release contains the images classified in 33 homogenized categories, as well as the metadata associated with them, reaching 3,114 profiles and ca. 8 million objects acquired between 2008–2018 at global scale. The geographical distribution of the dataset is unbalanced, with the Equatorial region (30° S – 30° N) being the most represented, followed by the high latitudes in the northern hemisphere and lastly the high latitudes in the Southern Hemisphere. Detritus is the most abundant category in terms of concentration (90 %) and biovolume (95 %), although its classification in different morphotypes is still not well established. Copepoda was the most abundant taxa within the plankton, with Trichodesmium colonies being the second most abundant. The two versions of UVP5 (SD and HD) have different imagers, resulting in a different effective size range to analyse plankton and detritus from the images (HD objects >600 µm, SD objects >1 mm) and morphological properties (grey levels, etc.) presenting similar patterns, although the ranges may differ. Therefore, recommendations are provided for the appropriate use of this data when conducting studies. A large number of images of plankton and detritus will be collected in the future by the UVP5, and the public availability of this dataset will help it being utilized as a training set for machine learning and being improved by the scientific community. This will reduce uncertainty by classifying previously unclassified objects and expand the classification categories, ultimately enhancing biodiversity quantification. The dataset that constitutes this first release is available at SEANOE.

title: Prospects and complexities in sustainability impacts of global residue-based bioenergy deployment
summary: Amid rising global demand for sustainable energy, agricultural and forestry residues (AFRs) emerge as a key yet underutilized resource in energy transition. Mechanisms of how optimizing multipath AFR utilization advances sustainability cont
content: Amid rising global demand for sustainable energy, agricultural and forestry residues (AFRs) emerge as a key yet underutilized resource in energy transition. Mechanisms of how optimizing multipath AFR utilization advances sustainability contributions in varied socioeconomic contexts remain underexplored. Integrating the Global Change Analysis Model and life cycle assessment within an optimized Integrated AFR-to-Energy System (IAES) framework, we evaluate the selected Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)-related contributions of global IAES deployment across combined Shared Socioeconomic Pathways-Representative Concentration Pathways scenarios until 2060. Our results reveal that regional disparities in the contributions to SDGs are driven by variations in AFR availability, technology configurations, and socioeconomic conditions. Most lower-middle-to-low income regions struggle to achieve meaningful sustainability benefits. Canada, where energy output from IAES deployment could meet nearly 20% of its energy demand by 2060, leads the sustainability gains excelling in SDG7 and SDG13, followed by Eastern Europe that strides in SDG1, while China shows comparatively limited prospects. This study offers a comparative, scenario-based basis for informing bioenergy deployment strategies across regional contexts to advance energy transition and the SDGs. This study shows that deploying agricultural and forestry residue-based bioenergy globally could advance multiple Sustainable Development Goals, with benefits varying substantially by region and socioeconomic scenario.

title: Rural eco-industries, livelihood capacity and farmers' income: an empirical study based on 913 survey data from farmers in the Three Gorges Reservoir area of Chongqing, China
summary: Developing regionally distinctive rural eco-industries is an important pathway for broadening farmers' income channels. While existing studies have largely focused on the income-enhancing effects of specific types of such industries, few ha
content: Developing regionally distinctive rural eco-industries is an important pathway for broadening farmers' income channels. While existing studies have largely focused on the income-enhancing effects of specific types of such industries, few have systematically examined their broad income-enhancing effects and micro-level mechanisms. Within a ‘rural eco-industries-livelihood capacity-farmers' income’ theoretical framework and using micro-survey data from 913 households in the Three Gorges Reservoir Area of Chongqing, China, this paper employs multiple regression, mediation and threshold models to examine the impact of rural eco-industries on farmers' income and the role of livelihood capacity. The results show that (1) rural eco-industries directly increase farmers' income, with participants earning 37.92% more than non-participants; (2) livelihood capacity serves as a significant partial mediator in this relationship, accounting for 5.20% of the total effect and (3) the impact of rural eco-industries on farmers' income exhibits a threshold effect with respect to livelihood capacity: the coefficient is 0.3472 when livelihood capacity is below 0.4172 and rises to 0.3980 once it exceeds this value. These findings provide empirical support for refining rural eco-industry policies, enhancing farmers' livelihood capacity and maximizing the income-enhancing potential of eco-industries.

title: Large and persistent social risks to forest carbon projects
summary: Despite the popularity of carbon credits as a tool to offset greenhouse gas emissions, there are growing concerns over whether their climate mitigation claims are robust. Most attention has focused on natural risks to forest carbon projects
content: Despite the popularity of carbon credits as a tool to offset greenhouse gas emissions, there are growing concerns over whether their climate mitigation claims are robust. Most attention has focused on natural risks to forest carbon projects, such as wildfire, while social risks (e.g., those driven by fraud, mismanagement, and land conflicts) remain largely unquantified. Here we analyze 244 forest-based carbon projects to assess the vulnerability of the voluntary carbon market to social risks and find that projects systematically underestimate their risk of failure. Even under optimistic assumptions, projects are roughly twice as likely to fail within 25 years as their self-assessed risk implies over a 100-year horizon. Projecting these trends forward, we show that credits issued to failed projects could exceed the reserves registries hold to mitigate these risks within 1-2 decades. Overall, our results suggest stronger mechanisms and reserves are needed to ensure carbon credits deliver the promised climate benefits.

title: Fire carbon emission constraints from space-based carbon monoxide retrievals during the 2019 intense burning season in Brazil
summary: Abstract. In 2019, Brazil experienced an intensive fire season, despite the absence of major climate anomalies to enhance fire activity. Existing carbon monoxide (CO) emission estimates from state-of-the-art fire emission inventories differ
content: Abstract. In 2019, Brazil experienced an intensive fire season, despite the absence of major climate anomalies to enhance fire activity. Existing carbon monoxide (CO) emission estimates from state-of-the-art fire emission inventories differ by a factor two for the period and region. We provide a top-down estimate on CO emissions from these fires using the new CarbonTracker Europe – Long/Short Window (CTE-LW/SW) inverse modelling framework driven by column-averaged dry air CO mole fractions (XCO) from the MOPITT and TROPOMI satellite instruments. Our analysis indicates that the 2019 fires in Brazil released approximately 47 TgCO. Although structural atmospheric-chemistry related uncertainties remain (±15 TgCO), the inversions converged strongly to a common posterior (46–48 TgCO) independent of the prior emission inventory (GFED5.1, GFAS v1.2) or assimilated dataset (TROPOMI, MOPITT). Posterior fire emissions closely resemble the newly released GFED5.1, supporting recent advances in bottom-up fire modelling. Nonetheless, at the biome level, our results reveal a systematic underestimation—by roughly a factor of two—in the Cerrado and Caatinga savannas relative to both fire emission priors. While more targeted uncertainty assessments are required, we speculate that this emission gap unlikely stems from inversion choices alone and may indicate an underestimation of fuel loads or emission factors. Overall, we demonstrate CTE-LW/SW effectively leverages XCO to complement existing fire emission monitoring capacities at increasingly fine spatial resolution—a capability that is especially valuable in Brazil, where different fire regimes occur in close proximity and fire activity has intensified in recent years.

title: Nematode rapid adaptative response to the massive Deepwater Horizon oil spill
summary: The Gulf ecosystem health was of great concern after the explosion of the Deepwater Horizon oil platform (April 2010). After the spill, a large volume of oil trapped in the deep-sea plumes was transported offshore and to deep-water sediment
content: The Gulf ecosystem health was of great concern after the explosion of the Deepwater Horizon oil platform (April 2010). After the spill, a large volume of oil trapped in the deep-sea plumes was transported offshore and to deep-water sediments, causing detrimental effects on the benthic fauna. In this study, the variability in nematode standing stock, structural and functional diversity has been investigated. Nematodes were collected in October 2010 from stations characterized by different levels of impact and along the sediment vertical profile. Immediately after the oil spill, nematode abundances rapidly increased moving towards impacted stations and reaching unusual abundances for the deep-sea. Despite the sediment toxicity, impacted stations showed dense populations of small-sized nematodes concentrated in the surface sediment, whereas no-impact stations displayed more even vertical distributions and more stable size spectra. High turnover across horizontal and vertical gradients demonstrated substantial species replacement linked to contamination. Impacted stations were dominated by opportunistic and tolerant species, while sensitive taxa were restricted to no-impact stations. Functional traits provided additional resolution: impacted stations exhibited a marked dominance of juveniles, indicating rapid population turnover and resilience to hydrocarbon contamination. In contrast, no-impact stations were characterized by a higher proportion of adults and k-strategist nematodes, reflecting more stable communities. Bacterivorous/deposit-feeding nematodes dominated the impacted stations, compared to a more diversified trophic community in no-impact stations. The combined use of standing stock, taxonomic, and functional descriptors offered a powerful framework for assessing deep-sea oil spill magnitude and impacts, highlighting the nematodes as reliable bioindicators of oil pollution.

title: Drizzle drives model differences in the Southeastern Atlantic Stratocumulus Transitions with Aerosol-Rain-Radiation interactions (SEA STARR) large eddy simulation intercomparison project
summary: Abstract. The transition from overcast stratocumulus clouds to broken cumulus cloud fields as air is advected over warmer waters is important for controlling cloud cover and thus the radiative budget in the subtropics. Stratocumulus clouds
content: Abstract. The transition from overcast stratocumulus clouds to broken cumulus cloud fields as air is advected over warmer waters is important for controlling cloud cover and thus the radiative budget in the subtropics. Stratocumulus clouds can transition into scattered cumulus via an entrainment-driven “deepening-warming” process or into an open mesoscale cellular convective organization via a precipitation-driven “drizzle-depletion” process. The Southeastern Atlantic Stratocumulus Transitions with Aerosol-Rain-Radiation interactions (SEA STARR) large eddy simulation (LES) intercomparison project described herein uses a composite trajectory of cloud transitions in the southeastern Atlantic to assess the extent to which different LES model setups simulate similar deepening-warming or drizzle-depletion transitions under identical meteorological and aerosol forcings. Results are evaluated in light of observations from the ORACLES, CLARIFY, and LASIC field campaigns. The default setup includes abundant smoke (~1,000 mg-1) from southern African biomass burning and is compared with simulations using the same large-scale meteorology but cleaner (100 or 30 mg-1) free tropospheric aerosol concentrations. In the control, all five LES models simulate deepening-warming transitions that track satellite observations in terms of cloud fraction; exhibit boundary layer deepening somewhat greater than is consistent with observations; and maintain higher cloud droplet number concentrations than observed during nearby aircraft campaigns despite similar below-cloud aerosol number concentrations. In the cleaner cases, however, some models produce drizzle-depletion transitions while others maintain deepening-warming transitions. LES model differences are tied to large discrepancies in simulated rain formation for a given cloud state in terms of total condensate and droplet concentration.

title: Microeukaryotic Diversity and Habitat Structuring in a Desiccating Alkaline Maar Lake (Central Mexico)
summary: Microeukaryotes are important components of microbial food webs in saline and alkaline lakes, yet their diversity and distribution across distinct microhabitats remain poorly understood. We characterized microeukaryotic communities associat
content: Microeukaryotes are important components of microbial food webs in saline and alkaline lakes, yet their diversity and distribution across distinct microhabitats remain poorly understood. We characterized microeukaryotic communities associated with microbialites, microbial mats, hypersaline waters, and sediments in the desiccating maar lake Rincón de Parangueo (central Mexico) using 18S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing. After quality filtering and rarefaction, 417 amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) belonging to 17 eukaryotic phyla were identified. Community composition differed among microhabitats, with mats harboring the highest number of exclusive genera and water containing the fewest. No genus was shared across all four microhabitats. The greatest taxonomic overlap occurred between mats and water, suggesting ecological connectivity between benthic and planktonic environments. Ordination analyses and environmental data indicated strong habitat filtering associated primarily with salinity and conductivity. Co-occurrence network analysis revealed a highly modular community structure (Q = 0.789), with distinct habitat-associated modules and limited connectivity among them. Chlorophyta dominated assemblages, particularly in microbialites and water, whereas Bacillariophyta, Amoebozoa, Discoba, Aphelidiomycota, and Rotifera were present. Recurrent taxa such as Dunaliella and Picocystis occupied central network positions. These results demonstrate strong microhabitat-scale structuring and highlight the importance of fine-scale environmental heterogeneity in shaping diversity within alkaline maar lakes.

title: From conservation to management: lessons from old-growth forests
summary: Interest in old-growth and virgin forests dates to the second half of the nineteenth century, when they became subjects of scientific investigation in search of inspiration for the development of close to nature silviculture as an alternati
content: Interest in old-growth and virgin forests dates to the second half of the nineteenth century, when they became subjects of scientific investigation in search of inspiration for the development of close to nature silviculture as an alternative to financial and production-oriented forestry. Research conducted across diverse environmental contexts revealed a remarkable diversity of forest structures and composition, showing that no single model of the “natural forest” exists. Today, there is growing recognition that attempting to manage complex, dynamic, and unpredictable ecosystems through deterministic models is a paradox. This perspective paper explores whether and how old-growth forests can inform closer-to-nature and silvosystemic forest management. Acknowledging their role in advancing ecological understanding, old-growth forests have much to teach us. Their value invites us to move beyond the traditional utilitarian paradigm of silviculture by embracing a deeper ecological comprehension and accepting complexity as an inherent feature of forest management.

title: Length of the growing season as a key determinant of spatial variation in forest surface litter quantity
summary: Forest surface litter is an integral component of forest ecology, it acts as bridge between biotic and abiotic components of any forest ecosystem. Comprehensive, wall-to-wall mapping of forest litter distribution can enhance our understandi
content: Forest surface litter is an integral component of forest ecology, it acts as bridge between biotic and abiotic components of any forest ecosystem. Comprehensive, wall-to-wall mapping of forest litter distribution can enhance our understanding of ecosystem processes and nutrient dynamics, and improve management interventions and strategies for forest fire prevention and control. Forest phenology refers to start of season (SOS), peak of season (POS), end of season (EOS) and length of season (LOS). Thereby can be a potential indicator of accumulated surface litter quantity. However, these parameters are seldom used in estimation of surface litter. This study explored the prospective use of optical satellite-derived forest phenological metrics along with vegetation indices, LiDAR canopy-height and C-band SAR backscatter in estimation of surface litter quantity. Interestingly, the study found LOS (31.39%) to be the most important contributor to litter quantity estimation, followed by comparable contributions from LSWI (23.01%) and CRI2 (20.15%). SOS, POS and EOS had negligible contribution in explaining the spatial variability of accumulated surface litter. The study highlights the integrated use of LOS with canopy parameters that are indicator of vegetation stress and phase of leaf development can help in reliable estimation of forest surface litter quantity.

title: FLOWS: a model to simulate water and solutes fluxes in agricultural and environmental systems: 2. Modules for specific applications in water and nutrient management
summary: Abstract This paper is the second of two companion studies. The first paper focused on describing the model FLOWS, theory and the model benchmarking. This paper addresses FLOWS modules on specific applications: irrigation, temperature, orga
content: Abstract This paper is the second of two companion studies. The first paper focused on describing the model FLOWS, theory and the model benchmarking. This paper addresses FLOWS modules on specific applications: irrigation, temperature, organic carbon processes and nutrient transformation and transport in the soil. It also includes applications of FLOWS model in real scenarios. In the irrigation module, FLOWS allows for different scenarios: (1) no irrigation, i.e., only rainfall; (2) irrigation introduced by the user as a top-boundary, temporally variable, input flux; (3) irrigation computed as the daily potential evapotranspiration demand; and (4) irrigation computed by the model. In the latter, FLOWS optimizes irrigation fluxes and schedule according to a criterion based on the average pressure head along a user-specified depth, e.g., the root zone. Since soil temperature influences several soil processes, FLOWS simulates the temperature distribution in depth and time by using a solution to heat flow equations proposed by van Wijk and De Vries. FLOWS simulates fertilizer applications as organic matter (manure and crop residues) or mineral fertilizers. It can either simulate organic matter decomposition with coupled carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus transformations governed by C:N and C:P ratios or simulate nitrogen transport alone using an empirical mineralization approach independent on organic matter dynamics. Two applications of the model are presented in this paper: (1) analysing the role of spatial variability in soil and vegetation for large-scale irrigation optimization, and (2) monitoring and modelling water and nutrient fluxes from irrigated fields to the surface drainage network. In the first application, FLOWS proved reliable for optimizing irrigation at large scales by accounting for the spatial variability of soil and vegetation properties and by enabling the analysis of the uncertainty associated with progressively overlooking this variability. In the second application, FLOWS was coupled with another physically based model (KWV) founded on kinematic wave theory. FLOWS was used to accurately simulate water, nitrate, and phosphorus fluxes to runoff, which were then routed through the KWV model to produce runoff hydrographs and nutrient concentrations at different sections of the drainage network and at the field outlet.

title: On-Water and In-Water Effects: May Natural Organic Matter Serve as an Interfacial Reaction Facilitator?
summary: Abstract This perspective builds on the concept of reaction facilitation, where certain complex reactions can be accelerated up to 700 times at interfaces between water and hydrophobic substances. These effects include the “on-water” phenom
content: Abstract This perspective builds on the concept of reaction facilitation, where certain complex reactions can be accelerated up to 700 times at interfaces between water and hydrophobic substances. These effects include the “on-water” phenomenon observed in emulsions formed by mixing hydrophobic reactants with water, and the “in-water” effect observed predominantly in the aqueous phase at organic-water interfaces, such as micelles. We suggest that similar reaction enhancements might also occur at the interfaces of natural organic matter (NOM) fractions that form supramolecular assemblies. Such interfaces could transform contaminants and potentially detoxify them in the environment. Initially, we review documented on-water and in-water effects described in the synthetic chemistry literature. Next, we examine evidence that some NOM fractions can form supramolecular assemblies under appropriate conditions. We then discuss experimental observations of reaction enhancements with NOM amendments─suggesting potential on-water- or in-water-like effects. Using these insights, we propose two mechanisms by which NOM could enhance reactions: 1) by stabilizing hydrogen-bonding transition states and 2) through hydrophobically driven interactions and/or a multisite functional group model. Finally, we outline future research directions to determine if such on-water- or in-water-like effects occur at NOM-supramolecular interfaces and discuss their potential environmental implications if confirmed.

title: Ultramafic weathering in tropical volcanic arcs: Geochemistry and inverse modeling of rivers draining the Zambales Ophiolite Complex (ZOC), Philippines
summary: Mafic and ultramafic rocks are highly susceptible to silicate weathering, a key negative feedback which modulates atmospheric CO2 over geological timescales. The tectonic exposure of these reactive lithologies, such as the Neogene uplift of
content: Mafic and ultramafic rocks are highly susceptible to silicate weathering, a key negative feedback which modulates atmospheric CO2 over geological timescales. The tectonic exposure of these reactive lithologies, such as the Neogene uplift of the volcanic islands in maritime Southeast Asia, has been hypothesized to enhance this global feedback and contribute to long-term global cooling. However, the extent of its contribution is not clearly expressed in marine radiogenic strontium isotopic records. Evaluating this hypothesis motivates improving constraints on solute fluxes across the geologically complex region to refine interpretations of geochemical proxies for weathering. This work characterizes the silicate weathering process in the Zambales Ophiolite Complex (ZOC), Philippines using an updated geochemical dataset of major ions (Ca2+, Mg2+, Na+, Cl-) and 87Sr/86Sr, combining published data with new measurements of water, soil, and rocks collected from three sampling campaigns covering wet and dry seasons across 25 catchments. We employ inversion modeling to partition river geochemistry, explicitly accounting for lithological complexity and incorporating 87Sr/86Sr data and clay formation as a solute sink. Sensitivity analysis shows that the incorporation of these constraints substantially influences the calculated contributions of sources to the overall weathering flux. This approach yields a long-term silicate weathering-derived CO2 consumption of 2.15 x 106 mol CO2 km-2 yr-1 ± 25.77% (1σ) in the ZOC, significantly higher than global average. While adopting a more conservative framework returned an estimate lower than previous studies, it reinforces the disproportionately high area-normalized weathering fluxes from the ZOC. Principal component analysis additionally shows association between CO2 consumption and watershed features related to topography and runoff. Combining our calculations with published data, we estimate that SEA, despite occupying <2% of the Earth’s continental surface, accounts for approximately 7.6% of the global silicate weathering budget. This regional CO2 consumption per unit area corresponds to approximately four times the global continental average. Further, several altered ultramafic samples exhibit higher 87Sr/86Sr values than expected for mantle-derived material, a signature also expressed in a subset of river water samples. Compiling published data for mafic and ultramafic rocks across the region also show a considerable range of 87Sr/86Sr ratios (0.702-0.709). These findings highlight the importance of incorporating the geochemical variability of mafic and ultramafic bedrocks in inversion models to estimate weathering fluxes and motivates further work on investigating its influence on marine isotopic records to better understand the role of SEA in the evolution of the global carbon cycle.

title: Effects of a low dose of 3-nitrooxypropanol and a combination of direct-fed microbials on methane emission, oral swab bacterial community, and performance in dairy cows
source: Journal of Animal Science and Biotechnology/Journal of animal science and biotechnology
summary: Abstract Background 3-Nitrooxypropanol (3-NOP) can inhibit ruminal methane production by inactivating the key enzyme during methanogenesis. Combining 3-NOP and direct-fed microbials (DFM) can potentially provide a dual-action approach to re
content: Abstract Background 3-Nitrooxypropanol (3-NOP) can inhibit ruminal methane production by inactivating the key enzyme during methanogenesis. Combining 3-NOP and direct-fed microbials (DFM) can potentially provide a dual-action approach to reduce ruminal methane production. The objective of this study was to investigate the effects of supplementation of a low dose of 3-NOP and a mixture of DFM, on methane emissions, performance, and rumen microbial community of dairy cows. Results Forty-eight Danish Holstein dairy cows were used in a 14-week randomized complete block design. Due to a mixing error, 3-NOP was included at an unexpected low dose (6.0 mg/kg DM). Cows were fed with one of four experimental diets: (1) control diet, and other treatment diets were control diet supplemented with (2) 3-NOP, or with (3) DFM (12 mg/kg P. acidipropionici strain P169 and 120 mg/kg Bacillus subtilis and B. licheniformis mixture), or with (4) a combination of 3-NOP and DFM. 3-NOP inclusion did not affect DMI, feed efficiency, or milk yield and composition. DFM supplementation reduced partial mixed ration intake and total DMI. 3-NOP supplementation significantly reduced CH 4 production (g/d) (8%) and CH 4 intensity (g/kg ECM) (9%) but did not affect CH 4 yield (g/kg DMI). Furthermore, 3-NOP supplementation increased H 2 production, yield, and intensity. DFM supplementation reduced milk yield from weeks 3 to 8 and ECM yield from weeks 3 to 7, but these effects diminished over time. 3-NOP alone or in combination with DFM resulted in higher abundance of Megasphaera and Prevotella genera in oral swab samples. DFM supplementation had no effect on gas emissions, and it only tended to improve feed efficiency (ECM/DMI, kg/kg) during the later stage of the experiment. DFM supplementation led to higher abundance of certain species within the Lactobacillaceae family particularly at later stages of the experiment. Conclusions An unforeseen reduced dose of 3-NOP supplementation still can effectively mitigate methane emissions (both production and intensity) and increase H 2 emissions without affecting DMI or performance. DFM supplementation reduced DMI and milk yield at the onset of the experiment, but the effects subsided over time, resulting in an increased feed efficiency by the end of the experiment.

title: Governance of dietary microplastic exposure risk in marine ranching in the context of climate change
summary: Aquaculture facilities in marine ranches continuously fragment and release microplastics, which accumulate in filter-feeding shellfish and enter residents’ diets. Climate change intensifies this pathway. Warming and ultraviolet exposure acc
content: Aquaculture facilities in marine ranches continuously fragment and release microplastics, which accumulate in filter-feeding shellfish and enter residents’ diets. Climate change intensifies this pathway. Warming and ultraviolet exposure accelerate the fragmentation of aquaculture plastics, while typhoons damage facilities and release microplastics in pulses and raise the health expenditure at stake for the government, enterprises, and households. This study constructs a tripartite evolutionary game model of the government, marine ranching enterprises, and consumers. Numerical simulation is used to examine how each actor’s strategies shape the system’s convergence path and speed and long-term residual exposure. The findings are as follows. Whether the government can sustain regulation depends solely on whether the process-based assessment payoff covers the cost of regulation, because the outcome-based performance payoff can be free-ridden and cancels out in the payoff differential. Once subsidies exceed this government-side ceiling, they crowd out regulation and cause exposure to rebound. Enterprises’ tolerance for plastic-reduction costs follows a tiered threshold structure, and the simultaneous phase-down of regulation and subsidies readily triggers a governance relapse, so a mature market premium mechanism must be in place first. Consumer participation is subject to a self-undermining mechanism whereby governance success erodes the incentive to participate. Sustaining it requires lowering information and oversight costs rather than heightening risk perception. Information disclosure relaxes the consumer participation constraint in all configurations without fiscal expenditure, making it the most cost-effective instrument. When none of the equilibrium conditions holds, the system oscillates periodically, and population-average exposure underestimates both the cumulative health cost and the risk borne by highly exposed subgroups. The results lock in the government’s presence through process-based assessment, cultivate market premiums before phasing down regulation, and integrate microplastic source control into climate adaptation planning for marine ranching.

title: Agrobacterium-mediated genetic transformation studies in soybean (Glycine max (L.) Merrill) for sustainable food and nutritional security: A Review
summary: Soybean (Glycine max (L.) Merrill), is a major legume crop in the family Fabaceae. It is significant source of plant-based protein and oil, which is important determinant in the food and nutritional security of the world. However, its produ
content: Soybean (Glycine max (L.) Merrill), is a major legume crop in the family Fabaceae. It is significant source of plant-based protein and oil, which is important determinant in the food and nutritional security of the world. However, its productivity is progressively being limited by the abiotic stresses (drought and salinity), and biotic stresses (diseases and pests). Conventional breeding has limited success due to the complex genetics of stress-responsive traits and prolonged breeding cycles. Therefore, this review critically evaluates recent advances in Agrobacterium tumefaciens-mediated transformation for soybean improvement, focusing on stress tolerance, nutritional enhancement, and transformation efficiency. This review explains about current knowledge on major stress-responsive genes and transcription factors, including DREB, NAC, bZIP, and WRKY families, in addition to Osmo protective, antioxidant, and protein/oil quality-associated genes that contribute to soybean improvement. Furthermore, optimized transformation parameters, including explant selection, infection conditions, and selection strategies, are comparatively discussed to highlight emerging trends in transformation efficiency. In spite of substantial progress, persistent challenges such as genotype dependency, limited transformation efficiency, low reproducibility, and regulatory constraints continue to hinder the large-scale application of transgenic soybean technologies. Henceforth, emerging strategies including gene stacking, genome editing, and advanced vector systems are discussed as promising approaches to overcome these limitations. Agrobacterium-mediated transformation is a valuable tool for functional genomics and soybean improvement. Its integration with genome-editing technologies, systems biology, and conventional breeding can accelerate the development of climate-resilient, nutritionally enhanced soybean cultivars.

title: Knowledge-based injection molding optimization framework under real manufacturing constraints
source: The International Journal of Advanced Manufacturing Technology
summary: Injection molding parameter selection requires the simultaneous balancing of product quality, cycle time, and process stability. The inconsistencies among shop-floor, polymer datasheet, plastic simulation, and Subject Matter Expert (SME) re
content: Injection molding parameter selection requires the simultaneous balancing of product quality, cycle time, and process stability. The inconsistencies among shop-floor, polymer datasheet, plastic simulation, and Subject Matter Expert (SME) recommended parameters may lead to uncertainty and impractical solutions in real manufacturing. Existing optimization and simulation-based approaches fail to account for this issue, thereby limiting industrial applicability. Consequently, this study proposes a knowledge-based integrated framework for robust and industry-applicable parameter optimization. The methodology employs Grey Wolf Optimization (GWO) as the primary optimization tool to perform global exploration and local exploitation of process parameters within defined bounds and ideal targets, as well as under constraint-driven conditions without predefined ideal values based on surface-finish requirements. Taguchi analysis and regression modeling are utilized to identify important parameters and provide statistical validation. The results demonstrate that melt temperature is the primary factor governing sink marks and cooling time, while mold temperature primarily controls volumetric shrinkage, confirming thermally driven process behavior. Although both parameter ranges, namely SME-guided theoretical ranges defined prior to production and SME-adjusted practical ranges used at the shop floor, originate from SME knowledge, they differ due to presumptions versus real process conditions. By incorporating these practical SME constraints into the GWO search, the framework achieves near-zero deviation, including 0% deviation in injection pressure, $$-3.45\%$$ in mold temperature, $$+0.18\%$$ in melt temperature, $$-8.33\%$$ in hold time, $$-11.11\%$$ in cooling time, and $$-6.94\%$$ in cycle time, from shop-floor conditions while effectively balancing quality and productivity, thereby enabling stable and industry-ready parameter selection. Further independent shop-floor validation showed close agreement with the GWO recommendations and achieved acceptable quality within three gate-seal trials.

title: Feedbacks between natural climate solutions and plant invasions
summary: Abstract Biological invasions and carbon sequestration guide many modern-day land management decisions. However, intersections between invasions and natural climate solutions (NCS) - actions to maintain or increase the land carbon sink - ha
content: Abstract Biological invasions and carbon sequestration guide many modern-day land management decisions. However, intersections between invasions and natural climate solutions (NCS) - actions to maintain or increase the land carbon sink - have not received adequate attention in either the invasion or climate mitigation literature. We therefore review how plant invasions affect NCS and vice versa, focusing on reductions in emissions and carbon removals associated with avoided habitat conversion, restoration, forest and cropland management, agroforestry, and optimal grazing. We find that plant invasions can interfere with rapid NCS implementation and reduce the durability of carbon storage in many systems, although there are cases in which invasive plants increase carbon storage, creating biodiversity-climate mitigation trade-offs. At the same time, studies find that several NCS increase community resistance/resilience to invasions, and do so in forests, in particular, which can suppress invasive species spread in these systems. These dynamics suggest a positive feedback loop between NCS and invasions, in which NCS facilitate invasion control, and successful invasion control, in turn, eases further NCS implementation. This feedback could accelerate gains in land-based carbon storage and generate co-benefits for biodiversity, provided that NCS projects receive resources for sustained invasive species management. We highlight areas in need of further research, including how financial mechanisms for climate action could be used to overcome invasion-induced implementation barriers.

title: Beyond ROI: the sustainability paradox of tourism investment in Sub-Saharan Africa—A critical systematic review of readiness, governance, and just pathways
summary: Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) holds extraordinary natural and cultural heritage yet captured less than 2% of global tourism foreign direct investment (FDI) between 2010–2024, representing US$8–12 billion in annual lost development finance. This
content: Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) holds extraordinary natural and cultural heritage yet captured less than 2% of global tourism foreign direct investment (FDI) between 2010–2024, representing US$8–12 billion in annual lost development finance. This critical systematic review asked not merely why investment remained low, but whose development was served, at what cost, and under what conditions tourism advanced sustainable outcomes. Synthesizing 124 academic studies and 53 gray literature documents published between 2000 and 2024, the review identified six binding constraints: land tenure insecurity (73% of sources), restrictive visas (67%), infrastructure deficits (61%), corruption (58%), profit repatriation (52%), and licensing burdens (44%). Empirical evidence on sustainability outcomes remained limited, only 18% of academic studies reported sustainability-related data, with literature dominated by capital flows rather than community wellbeing or ecological integrity. To address this gap, the study introduced the Sustainable Tourism Investment Readiness (STIR) framework, reframing investment readiness around three pillars: pro-poor outcomes, ecological limits, and procedural justice. Evidence from patient capital (US$1.4 billion committed in 2023, growing at 26.8% annually) and technology-enabled ventures (seed investments US$250,000–1.5 million, internal rate of returns (IRRs) 18–45%) demonstrated that alternative approaches could align financial returns with sustainability. Such alignment required governance reforms prioritizing community land tenure, equitable benefit-sharing, and institutional accountability. The investment–sustainability paradox is solvable, but not through technocratic ease-of-doing-business reforms alone. Visa liberalization, land tenure reform, and tourism zones could improve viability by 3–5 percentage points, yet without social safeguards and ecological conditionality they risk reinforcing enclave tourism, leakage, and dispossession. The review proposed a research agenda centered on sustainability-grounded metrics and offered actionable recommendations for investors, policymakers, and development finance institutions (DFIs) seeking to align capital with just and sustainable development.

title: Biodiversity safeguards ecosystem services and functions worldwide
summary: Abstract Biodiversity loss threatens ecosystem services on which humanity depends, yet the strength, form and context-dependency of biodiversity–ecosystem service and biodiversity–ecosystem function relationships remain poorly quantified. H
content: Abstract Biodiversity loss threatens ecosystem services on which humanity depends, yet the strength, form and context-dependency of biodiversity–ecosystem service and biodiversity–ecosystem function relationships remain poorly quantified. Here we synthesize 423 studies to determine how biodiversity affects ecosystem functioning and service delivery. We show that regulating services, including water quality and pollination, often exhibit linear relationships, suggesting an additive role for diversity. While biodiversity enhances most functions and services, our effect-size analysis shows that oceanic ‘blue carbon’ sequestration is exceptionally sensitive, revealing how critical marine biodiversity is for climate mitigation. Conversely, services such as hazard regulation appear relatively insensitive to biodiversity, instead depending on a few functionally unique foundational species whose persistence nonetheless is interdependent on the wider community. Our new synthesis enables the forecasting of impacts, for example, that biodiversity loss will reduce pest regulation in countries experiencing population growth and intensive development, and it also highlights how ecosystem services might be used to anticipate future problems.

title: Summer oxygen dynamics in the bottom waters of a wide, temperate shelf sea
summary: Abstract. Seasonal depletion of dissolved oxygen (DO) in stratified shelf seas has important consequences for benthic and pelagic ecosystems and biogeochemical cycling. There is a need to understand the importance of different processes con
content: Abstract. Seasonal depletion of dissolved oxygen (DO) in stratified shelf seas has important consequences for benthic and pelagic ecosystems and biogeochemical cycling. There is a need to understand the importance of different processes contributing to the bottom water oxygen budget, and how those processes might change in a warmer ocean. Using CTD observations from the UK Shelf Sea Biogeochemistry programme, we construct a summer DO budget for the bottom waters of the Celtic Sea and use the budget to assess how bottom water DO might change in a warmer climate. Across the shelf, bottom water DO concentration declined during summer stratification, with greater losses in shallow northern waters and slower depletion in deeper southern regions. At a well-sampled site in the central Celtic Sea, the bottom water shows a consistent net DO loss of –44 ± 4 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹. Respiration and remineralization dominate this decline (–54 ± 19 mmol m⁻² d⁻¹), while vertical turbulent fluxes from the subsurface chlorophyll maximum (SCM) form an important DO source (30 ± 17 mmol m-2 d-1). Episodic wind events enhance DO supply from the SCM, helping to offset some of the DO consumption in the bottom water. Benthic oxygen demand and horizontal transports make minor contributions to the DO budget. A +2 °C “business as usual” climate warming will reduce oxygen solubility and lead to a 12 mmol m-3 drop in DO concentration in the bottom water over the summer stratified period. However, we find that increased microbial metabolic rates in the warmer bottom water are more important for changes in bottom water DO concentrations, potentially driving a decrease in DO concentration of about 35 – 66 mmol m-3. Combined, these effects will lead to increased oxygen deficiency in the central and northern Celtic Sea. Our results demonstrate the importance of metabolic responses to a warmer ocean, but also the need to better understand changes in winds and wind-driven mixing across the seasonal thermocline.

title: Measuring large-scale mCDR using a novel Atmospheric CO₂ Perimeter Flux (ACPF) method
summary: Achieving net-zero CO₂ emissions globally requires an annual removal of on the order of 7–9 Gt CO₂; but current CO₂ removal (CDR) measurement methodologies are not designed to quantify marine CDR (mCDR) at the megaton-to-gigaton scales requ
content: Achieving net-zero CO₂ emissions globally requires an annual removal of on the order of 7–9 Gt CO₂; but current CO₂ removal (CDR) measurement methodologies are not designed to quantify marine CDR (mCDR) at the megaton-to-gigaton scales required for climate relevance. This perspective presents a new methodology, the Atmospheric CO₂ Perimeter Flux (ACPF) method, an atmospheric-domain framework for the monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) of marine carbon dioxide removal. ACPF relies on a network of autonomous surface vehicles (ASVs) that monitor CO₂ concentration and wind vector in the well-mixed marine boundary layer (MBL) above the mCDR region. The sensors integrate net CO₂ mass flux in the MBL across the perimeter in tonnes per hour. Paired upwind and downwind ASVs track the sampled air mass, suppressing synoptic-scale CO₂ variability common to both ends of the transect. The difference between upwind and downwind CO 2 values can be converted into XCO₂ difference values comparable to satellite retrievals. The framework constrains net surface exchange over the enclosed region without ocean-interior observations or a biological-pump model. Attributing that exchange to an intervention requires a baseline obtained by the same array, over the same region. The magnitude of the signal that ACPF must resolve is assessed against the surface CO₂ depletion implied by the post-Pinatubo atmospheric anomaly. The ACPF architecture applies to any bounded mCDR intervention that generates a measurable surface CO₂ depletion at the megaton-to-gigaton-per-year scale required by today’s net-zero commitments.

title: Safeguarding old-growth and primary forests: protection and forest landscape restoration to deliver Europe’s 30×30 commitments
summary: Safeguarding old-growth and primary forests is essential for biodiversity conservation, climate regulation, ecosystem resilience and cultural heritage, yet these forests remain rare, fragmented and increasingly threatened across the EU. Rec
content: Safeguarding old-growth and primary forests is essential for biodiversity conservation, climate regulation, ecosystem resilience and cultural heritage, yet these forests remain rare, fragmented and increasingly threatened across the EU. Recent assessments estimate that primary and old-growth forests represent <3% of EU forest extent, with substantial gaps in spatially explicit mapping; this rarity underscores the urgency of protection and evidence-based restoration strategies (European Commission 2021b; Sabatini et al., 2018 ). In alignment with the EU Biodiversity Strategy for 2030, the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (Target 3, “30×30”) and the EU Nature Restoration Regulation, this paper argues for a dual pathway: (i) protection and improved legal enforcement for remaining intact, high-integrity old and primary forests and (ii) forest landscape restoration (FLR) to strengthen buffer zones, recover old-growth attributes and reconnect landscapes (CBD, Convention on Biological Diversity, 2022; European Union, 2024). We outline governance strategies to harmonize implementation across scales and emphasize the role of participatory management, engaging landowners and communities to strengthen social legitimacy and reduce pressures on remaining forests. Additionally, we suggest practical restoration frameworks, such as the Restoration Opportunities Assessment Methodology (ROAM), that support evidence-based interventions. We conclude with priority actions for conserving primary forests, restoring ecological connectivity, and communicating the ecological, cultural, and socio-economic values of old-growth landscapes. By coupling protection with landscape-scale restoration, supported by robust social safeguards and monitoring, Europe can accelerate progress toward 30×30 targets while enhancing climate resilience and societal benefits.

title: Geographically close nearshore sites exhibit contrasting dissolved oxygen dynamics and ecosystem metabolism in eastern Lake Taihu
summary: Diel dissolved oxygen (DO) dynamics integrate biological metabolism and physical forcing and provide a powerful tool for investigating ecosystem metabolism in shallow lakes. However, whether geographically close sites exhibit similar metabo
content: Diel dissolved oxygen (DO) dynamics integrate biological metabolism and physical forcing and provide a powerful tool for investigating ecosystem metabolism in shallow lakes. However, whether geographically close sites exhibit similar metabolic behavior and environmental controls remains poorly understood. Here, three years (2022–2024) of high-frequency DO observations from three contrasting nearshore sites in eastern Lake Taihu were used to quantify diel and seasonal variability in net ecosystem production (NEP), gross primary production (GPP), and ecosystem respiration (R). Yidixuan (YDX) is strongly influenced by surrounding anthropogenic activities, Yuyangwan (YYW) has comparatively stable environmental conditions, and Xintiandi (XTD) is subject to an intermediate level of disturbance. All three sites exhibited clear diel cycles in DO and NEP but differed markedly in oxygen level, diel amplitude, and metabolic balance. YYW maintained relatively high DO, small diel fluctuations, and predominantly positive NEP, whereas XTD and especially YDX showed lower DO, larger diel oxygen oscillations, and predominantly negative NEP. At YDX, the pronounced diel oxygen amplitude suggested intensified oxygen turnover, with respiration exceeding production overall. XGBoost-SHAP analysis revealed site-specific environmental associations with NEP. Photosynthetically active radiation was the primary predictor at YYW, pH was the leading predictor at XTD, and oxidation–reduction potential and pH were most influential at YDX. Comparison of the two respiration formulations showed that their performance depended strongly on local DO regime, with the direct nighttime formulation performing more consistently under relatively stable oxygen conditions and the alternative formulation providing more interpretable estimates where diel oxygen variability was large. These results demonstrate that substantial ecological differences can occur among nearby nearshore sites within a single shallow lake and highlight the value of diel DO dynamics for understanding metabolic variability and guiding metabolism estimation in freshwater ecosystems.

title: Old-growth beech forests - Joint Natural Heritage of Europe
summary: ncient trees are witnesses of cultural and natural history. Old-growth forests are like the “backbone” or “lungs” of the Biosphere. The beech (Fagus sylvatica) is a miracle tree, and beech forests are an outstanding example for adaptation t
content: ncient trees are witnesses of cultural and natural history. Old-growth forests are like the “backbone” or “lungs” of the Biosphere. The beech (Fagus sylvatica) is a miracle tree, and beech forests are an outstanding example for adaptation to diverse site conditions and for resilience in changing environment. The expansion of beech from their glacial refuge areas to large parts of our continent, the succession of beech forests, the change from mixed deciduous forests to beech dominated deciduous forests, and the co-evolution with the cultural history in Europe is a fascinating story. And, as a specific European phenomenon beech forests promote a common European identity. The inscription of European Beech forests in the UNESCO World Heritage List improves the public awareness for the value and importance of virgin forests and supports the movement for the protection of remaining old-growth forests in Europe.

title: ECOLOGICAL RELATIONS OF NATURAL REGENERATION OF FOREST PHYTOCOENOSES IN THE LEFT-BANK POLISSIA OF UKRAINE
summary: This study aimed to identify the factors affecting the population density, viability, and structural stability of natural regeneration in leading forest species (Pinus sylvestris, Quercus robur, Acer platanoides) in the Left-Bank Polissia o
content: This study aimed to identify the factors affecting the population density, viability, and structural stability of natural regeneration in leading forest species (Pinus sylvestris, Quercus robur, Acer platanoides) in the Left-Bank Polissia of Ukraine. The research focused on four forest formations: Pineta sylvestris, Querceta roboris, Betuleta pendulae, and Populeta tremulae. Field surveys used stratified random sampling and elemental accounting of self-seeding cohorts. Key environmental factors influencing cohort conditions included soil water regime, nitrogen content, carbonates, habitat illumination, and thermal regime. The study revealed how cohort traits respond to gradients of these factors, showing both diversity and individuality, which are crucial for enhancing adaptive potential and environmental sustainability. The response of these young cohorts to ecological factors reflects species-specific regeneration requirements and their ability to adapt. In Pineta sylvestris hylocomiosa forests, conditions for successful natural regeneration were found to be favorable. However, anthropogenic pressure led to a 35-55% reduction in regeneration density, decreased vitality, and cohort imbalance. The study also found that natural regeneration is more cost-effective than plantation forestry, reducing costs by 2.3-3.5 times per hectare. These findings can inform sustainable forest management and predict forest ecosystem adaptability to climate change. Keywords: biodiversity; ecosystems; natural regeneration; integrated population analysis; population structure; mathematical modelling.

title: Psychotropic drugs in drinking water? A scoping review of evidence on diazepam and fluoxetine
summary: The global prevalence of mental disorders has increased considerably in recent decades. This evidence, associated with population growth and the expansion of access to medications, favors the growing global consumption of psychotropic drugs
content: The global prevalence of mental disorders has increased considerably in recent decades. This evidence, associated with population growth and the expansion of access to medications, favors the growing global consumption of psychotropic drugs. Consequently, an increasing load of these substances is introduced into the environment, especially into water bodies, characterizing them as emerging contaminants. This scoping review study aimed to integrate data and provide a global overview of the occurrence of widely used psychotropic drugs (diazepam, fluoxetine, and haloperidol) in drinking water. The search for studies was conducted across 7 databases, with no language or publication year restrictions. We included only original studies in this review and synthesized data from the included studies for water sampled, sampling location, year of sampling, analytical method used, psychotropic drug found, and concentration found. Our review identified 13 studies published between 2000 and 2024 on the occurrence of diazepam and fluoxetine in tap water, drinking water, bottled water, and drinking well water from 7 countries, with concentrations ranging from 0.2 to 300 ng/L. No studies on the occurrence of haloperidol in drinking water were found. Our data highlight that the occurrence of psychotropic drugs in drinking water is a growing global reality and also show a significant lack of research dedicated to the topic. Furthermore, the results of this scoping review reinforce the need to expand water quality monitoring, improve analytical techniques, invest in advanced water treatment technologies, and implement public policies on the proper disposal of medication and the control of drug pollution.

title: Processi ecofisiologici ed ecosistemici nei boschi vetusti
summary: I boschi vetusti rappresentano oggi un riferimento essenziale per orientare strategie adattative di gestione, conservazione e ripristino degli ecosistemi forestali: conservano grandi quantità di carbonio, ospitano biodiversità e mostrano pr
content: I boschi vetusti rappresentano oggi un riferimento essenziale per orientare strategie adattative di gestione, conservazione e ripristino degli ecosistemi forestali: conservano grandi quantità di carbonio, ospitano biodiversità e mostrano processi ecologici che nei boschi giovani o gestiti sono assenti o meno evidenti. Capire come funzionano aiuta a prevedere la stabilità futura delle foreste e la loro capacità di rispondere a siccità, aumento delle temperature e altri stress. Con l’aumento dell’età e delle dimensioni, gli alberi affrontano vincoli diversi da quelli delle piante giovani. Devono trasportare acqua più in alto, mantenere una maggiore massa viva e sostenere chiome complesse. Questi fattori possono ridurre la crescita e la produttività, sia del singolo albero sia dell’intero popolamento. A livello individuale, il rallentamento può dipendere da maggiori costi respiratori, limiti idraulici e minore efficienza fotosintetica. A livello di popolamento, può essere associato a minore disponibilità di nutrienti e a una maggiore allocazione di risorse verso componenti non legnose. Resta però incerto quanto questi processi causino davvero il declino produttivo osservato. Età, dimensioni, genetica, ambiente e disturbi interagiscono in modi ancora poco chiari, limitando la capacità di prevedere la risposta delle foreste vetuste al cambiamento globale.

title: Prototyping Chain-Elongation-Mediated Dehalogenation for Groundwater Bioremediation
summary: Abstract Chlorinated ethenes are widespread groundwater contaminants. Microbial reductive dehalogenation can detoxify chlorinated ethenes but requires sustained H2 delivery to organohalide-respiring bacteria. In enrichment cultures, microbi
content: Abstract Chlorinated ethenes are widespread groundwater contaminants. Microbial reductive dehalogenation can detoxify chlorinated ethenes but requires sustained H2 delivery to organohalide-respiring bacteria. In enrichment cultures, microbial chain elongation was shown to reliably provide H2 for dehalogenation from the conversion of ethanol and acetate to butyrate and caproate and subsequent fermentation of these carboxylates. Supported by robust laboratory testing, here, we document the first field-scale application of chain elongation-mediated dehalogenation in chlorinated ethene-contaminated groundwater. Native groundwater communities produced mainly propionate from ethanol and acetate in microcosms and the field, whereas bioaugmentation with a chain-elongating enrichment culture redirected microbial metabolism toward butyrate production and supported dehalogenation to ethene. Dehalogenation was favored at a lower organic carbon loading (900 mg C L–1 either as ethanol + acetate, butyrate, or caproate). Chain elongation was more strongly stimulated at higher ethanol to acetate molar ratios and organic carbon loadings (3500 mg C L–1). Bioaugmentation with chain-elongating bacteria in groundwater produced detectable butyrate concentrations, increased the molar ratio of ethene and ethane from 0.20 to 0.51 during monitoring, and did not stimulate methanogenesis. This study positions chain elongation-mediated dehalogenation as an effective strategy for groundwater bioremediation of chlorinated ethenes.
