title: From CO2-EOR Utilization to Verified Geological Storage: An Abu Dhabi Certification Readiness Framework
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Carbon dioxide utilization for Enhanced Oil or Gas Recovery (CO2-EOR/EGR) can contribute to the industrial decarbonization in the near term when it can be demonstrated that the injected CO2 is durably retained in a defined geologic
content: Abstract Carbon dioxide utilization for Enhanced Oil or Gas Recovery (CO2-EOR/EGR) can contribute to the industrial decarbonization in the near term when it can be demonstrated that the injected CO2 is durably retained in a defined geological storage system. This paper discusses a certification-readiness framework that converts CO2-EOR utilization into auditable associated storage evidence. Precisely, an Abu Dhabi-aligned certification framework is proposed applicable to associated geological storage in CO2-EOR/EGR operations, developed around the principles of ISO 27916 and other relevant standards and regulatory frameworks implemented around the world. The work responds to a practical challenge faced by the hard to abate sectors as emissions monitoring and reporting are required by domestic and international competent authorities or agents shaping the evolution of compliance and voluntary carbon markets. In this context, EOR/EGR operators that utilize CO2 from such hard to abate sectors and intend to claim safe, long-term associated geological storage that genuinely reduce operational CO2 emissions, by implementing a robust and transparent governance framework that can potentially obtain domestic regulatory endorsement and withstand international market scrutiny. The framework discussed in this paper integrates seven building blocks: 1) certification objective and system boundary definition 2) storage site screening and site characterization, 3) containment assurance in a closed loop system, 4) monitoring and measurement, 5) mass-balance quantification, 6) closure planning and 7) governance for independent verification and competent authority endorsement. The approach is illustrated using an Abu Dhabi case involving the Al Reyadah operation, where captured CO2 from steel production is transported by pipeline to several oil fields and injected in selected reservoirs to enhance oil recovery. The preliminary gap assessment indicates that existing operations provide important foundations, including a defined CO2 source, active injection, a monitoring plan in place suitable for operational performance tracking including flowmeters at key locations and well and reservoir surveillance including saturation monitoring, production logging, isotope analysis and corrosion monitoring. However, certification readiness requires additional definition of the storage boundary, closed-loop CO2 injection, traceable accounting, reservoir model calibration and matching, well integrity assurance, risk-based MMV and verification-ready data governance. The paper concludes that ISO 27916-aligned certification can create a credible pathway to distinguish CO2 utilization from auditable associated storage, supporting defensible claims for reduced embedded emissions and future carbon-differentiated product strategies.

title: Driving the GCC Energy Future: Flexible Pipe Systems for Long-Term Cost Reduction and Sustainable Development for Hydrocarbon Transport Systems
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Objectives/Scope This paper examines the strategic, technical, and economic advantages of flexible pipe systems across the GCC, focusing on TOTEX, installation efficiency, and decarbonization. With national operators prioritizing l
content: Abstract Objectives/Scope This paper examines the strategic, technical, and economic advantages of flexible pipe systems across the GCC, focusing on TOTEX, installation efficiency, and decarbonization. With national operators prioritizing low‑impact developments, it shows how flexible solutions for short tie‑backs (~5–10 km) can reduce manufacturing and installation CO2 emissions by 38–57%, providing a credible, lower‑carbon pathway compared with traditional rigid systems. Methods, Procedures, Process The study utilizes a techno-economic comparative assessment and analysis between rigid and flexible systems, focusing on a specific GCC shallow water case study. The assessment focuses on direct and energy‑related emissions across the system's lifecycle, evaluating impacts associated with operational activities and manufacturing processes too. The evaluation measures "Certainty of Execution" by analysing vessel requirements, weather window adaptability, and the elimination of heavy subsea hardware such as Pipeline End Terminations (PLETs) and rigid spools/jumpers. Results, Observations, Conclusions The analysis demonstrates that although rigid carbon steel is often perceived as a lower‑cost solution, it requires extensive offshore welding, NDT, and fit‑up activities, significantly increasing vessel days. Flexible pipes, delivered as a finished product, streamline execution and typically reduce installation time by several days per jumper. Key advantages include improved: Capital Efficiency, as reduced fabrication and offshore construction lower upfront expenditure and minimise lifecycle emissions.A strong lifecycle emissions advantage is demonstrated through reduced manufacturing and offshore installation impacts. Flexible systems achieve approximately 72-74% lower installation-related CO2 emissions by utilizing lighter installation spreads, reducing vessel-day requirements, and eliminating offshore welding activities. As a result, overall lifecycle emissions are reduced by approximately 38-47% compared with conventional carbon steel rigid pipeline alternatives.Operational Savings are realized through the absence of routine maintenance requirements, lowering OPEX over the asset life. Enhanced field optimisation is achieved by eliminating rigid spools and enabling tighter bend radii, reducing routing deviations and shortening pipeline length for short tie‑backs.Technical reliability is strengthened through digital monitoring of annulus conditions and tensile armour behaviour, supporting long‑term integrity and potential life extension. Overall, the paper concludes that prioritizing TOTEX rather than initial CAPEX enables GCC operators to deliver lower‑carbon, cost‑efficient hydrocarbon transport while maintaining robust project economics. title: Industrial Deployment of a Novel Methodology to Optimize Power Demand
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Reducing power demand is a key lever to decarbonizing upstream operations, where electricity generation typically represents a major share of Scope 1 emissions. This paper introduces a novel structured, asset-level methodology to i
content: Abstract Reducing power demand is a key lever to decarbonizing upstream operations, where electricity generation typically represents a major share of Scope 1 emissions. This paper introduces a novel structured, asset-level methodology to identify quick-wins and CAPEX projects that reduce power consumption. Deployment of the "Challenge Power Demand" methodology across TotalEnergies' operated oil and gas assets resulted in significant energy savings and associated CO2 reductions. An exhaustive checklist for challenging operating, maintenance, process & project practices was initially established by a transverse team. Then, a two-step methodology has been developed: first, the following preparatory information is gathered: full mapping of electrical consumers to establish a reliable baseline.critical review of existing improvement levers and implementation gaps, supported by the checklist.in-depth analysis of major consumers (>0.1 MW), focusing on compressors, pumps, and utilities. This serves as input for the second step: an on-site transverse workshop that drives ideation and prioritization of initiatives based on impact, complexity, and investment. The new methodology has been labelled as a must-do carbon footprint reduction project and has been deployed on TotalEnergies operated oil & gas production facilities. On several mature offshore assets of TotalEnergies, 5–15% reduction potential in total power demand have been identified, corresponding to 0.5–6 MW under stable operating conditions. This translates into an estimated 3–35 kt CO2eq reduction, depending on the fuel gas emission factor. Moreover, the reduction in total power sometimes enables the optimization of the power reserve (shutting down one gas turbine in the near future). Analysis of the results for several assets highlights that gas compression systems account for most savings, with key inefficiencies linked to suboptimal operating windows: excessive recycling flows, non-optimized anti-surge settings, and higher-than-required suction temperatures. Targeted optimization actions—such as compressor load redistribution, pressure ratio rebalancing, and improved cooling strategies—alone can deliver quick power savings on compression systems. More significant savings are expected from rebundling. In parallel, utilities optimization (e.g., seawater lift pumps, water injection systems) demonstrated that aligning equipment usage with actual production needs can deliver energy reductions with minimal CAPEX through actions such as reducing parallel equipment operation and optimizing setpoints. More significant savings are expected from rewheeling or impeller replacement. This paper moves beyond traditional audits by introducing a systematic methodology that bridges the gap between energy diagnostics and implementation. title: Well-To-Gate Life Cycle Assessment of Methanol Decarbonisation Pathways for the United Arab Emirates
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Methanol plays a crucial role in the chemical industry and is also emerging as a fuel. Currently the global production of methanol remains predominantly reliant on fossil fuels. This study evaluates the well-to-gate lifecycle asses
content: Abstract Methanol plays a crucial role in the chemical industry and is also emerging as a fuel. Currently the global production of methanol remains predominantly reliant on fossil fuels. This study evaluates the well-to-gate lifecycle assessment (LCA) of methanol production pathways for the United Arab Emirates. The different pathways considered are: (i) E-methanol production including three carbon capture scenarios: an ethanol refinery offset, solid sorbent DAC (direct air capture), and high-temperature (HT) liquid sorbent DAC. (ii) Biomethanol production using miscanthus, corn stover, landfill gas and switchgrass as the precursor. The analysis is conducted using R&D GREET 2025 model with UAE specific inputs, with a functional unit of 1 MJ of methanol evaluated against two metrics, GWP and total CO2, and benchmarked against fossil references from coal gasification (125.1g CO2 e/MJ). The most common is natural gas derived methanol (Feedstock split: approximately 65% natural gas, 35% coal, and only ~0.2% renewable sources) (IRENA, 2024). All pathways examined achieve lower GWP emissions and total CO2 than fossil-based methanol across both metrics. The strongest netnegative performance is -45.9 g of CO2 e/MJ, achieved by e-methanol using biogenic CO2. GWP emissions are reduced through hydrogen recycling across all CO2 capture configurations because recycling hydrogen prevents the CO2 burden from being shifted upstream to the electrolysis process.

title: Predicting Tomorrow's Failure Today: AI-Driven Time-To-Failure and Multivariable Deviation Analytics for Advancing Reliability and Production Excellence
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Oil and gas facilities operate as interconnected systems. A change in one part of the plant can affect equipment reliability, process stability, production, energy use, and emissions elsewhere. Conventional surveillance relies on a
content: Abstract Oil and gas facilities operate as interconnected systems. A change in one part of the plant can affect equipment reliability, process stability, production, energy use, and emissions elsewhere. Conventional surveillance relies on alarms, operating limits, inspections, and subject matter expertise. These safeguards remain essential, but they may not reveal the weak, multivariable patterns that develop before equipment degradation, process instability, production deferment, or increased flaring. This paper presents an integrated industrial artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) framework that combines time-to-failure (TTF) estimation, multivariable deviation detection, and process forecasting. The framework uses historical and real-time operati.ng data to characterize normal operation, degradation, and known failure events. It then compares current plant behavior with these learned patterns to identify emerging risk, show the variables associated with the change, and provide lead time for intervention. TTF modeling estimates the time remaining before a defined undesirable event. For suitable and validated failure models, the prediction horizon can extend to 7 days. Multivariable deviation analytics complements TTF by detecting abnormal relationships among process, mechanical, utility, and environmental variables. This method is particularly useful when few repeat failures are available. Forecasting can also be applied to continuous process measurements when a future value has operational value. Used together, the three methods provide a system-level view rather than a series of isolated tag assessments. The paper draws on deployments in oil and gas processing, gas compression, utilities, and production optimization. It then describes the extension of this approach to the Gas Treatment Plant and Onshore Gas Terminal (GTPOGT). The implementation links the Operation Process Playbook to a web-based, real-time analytics platform. For the high-pressure (HP), low-pressure (LP), and tank flare systems, the platform combines TTF, deviation analytics, and flare rate forecasting. Selected flare rates are forecast up to 4 hours ahead to support earlier investigation and intervention. The main finding is that a predictive model creates lasting value only when it is part of a disciplined operating workflow. Data readiness, clear event definitions, technical ownership, alert governance, engineering validation, response protocols, and model maintenance are as important as the algorithm. The proposed framework moves plant surveillance from alarm-driven response toward predictive, and eventually governed prescriptive, decision support. This shift can improve reliability, reduce exposure to unplanned deferment, increase production efficiency, and support lower carbon operations.

title: Cost Drivers and Deployment Barriers of CO2 Capture in Upstream Oil and Gas: A Techno-Economic Evaluation of the United Arab Emirates
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Objectives/Scope This paper develops a unified techno-economic and barrier framework to evaluate CCS deployment viability in the UAE upstream oil and gas sector, addressing the Euro-North American bias in existing cost literature.
content: Abstract Objectives/Scope This paper develops a unified techno-economic and barrier framework to evaluate CCS deployment viability in the UAE upstream oil and gas sector, addressing the Euro-North American bias in existing cost literature. It quantifies the Levelized Cost of Capture and Cost of CO2 Avoided for three archetypes — acid gas removal, offshore power generation, and LNG post-combustion capture — and identifies cost drivers, break-even carbon prices, and barrier profiles distinguishing applications by current viability, potential viability under stronger policy support, and persistent structural constraints. Methods, Procedures, Process: The study applies a cross-sectional techno- economic evaluation calibrated to 2023-2024 UAE conditions, generating 216 Monte Carlo observations around nine deterministic base cases (three archetypes × three capacity scales × three carbon-price scenarios). Uncertainty draws span the implemented NOAK capital multipliers, ±10% flue-gas CO2 concentration, and ±12% reboiler duty; WACC is held fixed at 10%. LCOC, CCA, and LCOE are computed with UAE- specific corrections for offshore retrofit premiums, power-island electricity costs, and EOR credits. The final analysis reports M3 cost-driver models with HC3 robust standard errors, M4 for IRR and break-even carbon price, and a descriptive barrier assessment, backed by Kruskal- Wallis tests and robustness checks. Results, Observations, Conclusions: The UAE upstream CCS cost landscape is sharply two-regime. Acid gas removal averages ~9.4 USD/tCO2 LCOC (11.8 CCA), while offshore power and LNG post-combustion cluster near 97-98 USD/tCO2 (119130 CCA) — roughly an order-of-magnitude gap. Archetype indicators dominate the M3 regression (R2 ~ 1.00); waste-heat fraction is the strongest within-archetype lever and log-TCC the second. Electricity price is effectively null in the calibrated model. Break-even carbon price for acid gas removal at the 10% corporate hurdle is approximately 43 USD/tCO2 with EOR; offshore and LNG remain unviable across the 0150 USD/tCO2 range. Barriers compound the cost penalty for dilute streams: offshore platforms face weight, footprint, and power-island constraints; LNG trains face dilute flue gas and steam-integration sensitivity. The conclusion is that UAE CCS should be sequenced, not uniform. Priority near-term deployment is acid gas removal connected to established onshore EOR/storage infrastructure, supported by a 4050 USD/tCO2 carbon-price range. Offshore and LNG capture require modular technology development, heat integration, shared hub infrastructure, and targeted public co-investment rather than carbon pricing alone. title: Bringing Synthetic Methane from Theory to Reality; Oman LNG as Case Study
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract The path to Net Zero Emissions by 2050 requires decarbonization initiatives across all energy systems. For the LNG industry, synthetic methane gas (SNG) is not only decarbonization initiative, but also alternative technical approac
content: Abstract The path to Net Zero Emissions by 2050 requires decarbonization initiatives across all energy systems. For the LNG industry, synthetic methane gas (SNG) is not only decarbonization initiative, but also alternative technical approach to harness renewable energy into creating low carbon fuel. It is a Key Power-to-Gas (PtG) technology that enables the production of methane (CH4) synthetically by reacting renewable hydrogen with carbon dioxide (CO2) through exothermic Sabatier reaction. The resulting SNG can be liquefied into synthetic LNG, stored, transported through pipelines or LNG carriers, without the need for infrastructure modifications benefiting from established LNG infrastructure. Where required, SNG can also be reconverted into hydrogen offering additional system flexibility and resilience in future energy systems. Despite higher Energy conversion losses than methanol or ammonia without heat recovery, SNG remains competitive due to its higher volumetric energy density and the compatibility with existing LNG infrastructure, resulting in favorable delivered fuel costs at port. Furthermore, safety risk for SNG is well understood and much lower compared to other products. At Oman LNG, the availability of a high-purity CO2 stream (~99%) enhances the attractiveness of the concept by ensuring a high-purity captured CO2 feedstock. Accordingly, this paper investigates an integrated process value chain for (SNG) production by combining captured carbon dioxide (CO2) from the Acid Gas Removal Unit (AGRU) at Oman LNG with green hydrogen produced via electrolysis. The study further assesses the technical and economic feasibility of the proposed system, including its viability as a business case. Oman LNG (OLNG), in collaboration with Kanadevia Corporation (Japan)-Isothermal Methanation Technology provider, adopts a phased study approach to evaluate the deployment of SNG production. The methodology follows two parallel workstreams. First, a pre–Front-End Engineering Design (pre-FEED) study is conducted at pilot-plant scale to de-risk the isothermal methanation technology with green hydrogen production via electrolysis and a concentrated CO2 source, in a full value chain interfacing with existing OLNG infrastructure and with intermittent feedstock. Second, a commercial-scale plant concept study is assessed in parallel to evaluate scale-up potential and associated economic performance, thereby supporting informed investment decision-making. In conclusion, the resulting SNG is fully compatible with existing natural gas infrastructure, presenting potential decarbonization pathway for Oman LNG and offering a sustainable low carbon fuel production option for Oman. The study demonstrated that pilot-scale deployment can support the transition to commercial-scale investment by identifying and mitigating key technical, operational, and integration risks, thereby de-risking subsequent billion-dollar scale-up plant investment. title: Closed-Loop Remote Optimization of ESP Systems Using Real-Time Voltage/Frequency Control: A Field-Proven Digital Method to Reduce Energy, Emissions, and Failure Risk
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract This paper presents a closed-loop, fully remote optimization framework for Electrical Submersible Pump (ESP) systems, validated across 9 wells in a mature field in Ecuador, that dynamically adjusts motor operating conditions. Unlik
content: Abstract This paper presents a closed-loop, fully remote optimization framework for Electrical Submersible Pump (ESP) systems, validated across 9 wells in a mature field in Ecuador, that dynamically adjusts motor operating conditions. Unlike conventional ESP tuning practices relying on periodic manual interventions or static design assumptions, this approach continuously optimizes the voltage/frequency (V/f) ratio based on real-time electrical readings. The objective is to reduce energy consumption, emissions, and equipment failures without interrupting production or requiring field intervention. The methodology integrates high-frequency telemetry with a real-time decision workflow that continuously evaluates motor loading, power consumption, and thermal behavior. Variable Speed Drive (VSD) parameters are remotely modified through dynamic adjustment of the Frequency Base (FBase), enabling continuous optimization of the Voltage/Frequency ratio. A data-driven diagnostic classifies operating regimes as over-magnetized or under-magnetized, and corrective actions are applied accordingly. Underloaded systems receive voltage reductions to eliminate excess magnetizing current; overloaded systems receive controlled voltage increases to restore torque capability. All adjustments are executed online, forming a closed-loop cycle with no well shutdowns, site visits, or production deferral. Field deployment across 9 pilot ESP units demonstrated average real power reductions of 2.5% for over-magnetized systems, with savings up to 4.9 kW per well. Annual CO2 emission reductions were estimated between 9.6 and 28.8 metric tons per ESP. Thermal stabilization was observed across several optimized systems, with motor temperature reductions of up to 3.7°F—directly contributing to insulation integrity and extended run life. Systems operating beyond nominal load (101%) exhibited measurable efficiency improvements following voltage correction, confirming that conventional derating strategies overlook optimization opportunities in under-magnetized cases. Average economic savings reached $225 USD per month per well, while eliminating deferred production and reducing exposure to start-up-related mechanical and electrical stresses—key contributors to premature ESP failure. This work redefines ESP optimization as a continuous digital process rather than a discrete field intervention. The demonstrated ability to simultaneously reduce energy consumption, lower carbon emissions, and extend equipment run life—while operating 100% remotely with zero HSE exposure—establishes a scalable pathway toward autonomous artificial lift management in mature fields. The finding that controlled voltage increases in under-magnetized motors yield measurable energy savings challenges established derating conventions and introduces a new optimization paradigm.

title: Environment-Related Technological Innovation and Ecological Footprint in India: Aggregate and Component-Wise Time–Frequency Analysis
summary: This study investigates the time-frequency dynamics between environment-related technological innovation and environmental quality using the ecological footprint as a comprehensive measure of environmental quality and its components for Ind
content: This study investigates the time-frequency dynamics between environment-related technological innovation and environmental quality using the ecological footprint as a comprehensive measure of environmental quality and its components for India. To capture time-varying and frequency-dependent relationships, the study adopts a wavelet coherence framework, which allows simultaneous analysis of short-, medium-, and long-run dynamics between environment-related technological innovation and environmental quality for the period between 1990Q1 to 2022Q4. The results indicate that the relationship between environment-related technological innovation and environmental quality is strongly time-varying and scale-dependent. In the aggregate ecological footprint, the significant coherence is concentrated on the short and medium horizons, while the long-run interactions are weak and non-persistent. The phase dynamics show that the rise in ecological footprint precedes the adoption of environment-related technological innovation. In components analysis, it shows a strong short-term coherence between technological innovation in the environmental field and single parts of the ecological footprint. At the same time, the medium-run effects are intermittent, and the long-run relationships are mostly insignificant or driven by boundary effects. The results suggest that the environmental benefits from environment-related technological innovation are gradual and uneven in ecological dimensions. Therefore, policymakers should complement technology-promotion strategies with regulatory and demand-side measures to avoid overreliance on long-term technological solutions and to better address short-term ecological footprint.

title: Life Cycle Analysis of Magnetosome Biomanufacturing
summary: Abstract Production of iron oxide magnetic nanoparticles using conventional chemical and physical methods presents sustainability challenges due to often high energy consumption and the use of hazardous reagents. Biological synthesis via ma
content: Abstract Production of iron oxide magnetic nanoparticles using conventional chemical and physical methods presents sustainability challenges due to often high energy consumption and the use of hazardous reagents. Biological synthesis via magnetotactic bacteria (MTB) offers a greener alternative, but its environmental performance remains unexplored at scale. This study addresses this gap by conducting a life cycle assessment (LCA) of magnetosome production and purification, using a ‘cradle-to-gate’ approach. Key findings identified environmental hotspots in both upstream and downstream processing, in particular, bioreactor fermentation and magnetically enhanced density separation (MEDS). MEDS showed the highest environmental burden, accounting for 61% of global warming potential (GWP), 70.6% of terrestrial ecotoxicity, 74.6% of marine eutrophication, and 91% of land use, primarily due to its reliance on the specialty surfactant, Eumulgin ES. Notably, the bioreactor unit accounted for 53.7% of water consumption, 52.4% of human non-carcinogenic toxicity, 38.0% of fossil resource scarcity, and 33% of the total GWP, driven by the requirements for bacterial culture media and energy inputs to maintain optimal temperature for bacterial growth. This study shows that recovering protein and PHA as co-products modestly improved environmental impact metrics (below 0.75%), while enabling process circularity. The sensitivity analysis revealed that increasing cellular iron uptake from 33.1 to 300 mg of iron per gram of dried cell weight (mg Fe g–1 DCW) could reduce environmental impacts by >10.4-fold, while raising the rotor-stator high-gradient magnetic separation (RS-HGMS) yield from 70 to 99% could reduce emissions by 1.4-fold.

title: Impact of Dry Docking on Sustainability: A Case Study of CO2 Reduction Under SEEMP
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Maritime industry is facing the high pressure in order to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emission and increase energy efficiency in response to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and international maritime regulations. The resea
content: Abstract Maritime industry is facing the high pressure in order to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emission and increase energy efficiency in response to the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and international maritime regulations. The research examine the regulatory framework of the Ship Energy Efficiency Management Plan (SEEMP) developed by International Maritime Organization (IMO). The focus of this study to align with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, with particularly with SDG 7 (Affordable and Clean Energy) SDG 13 (Climate Action) and SDG 14 (Life Below Water). There is a critical gap exists in the current IMO framework where conventional distance-based Energy Efficiency Operational Indicator (EEOI) metrics are not suitable for offshore support vessels (OSVs) that engage in dynamic positioning, towing, and anchor handling operations. This study identifies and addresses this measurement gap by developing and validating a time-based EEOI proxy for OSVs using an Anchor Handling Towing Supply (AHTS) vessel as a case study, in accordance with IMO and SEEMP guidelines. For the case study the data has been collected from Tug MV Hadi over a year that is covering the period of pre and post dry docking interval. The vessel underwent scheduled maintenance in July 2025, including hull cleaning, propeller polishing, and the overhaul of both main and auxiliary engines. EEOI has been calculated by using data from fuel consumption and engine operating-hour (SMU) records. These results shows the improvement in energy efficiency after dry dock. Average EEOI dropped from 863.4 g CO2/(GRT·h) to 708.5 g CO2/(GRT·h) as an 17.9% reduction in EEOI. The average CO2 emission rate per engine hour decreased by a comparable 17% (0.59 to 0.49 t CO2/hr), and average monthly fuel consumption reduced by over 36% (402 to 256 MT/month). The monthly variance in EEOI also decreased and the standard deviation decreasing by approximately 18 % ( from 39 to 32 g CO2 / GRT·h), indicating a more stable performance after the revision. The novelty of this paper is to demonstrate for the first validate application of the IMO time based EEOI proxy for offshore support vessels that is addressing a critical gap in offshore logistics support. This study confirms that SEEMP is not only a theoretical but also a practical tool for improving energy efficiency in the maritime sector. This study demonstrates the real impact of (Planned Maintenance System) PMS offering operators practical evidence to align maintenance planning with IMO decarbonization targets and company efficiency goals. These strategies could contribute to Scope 1 emissions reduction while supporting SPE's Grand Challenge of Net Zero Operations while aligning with the UN Sustainable Development Goals framework.

title: Unlocking Emissions Reductions in Offshore Drilling Through the Adoption of Electric Crew Transfer Technologies Such as Wing-In-Ground Effect Vehicles
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Offshore oil and gas operations depend on fossil-fuel burning helicopters, crew transfer vessels, and ferries to move crews between shore bases and platforms. As the industry works to decarbonize, crew transfer stands out as a visi
content: Abstract Offshore oil and gas operations depend on fossil-fuel burning helicopters, crew transfer vessels, and ferries to move crews between shore bases and platforms. As the industry works to decarbonize, crew transfer stands out as a visible source of Scope 1 emissions. This paper evaluates whether all-electric wing-in-ground-effect (WIG) craft can take over helicopter missions and cut emissions in the process. The analysis follows a two-step model. First, the total emissions of the global offshore helicopter fleet is estimated from annual flight hours, mix-weighted fleet characteristics, and a jet-fuel emissions factor, arriving at a total addressable market of roughly 1 billion kilograms of carbon dioxide per year. Second, that total is filtered by the operational limits of WIG craft, namely range from shore and sea state, to yield a serviceable offset of approximately 600.1 million kilograms of carbon dioxide annually. After taking into consideration the Scope 2 emissions of charging the electric craft under three charging scenarios, net reductions range from 450.6 to 600.1 million kilograms of carbon dioxide per year depending on the electricity source (diesel generator, grid, or fully renewable). A sensitivity analysis on the impact of wave tolerance limitations and electricity source showcases key levers on potential emission offsets. Electric WIG craft emerge as a credible tool for decarbonizing one of the industry's harder-to-abate activities.

title: From Flaring to Value: A Scalable and Digital Enabled Multi Well Pad Green Completion Model Delivering 94% Emissions Reduction in Oman
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Hydraulically fractured gas wells commonly require extended cleanup and testing periods during which significant volumes of hydrocarbons may be flared. Strategies to reduce emissions by capturing and exporting hydrocarbons during w
content: Abstract Hydraulically fractured gas wells commonly require extended cleanup and testing periods during which significant volumes of hydrocarbons may be flared. Strategies to reduce emissions by capturing and exporting hydrocarbons during well flowback, commonly called "Green Completions", have been deployed in several producing basins in the middle east, however widespread implementation remains challenged by facility interfaces, solids and water management requirements, process safety considerations, and operational complexity. The need for scalable solutions is increasing as operators seek to simultaneously reduce emissions and improve project value. Shell Development Oman is advancing Green Completions as a component of its low carbon strategy by deploying reduced emission completion frameworks with a focus on enhancing asset performance during post-frac flowback operations. This addresses the dual challenge of maintaining production excellence while meeting stringent decarbonization targets. This paper presents a novel case study of the design, planning, and execution of Green Completions in a tight gas condensate asset in Oman, constituting a next-generation model integrating multi-well pad operations, direct tie-in to production facilities, advanced four-phase separation and solids management, digital real-time surveillance, and simultaneous operations framework into a low-carbon value stream. The case study presents a roadmap for operators to reduce flaring while improving operational efficiency and value. The case study highlights the successful integration of decarbonization objectives, process safety, and digital operational excellence, positioning Green Completions as a scalable and commercially viable solution for sustainable upstream development.

title: Offshore Fleet Efficiency Improvement Through Hybrid Energy and Heat Recovery Systems
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract The offshore maritime sector faces increasing pressure to reduce greenhouse gas emissions while maintaining the high operational reliability required for offshore energy production and subsea construction activities. Offshore Suppo
content: Abstract The offshore maritime sector faces increasing pressure to reduce greenhouse gas emissions while maintaining the high operational reliability required for offshore energy production and subsea construction activities. Offshore Support Vessels (OSVs), Construction Support Vessels (CSVs), Diving Support Vessels (DSVs), and Subsea Intervention Vessels operate under highly dynamic load profiles driven by Dynamic Positioning (DP), heavy-lift crane operation, hotel loads, and mission-specific subsea equipment. These operational requirements necessitate continuous online generator capacity to satisfy single-failure redundancy mandates, frequency resulting in prolonged low-load engine operation, elevated Specific Fuel Oil Consumption (SFOC), accelerated mechanical degradation, and avoidable carbon emissions. While alternative zero-carbon fuels and radical vessel redesigns offer long-term decarbonization pathways, existing fleets represent substantial capital investments with 10 to 20 years of remaining operational lifespans. Brownfield energy efficiency and align with International Maritime Organization (IMO) carbon intensity mandates. This paper proposes an Integrated Offshore energy Optimization System that combines a Lithium Iron Phosphate Battery Energy Storge System (BESS), multi-stage Waste Heat Recovery (WHR) loops, an Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) generator, and Intelligent Load Management under a centralized Energy Management System (EMS). Unlike existing studies that independently evaluate energy storage or waste heat recovery, this work establishes a unified mathematical and operational framework integrating electrical storage, thermal recovery, auxiliary motor speed modulation, and predictive power dispatch into a single control topology. A baseline analytical assessment was conducted on a representative 16 MW DP2 offshore construction vessel using field-validated engine performance maps and tropical Middle Eastern operating profiles (ambient air temperatures up to 50°C and sea temperatures up to 35°C). results demonstrate that the IEOS framework can achieve annual fuel savings to 16.0%, a 16.0% reduction in carbon emissions, a 23.0% reduction in engine operating hours, and an optimal average generator loading increase from 32% to 64% during DP operations. Financial modelling yields a simple payback period of 3.71nto 6.15 years. This research provides vessel operators with a validated, scalable transition strategy to achieve immediate emissions compliance while preserving operational reliability and power system safety.

title: Decarbonizing Flare Operations Using Smart Plasma Ignition at Remote Degassing Stations
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract This paper presents the deployment of a Smart Plasma Ignition System (SPIS) as a replacement for conventional fuel gas based flare ignition systems at Remote Degassing Stations (RDS 1, RDS 2, and RDS 3). The objective is to elimina
content: Abstract This paper presents the deployment of a Smart Plasma Ignition System (SPIS) as a replacement for conventional fuel gas based flare ignition systems at Remote Degassing Stations (RDS 1, RDS 2, and RDS 3). The objective is to eliminate routine pilot gas consumption, reduce greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 218 tons of CO2 annually (equivalent to 4 MMSCF fuel gas), and enhance flare reliability, safety, and operational sustainability. The emissions reduction strategy involved replacing continuous pilot fuel gas based flare ignition systems with a Smart Plasma Ignition System (SPIS). The SPIS generates high-energy plasma directly at the flare tip, removing the need for permanent pilot flame combustion. The system is integrated with the Distributed Control System (DCS), utilizing vent gas flow signals and thermocouple flame feedback to initiate ignition only during venting events and to provide immediate reignition upon flame loss. This configuration minimizes unnecessary gas burning, reduces methane and CO2 emissions, and ensures stable flare operation under low vent rates and adverse weather conditions. The deployment of the Smart Plasma Ignition System (SPIS) at RDS(1,2,3) successfully eliminated continuous pilot fuel gas consumption, resulting in a measurable reduction in routine flaring-related greenhouse gas emissions. The system demonstrated reliable ignition performance under challenging operating conditions, including ultra-low venting rates, high wind speeds, and adverse weather, addressing common causes of flame instability and unburnt hydrocarbon release. Integration with DCS logic ensured ignition occurred strictly during venting events, preventing unnecessary combustion and improving overall combustion efficiency. Operational data confirmed high ignition success rates, reduced operator intervention, and enhanced flare availability over extended periods of operation. The results validate SPIS as a robust, low-emission alternative to conventional pilot-based ignition systems, supporting company decarbonization strategy while improving operational safety, reliability, and environmental performance across onshore oilfield facilities This work demonstrates large‑scale replacement of conventional pilot‑based flare ignition with a fuel‑free Smart Plasma Ignition System across multiple operational RDS facilities. The novelty lies in integrating plasma ignition with real‑time DCS logic to eliminate continuous pilot combustion while maintaining flare stability at ultra‑low flow conditions, offering a replicable pathway for reducing routine flaring emissions in onshore oilfield operations.

title: Performance of Cryogenic Carbon Capture for CO2 Purification and Near-Zero SO2 Emissions
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Post-combustion capture of carbon dioxide usually requires other upstream pollutant capture systems such as selective catalytic reduction for NOx, flue gas desulfurization, electrostatic precipitators, etc. Traditional carbon captu
content: Abstract Post-combustion capture of carbon dioxide usually requires other upstream pollutant capture systems such as selective catalytic reduction for NOx, flue gas desulfurization, electrostatic precipitators, etc. Traditional carbon capture technologies cannot be deployed at point emission sources that do not have these systems and use fuels containing sulfur (e.g., heavy fuel oil, sour gas, etc.). A novel pollutant capture system is being developed that eliminates this limitation. A Cryogenic Carbon and Sulfur Capture (CCSC) technology has been developed at KAUST in collaboration with SE. This technology focuses on post-combustion CO2 capture along with SO2, NO2, and other Particulate Matter (PM) pollutants. CCSC is modular in design and mounted on a 15-meter-long trailer. The multi-species co-capture system is mounted in the central section of the trailer and includes a separate control room and gas storage room on either end of the trailer. This trailer-mounted CCSC system has a nominal capacity of capturing 0.25 ton of CO2 /day. This CCSC process cools exhaust flue gases below the desublimating temperatures of CO2 where CO2 solidifies out of the flue gas. This separation process is done by bubbling the flue gas through the pool of cryogenic carrier fluid at cryogenic temperatures, which serves as a contact liquid. CO2 freezes into the contact liquid and flows out as a slurry. The contact liquid is regenerated via a mechanical solid-liquid separator, and then the CO2 product is recovered via distillation. An additional column is necessary for the separation of a third species SO2. The primary objective of the mobile CCSC rig is to serve as a flexible technology and IP development platform for the simultaneous capture of CO2 and other flue-gas pollutants using a single cryogenic process. The CCSC process is inherently capable of separating additional flue-gas constituents through temperature- dependent phase-change mechanisms within the cryogenic recuperation system. Detailed characterization of NOx separation and other co-pollutant removal mechanisms is outside the scope of the present study and will be reported separately. Building on the system configuration and performance framework previously reported in SPE-229102 (Sreedharan et al., 2025), the present work focuses on experimental validation of CO2 product purity and SO2 co-capture under representative heavy fuel oil (HFO) flue-gas conditions. Although the current system is configured for one of SE's HFO-fired power plant, the platform is designed to be flue-gas agnostic and adaptable to other stationary and mobile emission sources. In particular, the demonstrated capability for simultaneous pollutant removal provides a pathway toward marine applications, where compact integration of CO2, SOx, and potentially other pollutant-control functions is highly desirable. Ongoing technology and IP developments at KAUST (Wagstaff et al., 2022a) (Wagstaff et al., 2022b) are being evaluated to furt

title: Combined Cycle Power Plant with Carbon Capture: Adding Value Through System Integration
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Natural gas is traditionally considered a lower-carbon fossil fuel than coal, emitting roughly half the amount of CO2 per unit of electricity generated. Despite their comparative advantage, gas-fired power plants still contribute s
content: Abstract Natural gas is traditionally considered a lower-carbon fossil fuel than coal, emitting roughly half the amount of CO2 per unit of electricity generated. Despite their comparative advantage, gas-fired power plants still contribute significantly to anthropogenic CO2 emissions. As the world moves towards net-zero emissions, even low-carbon fossil assets like natural gas combined cycles (NGCC) must implement solutions to reduce their carbon footprints. In this context, carbon capture utilization and storage (CCUS) emerges as a critical enabling technology (Ritchie et al., 2023). Currently, carbon capture solutions are categorized into three types: post-combustion, pre-combustion, and oxy-fuel combustion technologies. Among these, post-combustion carbon capture is considered to have the highest technology readiness level (TRL) and deployment maturity. Post-combustion capture offers significant advantages for power plants, as it can be retrofitted to existing operational facilities. This helps preserve the capital already invested in these plants, minimizes disruption to the power systems, and facilitates a gradual transition to more sustainable energy sources. Currently, carbon capture plants primarily utilize an aqueous monoethanolamine (MEA) solvent to extract carbon dioxide from flue gases. This technology has been extensively studied, and solvent-based carbon capture systems have been successfully implemented in refineries, chemical industries, and for acid gas sweetening in the oil and gas sectors. It is important to recognize that CO2 concentrations in exhaust gas from different sources can vary significantly, impacting the performance, configuration, and selection of carbon capture plant (CCP) technologies, as well as capital and operational expenses. For example, the exhaust gas from industrial land-based gas turbines typically contains around 3%-4.5% CO2 at near-atmospheric pressure, depending on the specific gas turbine model. The low pressure and density of flue gas led to high volume flows, which necessitate larger equipment's. These factors subsequently influence the plant's footprint and total installed cost. Furthermore, lower CO2 concentrations require higher energy input for effective CO2 separation. As a result, removing CO2 from sources with lower concentrations, such as natural gas combined cycle (NGCC), necessitates careful consideration. This paper discusses the improvements of a post-combustion carbon capture plant integrated with a NGCC through the application of exhaust gas recirculation (EGR) and steam integration. The EGR technology implies recirculating a portion of the flue gas from the stack back into the gas turbine inlet, where it is mixed with ambient air. The application of EGR increases the concentration of CO2 in the exhaust gas while reducing the amount of flue gas sent to the CCP. This dual effect enables a reduction in both the total energy consumption and capital expenditures of the CCP. Further optimis

title: Wind Hybridization in Tierra Del Fuego
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Tierra del Fuego (TEP Austral) operates two plants, Río Cullen and Cañadón Alfa, connected by a medium-voltage cable. Electricity has historically been produced using gas turbines. The site is an isolated island with no connection
content: Abstract Tierra del Fuego (TEP Austral) operates two plants, Río Cullen and Cañadón Alfa, connected by a medium-voltage cable. Electricity has historically been produced using gas turbines. The site is an isolated island with no connection to the grid or nearby consumers, preventing access to external renewable energy. Additionally, its remote southern location offers poor conditions for solar photovoltaic (PV) development. The aim of this project is to reduce fuel gas consumption with low-carbon intensity power sources. All energy must be generated on-site in this isolated environment. While Tierra del Fuego benefits from exceptional wind resources (Luna, M. F. et al., 2026), with average speeds of 11 m/s, wind power remains inherently intermittent. To address this challenge, the project integrates wind turbines, Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), and a custom-designed advanced Energy Management System (EMS). This hybrid solution allows operation with a single gas turbine at low load, significantly reducing dependency on fuel gas while improving grid stability, operational flexibility, and overall reliability of the system. Commissioned and started up in January 2026, this project represents a Wind + BESS + Gas Turbine hybrid system deployed at a fully isolated facility without external grid support. Unlike conventional hybrids connected to strong grids or relying on solar PV, it operates in a remote, wind-driven environment where grid stability, inertia, and process continuity must be internally managed, making it truly first-of-a-kind for TotalEnergies. Its innovation lies in both technology integration and a new operating paradigm for isolated assets. A key breakthrough is the use of grid-forming inverter technology within the BESS, enabling batteries to actively control voltage and frequency, support large motor starts, and deliver dynamic stability services traditionally provided by thermal generation. It delivers significant benefits, including more than 50% reduction in emissions from power generation, improved operational efficiency and enhanced reliability. Fuel gas savings can be commercialized, while the EMS and BESS simplify grid operations and improve flexibility. The project demonstrates that deep decarbonization and high reliability can be achieved without grid connection. The project delivers tangible benefits beyond innovation, including reduced CAPEX and OPEX through lower reliance on gas turbines and less intensive maintenance. It increases gas commercialization by redirecting fuel savings to sales, boosting production and revenues. HSE conditions improve with reduced noise, fewer high-risk activities, and safer maintenance. It also enhances operational efficiency and asset longevity. Finally, the solution is scalable and can be replicated across isolated assets and other energy-intensive industries.

title: From Carbon Waste to Carbon Wealth – Maximising Condensate from Overlooked Gas Streams
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Objectives/Scope This paper aims to demonstrate how overlooked gas streams—specifically flare, fuel gas, reinjection gas, and sales gas—can be transformed into high-value condensate through additional condensate recovery systems. T
content: Abstract Objectives/Scope This paper aims to demonstrate how overlooked gas streams—specifically flare, fuel gas, reinjection gas, and sales gas—can be transformed into high-value condensate through additional condensate recovery systems. This approach directly maximises revenue while reducing emissions, thereby improving overall carbon intensity (CI) performance. These gas streams were previously unmonetized and contributed to poor emissions management. The scope of this study covers both offshore facilities and onshore gas receiving terminals that are lacking full gas processing capability, focusing on value creation, greenhouse gas emissions reduction, and improved gas quality compliance. Methods, Procedures, Process The approach integrates low- and high-pressure condensate recovery concepts, supported by dynamic process evaluation of operating conditions and gas compositions. A low-pressure condensate extraction unit was implemented at an offshore flare system, while high-pressure applications targeted C5+ extraction from reinjection, fuel gas, and sales gas streams. Process analysis assessed gas specifications against turbomachinery requirements and gas sales agreements, particularly regarding liquid dropout risks. The study also leveraged Joule–Thomson (JT) cooling behaviour to maximise molecular condensation, with additional focus on onshore pressure gradients between offshore landing points and receiving facilities. Results, Observations, Conclusions Field deployment of the condensate recovery system yielded incremental condensate recovery of ~40 bbl/MMscf, demonstrating strong commercial impact from previously overlooked gas streams. The initiative also delivered a 20% reduction in CO2 emissions from flare, highlighting its dual value as an emissions-mitigation and monetisation solution. Observations confirmed that enhancing the JT effect significantly improves C5+ extraction efficiency, particularly at onshore facilities where larger pressure differentials exist. High-pressure recovery successfully ensured compliance with compressor gas specifications while reducing risks of liquid dropout beyond delivery points—an essential requirement in gas sales agreements. Treating hydrocarbons at a molecular level, rather than as homogeneous product streams, proved critical in unlocking additional value. Heavy hydrocarbon molecules (C5+) were shown to be approximately 400% more valuable than lighter components (C1), reinforcing the strong economic incentive for recovery. The results validate the strategic shift toward "right molecules to the right market," improving profitability and reducing carbon intensity across upstream operations. The approach introduces a novel molecular-level hydrocarbon management strategy that has not bee

title: Hydrogen Fuel Switching in Refining Assets: Technical Integration and Economic Barriers to Large-Scale Deployment
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract The increased risks of climate change are becoming increasingly prevalent worldwide. Many refiners and operators have therefore made ambitious pledges to meet net zero emissions. This has led to growing interest in decarbonization
content: Abstract The increased risks of climate change are becoming increasingly prevalent worldwide. Many refiners and operators have therefore made ambitious pledges to meet net zero emissions. This has led to growing interest in decarbonization opportunities to reduce Scope 1 greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions. While hydrogen firing has been demonstrated on individual refinery assets, refinery-wide deployment remains largely unexplored. This paper presents one of the first published refinery-scale assessments of hydrogen fuel switching, evaluating the technical integration requirements, economic performance, and decarbonization potential of large-scale deployment across a representative Middle Eastern refinery. A structured methodology was developed using experience from multiple refinery concept studies to assess hydrogen production, distribution, combustion equipment modifications, refinery fuel gas (RFG) management, and site integration requirements. Four fuelswitching pathways were evaluated: Existing Hydrogen Capacity - Partial Fuel Switching,Existing Hydrogen Capacity - Full Fuel Switching of Selected Consumers,Additional Blue Hydrogen Capacity - Full Fuel Switching,Additional Green Hydrogen Capacity - Full Fuel Switching. Economic performance was assessed using the levelized cost of abatement (LCOA) over a 25-year project life. The assessment identified fuel gas network limitations, hydrogen distribution infrastructure, management of displaced RFG, and plot space availability as the principal factors governing refinery-scale implementation. Results show that large-scale blue hydrogen production with integrated carbon capture emerged as the most economically attractive hydrogen fuel-switching option. The process proved to be more energy efficient for hydrogen production and carbon capture compared to the case using existing hydrogen capacity. This meant that over the 25 years operation it was much more economically attractive, as the fuel gas requirements make up a large proportion of overall project costs. Compared to the green hydrogen case the CAPEX costs are substantially lower. Green hydrogen production requires significant infrastructure for electricity production, electrolysis and energy storage. Comparison with a representative refinery Carbon Capture, and Storage concept demonstrated that under the baseline pricing conditions the CCS concept returns slightly better economics for carbon abatement. However, sensitivity analysis showed that hydrogen fuel switching becomes increasingly competitive under conditions of high fuel gas prices, low electricity prices, and refinery layouts that constrain CCS deployment. The study demonstrates that no single decarbonization pathway is universally optimal and highlights the importance of refinery-wide techno-economic assessments to identify the most effective site-specific decarbonization strategy and support long-term investment decisions.

title: The UV-A receptor CRY-DASH1 regulates ciliary length and mating efficiency in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii
summary: The biflagellate green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii encodes two DASH ( Drosophila , Arabidopsis , Synechocystis , Homo )-type cryptochromes. One of them, CRY-DASH1, absorbs mainly in the UV-A area and is localized in the chloroplast. Prev
content: The biflagellate green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii encodes two DASH ( Drosophila , Arabidopsis , Synechocystis , Homo )-type cryptochromes. One of them, CRY-DASH1, absorbs mainly in the UV-A area and is localized in the chloroplast. Previous studies have shown that CRY-DASH1 balances the photosynthetic machinery. It acts as a repressor of chlorophyll and carotenoid biosynthesis as well as of thylakoid membrane hyperstacking and it is an activator of specific pathways of the central carbon metabolism and of histidine biosynthesis. Environmental conditions influence the expression of CRY-DASH1; in addition, such conditions cause variations in the length of the algal cilia (also known as flagella). Here, we analyzed whether CRY-DASH1 may be involved in regulating the length of the cilia in C. reinhardtii by using wild-type cells and a backcrossed cry-dash1 knock-out mutant ( cry-dash1 mut ). We find that the ciliary length is significantly increased in vegetative cells of cry-dash1 mut compared to wild-type cells. Frequency distribution histograms suggest that the ciliary length of the entire algal population has shifted toward the longer values. According to prior findings, we corroborate that the ciliary length of C. reinhardtii wild-type gametes is increased compared to that of vegetative wild-type cells. Cilia of cry-dash1 mut cells are even further lengthened. Moreover, we find that the mating efficiency of plus and minus gametes of cry-dash1 mut strains is enhanced. All phenotypes were rescued to a significant extent in partially complemented CRY-DASH1 lines. Our results demonstrate that CRY-DASH1 is involved in the regulation of ciliary length in vegetative cells and gametes across the entire population. As cilia get longer in cry-dash1 mut , CRY-DASH1 acts as a repressor of ciliary length. Additionally, CRY-DASH1 functions as a negative regulator of mating efficiency in C. reinhardtii . Together, these findings expand the known functional roles of CRY-DASH1 beyond photosynthetic and metabolic regulation and suggest a relationship between photoreceptor-associated regulation and ciliary-associated cellular processes in this green alga.

title: Revenue Up, Carbon Down, Cost Zero – Simple Tuning for Higher C5+ Recovery
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: ABSTRACT Objectives/Scope This paper aims to demonstrate how simple, zero-investment operational tuning of a Dew Pointing Control Unit (DPCU) can significantly increase C5+ condensate recovery, improve gas quality compliance, and reduce car
content: ABSTRACT Objectives/Scope This paper aims to demonstrate how simple, zero-investment operational tuning of a Dew Pointing Control Unit (DPCU) can significantly increase C5+ condensate recovery, improve gas quality compliance, and reduce carbon intensity. The scope covers legacy turbo-expander (TEX) and Joule–Thomson (JT) valve systems at an onshore gas terminal that were previously operated under sub-optimal and risk-prone conditions, causing value leakage, equipment reliability issues, and poor emissions management. Methods, Procedures, Process A systematic diagnostic was conducted on Terminal A's DPCU using process simulation, historical operating trends, and dynamic upset behaviour modelling. The study evaluated TEX and JT valve interactions, hydrate formation risks, impeller failure modes, and sluggish automated JT response during TEX disturbances. Detailed simulations were used to identify pressure–temperature "sweet spots" that maximise C5+ condensation while staying within safe operating limits. Step-by-step operational tuning guidelines were developed to ensure robustness against past legacy issues, maintain production continuity, and safeguard compliance with sales gas specifications and downstream customer equipment limits. Results, Observations, Conclusions The optimisation revealed that dual operation of TEX and JT—previously implemented to avoid production interruptions—introduced significant inefficiencies, under-recovered condensate, and heightened risks of liquid carryover to customer facilities. Sub-optimal cooling from both streams contributed to condensate mismanagement, including misclassification as scheduled waste, while also weakening decarbonisation performance. Through targeted tuning, the team restored DPCU operation to a high-efficiency regime without requiring new equipment or CAPEX upgrades. The optimised settings delivered an 83% increase in C5+ condensate production at the same gas throughput, increased revenue generation, and reduced carbon intensity due to improved liquid extraction. The approach also mitigated hydrate formation risks, reduced exposure to compressor specification breaches, and prevented expensive customer-end equipment failures. The zero-investment optimisation is projected to save PETRONAS millions of ringgit through cost avoidance (downtime, repairs, penalties) while generate additional revenue by unlocking additional condensate throughput from existing assets. This establishes a practical pathway to value creation and emissions reduction, aligned with PETRONAS' NZCE aspirations. title: Transforming Gas Plant Performance Through First-Principle Digital Twin Integration: Enhanced Visualization with Intelligent Engineering Deployment at GTPOGT, Turkmenistan
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract As the global energy sector intensifies its focus on efficiency, reliability, and lower carbon operations, industrial digital twins are becoming critical enablers for operational optimization and GHG emissions reduction. Enhanced V
content: Abstract As the global energy sector intensifies its focus on efficiency, reliability, and lower carbon operations, industrial digital twins are becoming critical enablers for operational optimization and GHG emissions reduction. Enhanced Visualization with Intelligent Engineering is a new generation, first-principle-based digital twin designed to provide continuous performance insights for complex processing facilities. This paper presents the first deployment of digital twin integration at an international asset, specifically the Gas Treatment Plant and Onshore Gas Terminal (GTPOGT), in Turkmenistan. The deployment demonstrates how process-engineering-led digitalization can translate plant data into operationally relevant insights and measurable value across an integrated gas processing value chain. Digital twin integration was developed using a fully integrated steady-state process simulation software model representing the major gas and condensate processing systems in GTPOGT. Its scope encompasses feed gas and condensate reception, feed gas separation, acid gas removal, gas dehydration, hydrocarbon dewpoint control, propane refrigeration, flash gas compression, and condensate stabilization. The solution integrates process simulation with plant historian data, Plant Information Asset Framework, Plant Information Visualization Platform dashboards, automated data conditioning, model-informed key performance indicators, and virtual measurements. This architecture establishes continuous mass balance visibility and enables equipment-level performance diagnostics using a unified engineering model. Process studies covering October 2024 to June 2025 identified optimization opportunities in the hydrocarbon dewpointing, propane refrigeration, and flash gas compression systems. Simulation results indicated that achieving the intended temperature profile could increase condensate recovery by up to 28%, representing an estimated margin opportunity of USD 10,000 to USD 30,000 per day on the basis of the stated economic assumptions. Post-cleaning observations showed a 2 to 3°C improvement in performance. Flash gas compressor analysis showed that the antisurge valves were frequently open by more than 25% in the first-stage and more than 50% in the second-stage. Simulation estimated that rerouting approximately 2.9 MMscf/D of triethylene glycol (TEG)-treated gas to the compressor suction could reduce dependence on internal gas recycling and improve compressor loading. The value assessment associated compressor trip avoidance and approximately 8 MMscf/D of flaring with a cost avoidance potential of USD 593.75/hour. The digital twin integration deployment demonstrates how a first-principle digital twin can transform gas plant performance management from retrospective data review toward model-informed engineering oversight. title: Enabled Energy Transition Approach to Off-Grid Diesel Displacement in Oman
source: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
summary: Abstract Remote exploration and production (E&P) operations in off-grid environments are characterized by intensive diesel dependency and high operational complexity. Under standard Exploration and Production Sharing Agreements (EPSA), the
content: Abstract Remote exploration and production (E&P) operations in off-grid environments are characterized by intensive diesel dependency and high operational complexity. Under standard Exploration and Production Sharing Agreements (EPSA), the fiscal burden of diesel fueled power generation is assumed by the host government through cost-recovery mechanisms. These fuel subsidies can represent 36% to 40% of a nation's total energy subsidy budget. This fiscal structure inherently disincentivizes operators from pursuing fuel reduction strategies. This paper proposes a "Zero-CAPEX" Diesel Energy Service Contract (D-ESCO) model designed to align governmental fiscal recovery with systematic decarbonization of remote industrial assets. The proposed methodology involves deploying a "Hybrid Triad" integrating Solar PV, Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS), and Diesel Generation (DG) through a performance-based commercial framework. Under this structure, OQAE acts as the project aggregator, assuming 100% of the project development risk, and project management responsibility, while also serving as the aggregating entity across multiple sites and operators by mobilizing the resources and upfront investment required for implementation at scale. Conversely, the Government is insulated from project-level risk through zero capital contribution and no operational liability. This structure can be adapted to project-specific requirements, deployment horizons, and operating conditions, enabling either mobile or long-term fixed solutions under a tariff based commercial arrangement. In doing so, it enables operators to capture decarbonization benefits, improve operation reliability, and reduce production deferment risk, while also generating government value through lower cost-recovery exposure and emissions reduction in support of national NDC commitments. Scenario-based financial modeling indicates that reducing diesel consumption can yield up to a 47% reduction in government cost-recovery expenditure, with fiscal benefits enhanced by optimized fuel logistics, reduced storage requirements, and extended maintenance intervals for thermal assets. In parallel, lower diesel throughput reduces greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, with cumulative avoided emissions representing nearly 1% of country's 2021 emissions baseline. Beyond emissions and fiscal savings, the approach could support skilled employment, reinforcing economic diversification and In-Country Value objectives. If extended beyond remote E&P operations to mining and power generation, diesel and emissions reductions could be materially greater The novelty of this framework lies in its integration of an OQ Alternative Energy enabled DESCO model as project aggregator with off-grid hybrid deployment to address both fiscal and decarbonization challenges in Oman's remote E&P operations.
