This study shows that the timing of consecutive events is statistically associated in European trees, but that the association between fruiting and leaf coloration has weakened in some species as the interval between these phases has increased.

title: Carbon Dioxide Sequestration Potential of Rice (Oryza Sativa) Plant
source: International Journal of Educational Innovations and Research
summary: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is a naturally occurring component of the atmosphere, comprising approximately 0.04% of atmospheric gases. In recent years, increasing atmospheric CO₂ has received significant attention because of its potential influenc
content: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is a naturally occurring component of the atmosphere, comprising approximately 0.04% of atmospheric gases. In recent years, increasing atmospheric CO₂ has received significant attention because of its potential influence on global climate patterns. Anthropogenic activities, including industrialization, deforestation, forest degradation, and fossil fuel combustion, have contributed to increased atmospheric carbon levels and disrupted the global carbon cycle. Plants play an essential role in this cycle by serving as carbon sinks in terrestrial ecosystems. Carbon stored in plants is largely represented by their biomass, with above-ground biomass constituting a major portion of the terrestrial carbon pool. Estimating plant biomass is therefore important for determining carbon storage capacity and assessing carbon loss associated with deforestation. This study investigated the above-ground biomass and carbon dioxide absorption of rice plants, particularly their stems and leaves, and compared carbon capture during the vegetative and reproductive stages. The study was conducted in the Water Quality Analysis Laboratory using 21 samples of rice plant stems and leaves. Results showed that the leaves absorbed more carbon dioxide (0.74739 kg) than the stems (0.64011 kg), which may be attributed to the leaves’ primary role in photosynthesis and their greater availability of materials required for the process. The findings also revealed that rice plants captured a higher average amount of CO₂ during the vegetative stage (66.071 g) than during the reproductive stage (27.407 g). These results demonstrate the significant contribution of rice plant biomass, particularly leaves, to carbon sequestration and emphasize the importance of understanding carbon storage across different growth stages.

title: Electric-field-induced fully spin-polarized current in ferromagnetic bipolar Ag, Cr, or Sc-decorated AlN monolayer at room temperature
summary: In this study, we systematically unveil the pivotal role of transition metal adatoms (Ag, Cr, and Sc) in the atomic configuration, electronic structure, and magnetic properties of the aluminum nitride(AlN) monolayer using spin-polarized den
content: In this study, we systematically unveil the pivotal role of transition metal adatoms (Ag, Cr, and Sc) in the atomic configuration, electronic structure, and magnetic properties of the aluminum nitride(AlN) monolayer using spin-polarized density functional theory calculations. A pristine AlN monolayer is a direct p-type semiconductor with a non-magnetic nature. Decoration of the AlN monolayer with transition metal atoms induces a transition from non-magnetic to antiferromagnetic states. Bipolarity emerges in the decorated AlN monolayer once the temperature exceeds the magnetic transition temperature. Based on the first-principle calculations, the magnetic transition temperature turns out to be 21, 494.075, and 57.39 K for the AlN monolayers decorated with Ag, Cr, and Sc, respectively. The adatoms’ partially filled valence orbitals hybridizing with the host material is responsible for the ferromagnetic state of each compound. Further investigation demonstrates that stronger chemical adsorption and higher charge transfer are achieved for the Sc-decorated AlN monolayer. The tight bonding of the Sc atom, relative to other adsorbate species, is attributed to the formation of polar covalent bonds between the Sc atom and the nearest N atoms of the AlN monolayer. We further extended our investigation to explore the adsorption properties of decorated AlN monolayers under an external electric field. The energy band gap in all structures begins to decrease as the applied external electric field increases, and half-metallicity occurs when a threshold electric field is reached. These results underscore the significant potential of adatom embellishment of the AlN monolayer for future electronic and spintronic devices.

title: Rapid generation advancement in soybean: approaches, constraints, and the stage-dependent photoperiod window
summary: Long generation intervals constrain realized genetic gain in soybean ( Glycine max (L.) Merr.) breeding. Speed-breeding protocols developed for long-day and day-neutral crops use an extended photoperiod throughout the entire life cycle. The
content: Long generation intervals constrain realized genetic gain in soybean ( Glycine max (L.) Merr.) breeding. Speed-breeding protocols developed for long-day and day-neutral crops use an extended photoperiod throughout the entire life cycle. They are not directly applicable to soybean, because the E1 family represses the florigen genes GmFT2a and GmFT5a under long days and delays flowering. Rapid generation advancement in soybean therefore depends on a stage-dependent photoperiod window. Before flowering, the photoperiod (10–12 h in published stage-dependent protocols) must remain below the genotype-specific critical photoperiod, and an extended photoperiod can be introduced only after flowering (R1 stage), to accelerate seed maturation. Optimized continuous short-day systems are reported to allow up to five generations per year, and six are reported by one study that combined a post-flowering 22-h photoperiod with germination of immature seed. These figures come from different studies, genotypes and facilities. To our knowledge, no study has yet compared cycle length under a post-flowering long day with a corresponding short-day control in the same genotypes. A post-flowering 22-h photoperiod also reduced leaf photosynthetic capacity, and applying the same early harvest date to all plants may change allele frequencies in segregating populations. This review summarizes soybean speed-breeding protocols, their infrastructure requirements, and their physiological and genetic limitations. It also evaluates the integration of these protocols with marker-assisted selection, genomic selection and genome editing. Early seed harvest and high-density planting can be transferred between crops, but the photoperiod regime must be tailored to soybean. We conclude that the evidence supports soybean speed breeding as a method for accelerating generation turnover, and that phenotypic selection in the chamber needs to be validated in the field. Published controlled-environment soybean protocols do not report changes in allele frequency during accelerated advancement or genetic correlations between traits measured in the chamber and in the field. Both are needed to show whether rapid cycling translates into genetic gain in the field.

title: Exploratory profiling of Rhizophora apiculata root-associated fungi and preliminary polycaprolactone surface modification assessed using amplicon sequencing and culture-based approaches
summary: Microplastics are persistent environmental contaminants, and fungi associated with mangrove roots may offer a source of isolates for studying interactions with polymeric materials.This exploratory study profiled fungal DNA in a single poole
content: Microplastics are persistent environmental contaminants, and fungi associated with mangrove roots may offer a source of isolates for studying interactions with polymeric materials.This exploratory study profiled fungal DNA in a single pooled sample of Rhizophora apiculata roots using ITS amplicon sequencing and examined the FTIR spectra of polycaprolactone (PCL) samples following exposure to five cultured fungal isolates, designated fungal isolates S2-S6.Amplicon sequencing detected 48 fungal taxa, predominantly assigned to Ascomycota, with Aspergillus as the most abundant genus.The diversity indices suggested moderate diversity and relatively low dominance within the pooled sample.FTIR analysis revealed differences in PCL associated spectral features following exposure to the isolates, while principal component analysis (PCA) showed preliminary spectral differentiation among the analyzed samples.These observations indicate differences in the chemical or surface associated characteristics of the tested PCL samples; they do not demonstrate polymer mass loss, depolymerization, assimilation, or mineralization.The sequencing results represent fungal DNA detected in one pooled biological sample and do not establish the viability or endophytic status of the detected taxa.A correspondence between the cultured isolates and the detected amplicon sequence variants was not established.Quantitative mass-loss measurements, molecular weight and degradation product analyses, and experiments with appropriate controls and biological replication are needed to determine the nature and cause of the observed PCL associated spectral changes.

title: Reduced fertilizer with amino acids improves soil, yield, and quality of edible rose
summary: Abstract Long‐term excessive inorganic fertilizer application disrupts soil biological processes, diminishes nutrient use efficiency, and ultimately constrains sustainable production of edible roses. A 2‐year field experiment was carried ou
content: Abstract Long‐term excessive inorganic fertilizer application disrupts soil biological processes, diminishes nutrient use efficiency, and ultimately constrains sustainable production of edible roses. A 2‐year field experiment was carried out to explore the regulatory effects of reduced inorganic fertilizer combined with amino acid fertilizer on rhizosphere soil environment, yield, and quality. The experiment followed a two‐factor design comprising inorganic fertilizer and amino acid fertilizer. Treatments consisted of five levels of inorganic fertilizer (F 500 : 500, F 700 : 700, F 900 : 900, F 1100 : 1100 and F 1300 : 1300 kg ha −1 year −1 of blended NPK fertilizer [N:P 2 O 5 :K 2 O = 20–20–20]) and two amino acid fertilizer level (M 0 : 0, M 150 : 150 kg ha −1 year −1 ). Soil nutrient availability, enzyme activities, microbial abundance, yield, and quality were systematically evaluated. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM) and entropy weight‐technique for order preference by similarity to ideal solution (TOPSIS) were integrated to evaluate fertilization performance. Compared with single inorganic fertilization, the combined practice significantly improved soil nutrients, enzyme activities, and microbial abundance, and promoted yield and quality, with respective increases of 6.88%–40.02%, 3.82%–27.37%, 3.16%–15.71%, 6.24%–31.93%, and 1.38%–20.39%. PLS‐SEM suggested that fertilization was associated with yield and quality via soil nutrient availability, enzyme activities, and microbial abundance. TOPSIS evaluation identified the treatment with 900 kg ha −1 year −1 (N:P 2 O 5 :K 2 O = 20–20–20) inorganic fertilizer combined with 150 kg ha −1 year −1 amino acid fertilizer as the optimal regime. Integrating reduced inorganic fertilizer with amino acid fertilizer can improve rhizosphere nutrient status while sustaining high yield and quality, providing theoretical and technical support for edible rose cultivation.

title: Exploring the Variability in Growth and Yield‐Related Responses of Soybean Under Rainfed Conditions in Central Europe
summary: ABSTRACT To diversify cereal‐dominated rotations and increase protein supply for feed and plant‐based diets, soybean cultivation in nontraditional areas of Europe is encouraged. However, regional data and knowledge about nodulation, biomass
content: ABSTRACT To diversify cereal‐dominated rotations and increase protein supply for feed and plant‐based diets, soybean cultivation in nontraditional areas of Europe is encouraged. However, regional data and knowledge about nodulation, biomass and yield performance of different cultivars are still scarce. Field trials with nine soybean cultivars were implemented over 3 years in Berlin‐Dahlem, Germany. The main objective was to evaluate the responses and quantify growth, nodulation and yield of diverse feed‐ and food‐grade soybean cultivars under rainfed conditions. Nodulation varied across years, with minor differences among soybean cultivars. Nodule dry weight negatively correlated with numerous growth and yield‐related traits, including plant height, aboveground biomass, grain yield, pod number and harvest index, in comparison to nodule number. The average aboveground biomass ranged from 3101 kg ha −1 in the early food‐grade cultivar Tofina to 2521 kg ha −1 in the late food‐grade cultivar Siroca. Average grain yield ranged between 2317 and 1849 kg ha −1 for feed‐grade cultivars Acardia (early) and Antigua (very early), respectively. Environment contributed 87.0% to the variance in grain yield; year–cultivar interactions contributed 5.2%, whereas cultivar accounted only for 2.4%. There was considerable year‐to‐year variability in soybean yield, attributable to differences in climatic conditions, particularly during pod filling. The 2021 growing season, characterized by comparatively higher and uniformly distributed precipitation, lower evapotranspiration and reduced precipitation deficit during pod filling, had the highest soybean yield and superior grain quality. Our findings indicate that interannual precipitation variability represents a key constraint to achieving stable soybean cultivation in Northern Germany.

title: Living evidence map of the global climate and health literature
summary: OBJECTIVES: This is a protocol for a Cochrane review (flexible). The objectives are as follows: The objectives of this living evidence map are to: systematically map the breadth, scope, and characteristics of the global literature on the re
content: OBJECTIVES: This is a protocol for a Cochrane review (flexible). The objectives are as follows: The objectives of this living evidence map are to: systematically map the breadth, scope, and characteristics of the global literature on the relationship of climate change, climate variability, weather, climate-forcing agents, and fossil fuels with human health and well-being; enable ongoing, up-to-date access to the evolving evidence base through a living approach (encompassing content currency and adjustment of methods); enable identification of clusters of well-researched areas and evidence gaps; enable flexible, accelerated identification, visualization, selection, analysis, and export of records according to the needs of a diverse group of interest holders via an interactive interface and filtering via a dedicated taxonomy; enable the continuous monitoring of a specific topic of interest; and evaluate the rigor, legitimacy, and utility of an AI-supported living evidence mapping approach. Specifically, we envision the map to enable: researchers to identify, collate, and select existing evidence and diverse study designs, explore clusters and gaps, and produce evidence syntheses in a more efficient way; policymakers and international and intergovernmental organizations (such as the World Health Organization or the Sustainable Development Goals Synthesis Coalition) to understand the scope, scale, and distribution of the evidence; research funding bodies to take a more evidence-based approach to funding decisions and identify and fund priority topics, where evidence is most needed and duplication of efforts is avoided; science assessment bodies such as the IPCC or the Lancet Countdown on Climate Change and Health to obtain a comprehensive overview of the research landscape and obtain easy access to relevant lines of evidence for their assessment; health professionals and health systems decision-makers to monitor emerging evidence and evidence syntheses in specific areas that can inform clinical and public health practice and guidelines; and patients and communities directly affected by climate change to gain an overview of the literature relevant to the health risks they face and support the development of evidence-based preparedness and resilience strategies.

title: Reassessing carbon sink fisheries: biogeochemical constraints and ecological-economic-social coupling and governance
summary: Fisheries and aquaculture influence marine carbon cycling, but biological carbon-retention does not necessarily constitute atmospheric carbon dioxide removal. This critical narrative review reassesses carbon sink fisheries, a concept develo
content: Fisheries and aquaculture influence marine carbon cycling, but biological carbon-retention does not necessarily constitute atmospheric carbon dioxide removal. This critical narrative review reassesses carbon sink fisheries, a concept developed in Chinese fisheries research, through an ecological-economic-social framework. Seaweed cultivation, bivalve aquaculture, integrated multi-trophic aquaculture, and fisheries management are distinguished by carbon pathways and evidentiary requirements. Calcification, respiration, atmospheric replenishment, counterfactual production, postharvest fate, and storage durability constrain carbon claims. Recent observations support enhanced carbon burial in some depositional farming environments, whereas carbonate chemistry and system-level analyses do not justify classifying conventional bivalve production as verified marine carbon dioxide removal. These findings are reconciled by distinguishing measured transfers and stocks from additional atmospheric removal that persists over a specified horizon. A practical governance sequence is proposed: define the intervention and baseline, evaluate claim-specific evidence, report removal and avoided emissions separately, and assess economic performance alongside enforceable social and ecological safeguards. Shared monitoring, tenure protection, transparent benefit allocation, and a zero-carbon-credit financing scenario make the framework relevant to small producers. System dynamics is retained as a prospective tool for testing feedback and policy trade-offs; no calibrated simulation is presented. Climate claims should follow demonstrated carbon outcomes, while food production, nutrient removal, habitat protection, and livelihoods can justify distinct policy instruments.

title: Beyond The Energy Bill: Direct Emissions, Sludge and The Climate Footprint of Wastewater Reuse Trains in Lebanon
summary: Water reuse is central to water security in Lebanon, but the climate burden of producing reclaimed water is rarely assessed under the country's conditions of diesel-dependent electricity and uncontrolled sludge disposal. This study compares
content: Water reuse is central to water security in Lebanon, but the climate burden of producing reclaimed water is rarely assessed under the country's conditions of diesel-dependent electricity and uncontrolled sludge disposal. This study compares seven complete treatment trains, from conventional activated sludge (CAS) with UV disinfection to reverse osmosis, each matched to a Lebanese reuse category. The functional unit is 1 m³ of reclaimed water. A streamlined LCA combines a technology inventory with IPCC 2019 methods for direct N₂O and CH₄, dissolved methane and sludge disposal, five improvement scenarios and a 10,000-run Monte Carlo analysis. Gross climate impacts range from 1.24 kg CO₂ eq/m³ for an anaerobic membrane bioreactor (AnMBR) to 2.34 for a train with reverse osmosis. Direct emissions and sludge disposal account for 50–91% of the impact of every train except reverse osmosis. AnMBR, CAS + UV and a constructed wetland overlap within uncertainty, while reverse osmosis is the highest in 94% of runs. Upgrading from restricted to unrestricted irrigation quality adds only 0.15–0.20 kg CO₂ eq/m³ without reverse osmosis. Recovering 70% of dissolved methane lowers AnMBR to 0.68, a vertical-flow wetland reaches 0.98, and solar power cuts the MBR and reverse osmosis trains by 40–46%. Displacing groundwater pumping roughly halves every train's net footprint. The results indicate that methane and N₂O control, controlled sludge management and renewable electricity should be core design criteria for wastewater reuse in Lebanon.

title: An innovative quaternary hybrid nanocomposite model for improved heat transfer through curved configuration
summary: Investigation of heat transfer using thermal radiation effects is of utmost interest particularly in renewable energy systems and improving the efficiency of curved surface flow model which is important for heat transfer applications. Thus,
content: Investigation of heat transfer using thermal radiation effects is of utmost interest particularly in renewable energy systems and improving the efficiency of curved surface flow model which is important for heat transfer applications. Thus, aim of this work is to formulate an advanced nanofluid model accommodating an external influence of thermal radiations through curved configuration is considered. The governing problem formulated using thermophysical characteristics of tetra-nanofluid (Al2O3, MgO, Cu, and Ag), similarity transforms. The numerical solver bvp4c in MATLAB is then implemented for multi-range parametric output for comparative nanofluids and examined that the curvature and nanomaterial concentration regulate the flow while stretching of the domain enhances it. Further, the use of nonlinear radiations, temperature ratio, NPs concentration, and varying curvature of the surface provided valuable insights for thermal transport improvement. It is examined that skin friction varies from $$\:6.37974$$ to $$\:5.56863$$ , $$\:5.97797$$ to $$\:5.25798$$ , $$\:5.58160$$ to $$\:4.94978$$ , and $$\:5.59535$$ to $$\:4.96051$$ multiple types of fluids against increasing $$\:k$$ from 5 to 20. Moreover, the comparative output highlights that newly tetra-nanofluid has much ability to transform heat than previous classes. Thus, these nanofluids will be better for enhanced thermal applications.

title: Mapping actor diversity is essential for advancing global seagrass conservation
summary: Seagrass conservation is increasingly organised around global agendas for protection, restoration, climate mitigation, biodiversity recovery and nature-positive finance. The actor systems that determine whether these agendas succeed remain
content: Seagrass conservation is increasingly organised around global agendas for protection, restoration, climate mitigation, biodiversity recovery and nature-positive finance. The actor systems that determine whether these agendas succeed remain poorly described, if at all. We developed a heuristic actor-centred framework for seagrass social-ecological systems, combining a literature scan with expert-informed scoring of 22 actor profiles across nine attributes. Actor-relevant seagrass research was concentrated around governance, pressure and dependent actors, while intervention and finance actors were rarely foregrounded. More importantly, material leverage, literature visibility and accountability were misaligned. Several actors with high capacity to shape seagrass outcomes, including fisheries managers, donors, government agencies, and commercial fisheries actors, were less visible than their potential influence suggests. We identify recurrent authority-dependence, impact-visibility and finance-accountability asymmetries that reveal hidden leverage points for conservation. Seagrass conservation must move beyond generic stakeholder language towards actor mapping that links ecological recovery with authority, incentives, legitimacy, knowledge and accountability.

title: Observed substantial South Atlantic Upper-Ocean Water Mass changes over the past 45 years
summary: Abstract. Global climate change is driving widespread transformations in the ocean. The South Atlantic, a key component of the global meridional overturning circulation that regulates the climate, is thought to be undergoing large-scale and
content: Abstract. Global climate change is driving widespread transformations in the ocean. The South Atlantic, a key component of the global meridional overturning circulation that regulates the climate, is thought to be undergoing large-scale and deep-reaching compound state changes in temperature and salinity throughout the basin, but the underlying physical processes remain unclear. In this study, leveraging advanced ocean observing networks, we investigate the observational evidence and the physical processes shaping both individual and compound (temperature–salinity coupled) changes from a water-mass perspective based on rigorous analyses of observational uncertainty. We find that there are substantial properties changes in all upper-ocean water masses in the South Atlantic over the past 45 years, in which the physical contributions of these changes are due to distinct dynamic and thermohaline processes across different water masses: Surface Water has warmed and become saltier since the 1980s, accompanied by a ~10 % increase in volume driven. The South Atlantic Central Water has expanded vertically by ~1.15 times driven by vertical displacement. The Antarctic Intermediate Water has warmed by roughly 0.25 °C, leading to a density decrease dominated by thermal effects. The pronounced intermediate water warming signal represents a potential early fingerprint of anthropogenic change, now affecting ~70 % of the basin. It has been mixed and advected near-isopycnally into the South Atlantic from the Subpolar Front, Southern Ocean and the Indian Ocean. This study advances basin-scale observational evidences and the physical mechanisms underlying regional individual and compound changes, providing new insight into regional climate variability and long-term changes in a warming climate.

title: Water stable isotopes reveal surface water–groundwater relations, risks and opportunities for a small lake: Paardevlei, Cape Town
summary: Wetlands are valuable ecosystems providing multiple benefits to humans, animals and the environment, but are endangered due to destruction or damage caused by human activity. Paardevlei near Somerset West, Cape Town, was investigated by mea
content: Wetlands are valuable ecosystems providing multiple benefits to humans, animals and the environment, but are endangered due to destruction or damage caused by human activity. Paardevlei near Somerset West, Cape Town, was investigated by means of water chemistry and stable isotope analysis, including surrounding rain, surface water and groundwater. The dissolved ions of all these waters were within acceptable drinking water limits, except for autumn in Paardevlei, due to evaporative enrichment. The d2H and d18O values of water in the vlei showed large increases over the summer (September 2023 to February 2024: d2H from −4 to +60‰ and d18O from −1.7 to +11.0‰), in contrast to groundwater and the Lourens River, which remained more stable (average: −15 and −4‰), suggesting the Lourens River receives baseflow all year, whilst Paardevlei receives less or no groundwater input. Management of Paardevlei therefore needs to consider that rainfall is the primary replenisher of water and with climatic changes forecast for the future, plans should be made to ensure the long-term viability of this water resource.

title: Hazards and Safety Management in Pharmaceutical Industries
summary: As the pharmaceutical industry continues to evolve, ensuring safe working environments and effective risk management has become more important than ever. This volume provides a practical and comprehensive guide to understanding, identifying
content: As the pharmaceutical industry continues to evolve, ensuring safe working environments and effective risk management has become more important than ever. This volume provides a practical and comprehensive guide to understanding, identifying, and controlling the wide range of hazards encountered throughout pharmaceutical manufacturing and operations. Beginning with the multidisciplinary foundations of environmental studies, the book examines the classification and characteristics of physical, biological, chemical, ergonomic, and psychosocial hazards that affect pharmaceutical workplaces. It explores major industry risks, including air- and chemical-based hazards, fire and explosion hazards, and the inherent dangers associated with pharmaceutical production processes. Each topic is supported by practical control measures and preventive strategies designed to reduce risk and promote a strong culture of workplace safety. The volume also presents a cohesive framework for hazard management by integrating regulatory requirements, industry standards, and best practices. From hazard identification and risk assessment to personal protective measures, organizational safety perspectives, and emergency preparedness, it provides readers with the knowledge needed to develop and implement effective safety programs. Real-world case studies, practical examples, and discussions of emerging technologies further demonstrate how modern approaches can strengthen safety performance and regulatory compliance. Serving as both a reference and practical guide, Hazards and Safety Management in Pharmaceutical Industries is an invaluable resource for researchers, industry professionals, safety officers, faculty, and students involved in pharmaceutical manufacturing, industrial safety, regulatory affairs, and environmental health. It offers the essential knowledge required to foster safer, more efficient, and more sustainable pharmaceutical operations.

title: Effect of indole-3-butyric acid concentrations on root and shoot morphogenesis and nursery establishment of dragon fruit (Hylocereus undatus (Haw.) Britton & Rose) stem cuttings
summary: The rapid expansion of commercial dragon fruit (Hylocereus undatus (Haw.) Britton & Rose) cultivation necessitates the standardisation of reliable vegetative propagation protocols for producing high-quality planting material. A 2-year field
content: The rapid expansion of commercial dragon fruit (Hylocereus undatus (Haw.) Britton & Rose) cultivation necessitates the standardisation of reliable vegetative propagation protocols for producing high-quality planting material. A 2-year field investigation (2023–24 and 2024–25) was conducted at the Central Nursery, Vasantrao Naik Marathwada Krishi Vidyapeeth, Parbhani, Maharashtra, India (19.26° N, 76.78° E, 409 m above mean sea level), to evaluate the effects of different indole-3-butyric acid (IBA) concentrations (I1 = 5000 ppm, I2 = 6000 ppm and I3 = 7000 ppm; quick dip for 10–15 sec) on adventitious rooting, shoot morphogenesis, sapling survival and economic returns. Exogenous IBA treatments induced significant (P < 0.05) variation in all evaluated parameters. Application of IBA at 6000 ppm (I2) consistently gave superior performance in both seasons and in the pooled analysis. The minimum number of days to shoot initiation was recorded under I2 (34.34 days) and this treatment also gave the greatest shoot length at 120 days after sprouting (DASp) (38.13 cm), absolute growth rate (0.25 cm day-1), relative growth rate (0.019 cm cm-1 day-1), shoot fresh weight (130.63 g) and shoot dry weight (26.10 g). For rhizogenesis, IBA at 6000 ppm produced the highest number of primary roots per cutting (18.20 at 120 DASp), maximum root length (25.20 cm), root density (0.112 mg cm-3, equivalent to 1.84 mg in-3), root fresh weight (15.20 g) and root dry weight (5.28 g). The same treatment optimised nursery establishment, with a peak survival of 83.07 %, lowest mortality of 16.93 % and a balanced root-to-shoot length ratio of 0.80. Increasing the concentration to 7000 ppm (I3) produced supra-optimal auxin inhibition, delaying sprouting (36.96 days), reducing primary root number (16.70) and root density (0.094 mg cm-3) and raising mortality to 32.77 %. Economic evaluation, recomputed treatment-wise, established IBA at 6000 ppm as the most profitable treatment (gross B:C ratio 2.33; net B:C ratio 1.33). A quick-dip treatment of IBA at 6000 ppm is therefore recommended for efficient, high-quality and commercially viable nursery production of dragon fruit saplings.

title: Bayesian optimized neural network modeling for radiative flow of MHD hybrid nanoliquid with oxytactic microbes for biomedical applications
summary: This work examines the impacts of Joule heating and viscous dissipation on the bioconvection flow of a CNTs-water hybrid nanofluid over a sheet while optimising for the Soret and Dufour effects. The complex relationships governing the syste
content: This work examines the impacts of Joule heating and viscous dissipation on the bioconvection flow of a CNTs-water hybrid nanofluid over a sheet while optimising for the Soret and Dufour effects. The complex relationships governing the system are simulated and comprehended using a neural network technique based on Bayesian Regularized Optimizers. In commercial and ecological uses, oxytactic and gyrotactic microbes are significant. While oxytactic microbes improve wastewater treatment by migrating into oxygen-rich areas and speeding up pollutant destruction, gyrotactic microorganisms aid mineral transport by lining up with fluid motion. While microbial activity improves mixing and transport, the introduction of CNTs-based hybrid nanofluids increases thermal conductivity, allowing sophisticated bioreactors and diagnostic systems. All things considered, the model enables bioengineering and biomedical applications that call for exact thermal and solutal control. To reduce error and get approximation results for various CNTs-water hybrid nanofluid's system scenarios, the generated synthetic data is subjected to the Bayesian-Regularized approach. The effectiveness of the Bayesian Regularized technique, developed for computational fluid dynamics of hybrid nanofluid, is demonstrated by learning curves on mean square error, regression analysis, transition state index, error distribution histogram, and fitness plots.

title: Brazil’s climate targets impaired by the potential cessation of the Amazon carbon sink
summary: In accordance with the recommendations of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), countries utilize the "managed land" proxy for their national greenhouse gas (GHG) emission inventories. This implies deducting “passive” carbon
content: In accordance with the recommendations of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), countries utilize the "managed land" proxy for their national greenhouse gas (GHG) emission inventories. This implies deducting “passive” carbon removals from countrywide gross GHG emissions. Long-term forest plots indicate that the carbon sink in structurally intact Amazon forest has weakened by roughly 30% since the 1990s, as CO₂-driven growth is increasingly offset by warming. This matters for accounting, given that the majority of the carbon removal reported by countries such as Brazil is passive uptake on managed land. That carbon sink is now being eroded by the same warming it is expected to help limit. Statistical extrapolation of that observational evidence indicate the Amazon carbon sink may cease by mid-2030s. Here we evaluate the impact of this potential cessation of the Amazon carbon sink in the mid-2030s on Brazil's future emissions, in the context of its Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC) to the Paris Agreement. This is achieved by rescaling the forest carbon removal term embedded within Brazil’s NDC target, which was determined with the support of an integrated-assessment model scenario. Our results indicate that the potential cessation of carbon removals by structurally intact Amazon forests will imply in an increase of 21% to 26% in Brazil's total (economy-wide) net emissions in 2035, in comparison with its NDC pledge. This finding may be relevant also for other regions, e.g. Africa, where comparable reductions in the carbon sink of their forests are also predicted to occur in the subsequent decades. It is crucial that Brazil and other forest nations that rely on currently strong passive sinks adjust their climate targets, for example by anticipating the timing of their net-zero pledge (currently set to 2050 in Brazil), and increasing its GHG emission cuts in sectors such as energy and transport.

title: The Alternative to “Harm” in the ESA “Take” Claims
summary: Wildlife agencies recently finalized major changes to regulations interpreting the Endangered Species Act (ESA). These regulations remove longstanding habitat protections for endangered and threatened species. To better protect wildlife and
tags: North American Model of Wildlife Conservation
content: Wildlife agencies recently finalized major changes to regulations interpreting the Endangered Species Act (ESA). These regulations remove longstanding habitat protections for endangered and threatened species. To better protect wildlife and to solidify habitat protection’s role in Section 9 ESA litigation, conservation groups should bring more claims arguing that proposed projects “harass” wildlife by changing or destroying their habitat. This Note explores the potential effectiveness of “take” claims that allege “harass,” rather than “harm,” in the habitat modification context.

title: Biomass stock and carbon accumulation potential of Quercus lanata Sm. dominated forest in the central Himalayan region
summary: Forests play a vital role in global carbon cycles by storing large amounts of biomass and serving as major carbon sinks. This study quantified tree biomass, carbon stock, productivity and carbon sequestration potential across three Quercus
content: Forests play a vital role in global carbon cycles by storing large amounts of biomass and serving as major carbon sinks. This study quantified tree biomass, carbon stock, productivity and carbon sequestration potential across three Quercus lanata (Syn. Quercus lanuginosa) dominated forest sites in the Kumaun Himalaya, Uttarakhand, of which two are located in Nainital and one in Pithoragarh districts, at elevations ranging from 1950 to 2200 m. Across all the sites, total tree density varied between 590 and 1115 individuals ha-¹. The tree biomass was estimated by measuring the circumference of trees at breast height. Biomass was estimated using non-destructive allometric equations and carbon stock and sequestration rates were calculated. Across all 3 sites, the tree biomass ranged between 298.49 t ha-¹ and 441.79 t ha-¹ and the carbon stock varied between 141.78 t C ha-¹ and 209.85 t C ha-¹. Forest productivity ranged between 5.39 t ha-¹ yr-1 and 12.34 t ha-¹ yr-1, while carbon sequestration ranged from 2.56 to 5.86 t C ha-¹yr-¹. Quercus lanata was the dominant species at all sites, contributing the largest share in total tree biomass and carbon. The findings emphasise the important role of Q. lanata forests in carbon storage and climate change mitigation. This study provides key baseline data to support strategies aimed at increasing carbon sequestration and maintaining forest ecosystem functions in Himalayan temperate forests.

title: Climate-change-driven shifts in secondary metabolism of oat ( Avena sativa L.): toward candidate metabolite markers for drought and waterlogging stress
summary: Climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of drought, waterlogging, and other environmental extremes that threaten oat (Avena sativa L.) production and quality.This review examines oat secondary metabolites, including avenant
content: Climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of drought, waterlogging, and other environmental extremes that threaten oat (Avena sativa L.) production and quality.This review examines oat secondary metabolites, including avenanthramides, phenolic acids, flavonoids, avenacins, and avenacosides, in relation to primary metabolism and physiological responses to contrasting water stresses.Oat drought research links salicylate signaling with the modulation of carbon, antioxidant, and photo-oxidative metabolism, whereas oat-specific evidence for waterloggingresponsive secondary metabolites is much more limited.Stressresponsive metabolites are therefore distinguished from candidate metabolite markers and from independently validated markers.An evidence matrix separates four levels: validated oat markers, oat stress-associated candidates, oat biochemical candidates lacking water-stress-specific validation, and cross-species or mechanistic hypotheses.The matrix also identifies gaps in tissue, developmental stage, analytical identification, response magnitude, and association with tolerance phenotypes.Neither metabolite accumulation nor antioxidant activity alone establishes predictive value for stress tolerance.A mechanistic framework connects osmotic adjustment and carbon allocation under drought with oxygen-limited energy metabolism and reoxygenation-related redox responses under waterlogging.Targeted identification, genotype-resolved physiological phenotyping, independent validation, and field evaluation are required before candidate metabolite markers can be used in oat breeding.Stress resilience and functional grain quality should be evaluated as related but distinct outcomes.

title: More Than Two Decades of Ungulate Exclusion Did Not Alter Soil Organic Carbon Stocks in a Temperate Primeval Forest
summary: ABSTRACT The effects of long‐term wild ungulate exclusion on soil organic carbon (SOC) storage and soil organic matter (SOM) properties in forest ecosystems remain uncertain. Past research has been limited by short exclosure duration, shall
content: ABSTRACT The effects of long‐term wild ungulate exclusion on soil organic carbon (SOC) storage and soil organic matter (SOM) properties in forest ecosystems remain uncertain. Past research has been limited by short exclosure duration, shallow sampling depth, and confounding factors. We addressed these shortcomings by studying 23‐year‐old ungulate exclosures in the strict reserve of the Białowieża National Forest (eastern Poland) that has been protected from major human disturbances for centuries. The study also evaluated the effects of tree species composition, tree species diversity, and soil texture. Large ungulate exclusion decreased bulk density in the mineral soil, increased the C:N ratio in 5–10 cm and 10–25 cm soil layers but did not affect SOC stocks in the forest floor (FF) or mineral soil. Additionally, exclusion did not affect the partitioning of carbon between mineral‐associated organic matter (MAOM) and particulate organic matter (POM) fractions in the uppermost soil layer (0–5 cm). Higher tree species diversity was associated with lower soil C:N ratios, whereas a greater conifer proportion was associated with higher FF and soil C:N ratios. Soil texture had no significant impact on FF or mineral SOC stocks but did influence carbon partitioning among SOM fractions and soil C:N ratios. In summary, while large herbivores can impact soil C‐storage characteristics in open temperate ecosystems, we find that, on decadal timescales, tree species composition and diversity and soil texture exert greater control over these parameters in a temperate primeval forest. Therefore, large ungulate exclusion is unlikely to provide soil C storage benefits in similar forest systems.

title: Advances in the transcriptional regulation of seed vigor and its application in molecular breeding for rice
summary: Rice seed vigor is a life-cycle trait whose performance after sowing depends on physiological capacity established during seed development, preserved during storage, and reactivated during germination and seedling establishment. Rather than
content: Rice seed vigor is a life-cycle trait whose performance after sowing depends on physiological capacity established during seed development, preserved during storage, and reactivated during germination and seedling establishment. Rather than functioning as isolated stage-specific pathways, transcriptional networks coordinate a series of transitions between protection and growth. During seed development, transcription factors establish embryo competence, reserve organization, desiccation tolerance, and proteostasis, thereby creating the physiological capacity for subsequent performance. During storage, ABA- and auxin-associated bZIP networks, including the OsARF12-OsbZIP23 and OsbZIP23-PER1A modules and SAG9-associated regulation, maintain longevity through antioxidant and protective processes; emerging salicylic acid-associated signaling further extends this hormone-redox regulatory framework. After imbibition, ABA-GA balance, sugar and energy signaling, reserve mobilization, reactive oxygen species homeostasis, and cell expansion determine the timing and uniformity of germination, while related regulatory modules support establishment under salinity, chilling, water deficit, and oxygen limitation. Importantly, current evidence varies substantially in strength: some regulators are directly supported by germination, longevity, dormancy, or stress-vigor phenotypes, whereas others remain developmental candidates inferred mainly from grain composition or seed-development traits. Field-emergence validation and natural-storage evidence also remain limited. We therefore propose that rice seed-vigor improvement should prioritize stage-appropriate regulatory alleles and precise modulation of transcription-factor activity, while jointly considering storability, dormancy and pre-harvest sprouting resistance, field establishment, yield, and grain quality.

title: Biosynthetic additive manufacturing through mycelium-bacteria consortia
summary: Lignocellulosic biomass is the most abundant renewable raw material on Earth, yet its structural and carbon-storage potential remains unrealized: microbial decomposition returns stored carbon to the atmosphere before it can be harnessed as
content: Lignocellulosic biomass is the most abundant renewable raw material on Earth, yet its structural and carbon-storage potential remains unrealized: microbial decomposition returns stored carbon to the atmosphere before it can be harnessed as a durable material. Distinct microbial processes, such as biosynthesis and biomineralization, offer a natural counterpoint, converting organic carbon into mechanically robust, persistent materials such as polymers and minerals. Here, we establish a biosynthetic additive manufacturing strategy through mycelium-bacteria consortia, by coupling fungal self-assembly with bacterial biomineralization inside fabricated three-dimensional scaffolds derived from lignocellulosic biomass. Trametes versicolor forms a continuous living mycelial network that serves as both a structural template and a transport pathway, guiding the spatial colonization of Sporosarcina pasteurii and enabling volumetric calcium carbonate deposition throughout the scaffold interior, overcoming the surface-limited mineralization of conventional microbial systems. Integration with helicoidal Bouligand architectures translates microscale mineral reinforcement into macroscale performance, increasing compressive Young's modulus by 7-14-fold and ultimate strength by 5-fold relative to unmineralized conventional mycelium-based living composites. The living mycelial network also enables autonomous self-healing and modular self-assembly through hyphal bridging without external adhesives or energy input. This work establishes a scalable route for converting and upcycling transient biomass carbon into durable living structural materials for sustainable construction.

title: How Fire Moves Carbon in North American Ecosystems Shaped by Fire and Grazing
summary: ABSTRACT Fire interacts with ecosystem carbon in North American fire-grazing rangelands through processes that span chemical forms, soil depths, and temporal horizons. We synthesize empirical evidence on fire-driven carbon redistribution ac
content: ABSTRACT Fire interacts with ecosystem carbon in North American fire-grazing rangelands through processes that span chemical forms, soil depths, and temporal horizons. We synthesize empirical evidence on fire-driven carbon redistribution across the continental region where frequent fire and bison grazing historically co-occurred. Across these rangelands, temperate grasses allocate roughly 75–80% of biomass belowground, outside the combustion zone. Herbaceous aboveground biomass typically recovers within one to three growing seasons. Incomplete combustion produces pyrogenic carbon (PyC) amounting to ∼12% of the carbon emitted by fire. The stable component of that PyC persists in soil on centennial to millennial timescales. Frequent burning can reduce bulk soil organic carbon relative to fire exclusion, especially in dry systems, while shifting carbon inputs toward pyrogenic material. Across the Great Plains, shorter modeled fire intervals are associated with a larger mineral-associated fraction and a smaller particulate fraction, whereas the pyrogenic fraction changes little. Where fire is excluded, woody plant encroachment shifts a larger share of ecosystem carbon into aboveground biomass exposed to fire, drought, and dieback, while altering hydrologic function, biodiversity, and resilience to disturbance. The fire-grazing interaction distributes combustion and recovery across a shifting patch mosaic in which litter retention, grazing pressure, and belowground carbon inputs vary among patches. Carbon accounting frameworks that measure only stock size can mistake the carbon vulnerability created by fire suppression for carbon gain, inadvertently penalizing disturbance that sustains persistent soil carbon in these systems.

title: Geographic gradients reshape dissolved organic matter activity to regulate microbial metabolic strategies and greenhouse gas production across alpine aquatic systems
summary: Abstract As a sensitive region of global climate change, the Qinghai‐Tibet Plateau is experiencing permafrost degradation, leading to the release of sequestered carbon and nitrogen into aquatic ecosystems. However, the spatial heterogeneity
content: Abstract As a sensitive region of global climate change, the Qinghai‐Tibet Plateau is experiencing permafrost degradation, leading to the release of sequestered carbon and nitrogen into aquatic ecosystems. However, the spatial heterogeneity and underlying drivers of greenhouse gas concentrations across diverse water body types remain unclear. Here, we investigated the concentration patterns of greenhouse gases (CO 2 , CH 4 , and N 2 O) in rivers, lakes, and thermokarst lakes along an elevational gradient of 4382 m on the plateau. Results showed that mean CO 2 , CH 4 , and N 2 O concentrations were 74.39, 0.67, and 0.065 μ mol L −1 , respectively. Rivers exhibited the highest CO 2 , thermokarst lakes the highest CH 4 , and N 2 O followed a lakes > thermokarst lakes > rivers pattern. The concentrations of CH 4 and N 2 O declined with elevation, especially in lakes. Mechanistic analyses revealed that complex macromolecules, especially highly unsaturated and phenolic compounds, were closely involved in microbial carbon and nitrogen cycling. Dissolved organic matter meta‐metabolomics further indicated a high proportion of lignin compounds within the active dissolved organic matter pool, suggesting that these traditionally recalcitrant molecules play a more dynamic biogeochemical role in alpine waters than previously recognized. Moreover, microbial life‐history strategy analyses demonstrated that communities adapt to variations in dissolved organic matter bioavailability by shifting metabolic priorities from central metabolism toward polymer degradation. Our findings elucidate how macro‐geographic gradients shape the spatial patterns of greenhouse gas by driving microenvironmental differentiation. These insights have important implications for predicting future trajectories of carbon and nitrogen cycling on the plateau and for informing adaptive management strategies in fragile alpine ecosystems.

title: Researchers as predators: are field biologists altering traits of the populations that they study?
summary: Field biologists rarely directly measure the long-term impact of their work on the populations they study. However, heavy or repeated sampling (with or without release) could potentially alter population traits and even bias study conclusio
content: Field biologists rarely directly measure the long-term impact of their work on the populations they study. However, heavy or repeated sampling (with or without release) could potentially alter population traits and even bias study conclusions. Trinidadian guppies (Poecilia reticulata) are a frequently-studied species in evolutionary biology, particularly in the context of variation in predation. Here, we tested how research sampling intensity might be associated with behavioral traits (boldness, exploration, and shoaling), coloration (relative black and orange area), or size (body mass) in two low predation guppy populations. We carried out a literature review and identified paired sites in the Aripo and Paria rivers that have been either weakly-sampled or heavily-sampled for research, collected guppies from these sites, and measured traits. None of the behavioral traits, orange colouration, or mass showed any detectable impact of sampling intensity, which is reassuring for long-term guppy research. However, guppies from heavily-sampled sites had greater relative black area than did those from weakly-sampled sites. This last result suggests that guppy researchers could have unintended impacts on some guppy traits, and highlights the importance of considering long-term researcher-induced effects in study design.

title: Short-term impacts of fuel treatments to above-ground forest carbon storage and stability in southeastern British Columbia, Canada
summary: Abstract Background Extreme wildfires produce substantial carbon emissions and are increasingly causing some forests to transition from carbon sinks to net carbon sources. Fuel treatments are often implemented to proactively reduce the risk
content: Abstract Background Extreme wildfires produce substantial carbon emissions and are increasingly causing some forests to transition from carbon sinks to net carbon sources. Fuel treatments are often implemented to proactively reduce the risk of severe wildfire and resulting emissions; however, there is limited existing research characterizing the effects of these treatments on forest carbon storage and stability in the seasonally dry, fire-prone forests of southeastern British Columbia, Canada. We partnered with five community forests that implemented different types of fuel treatments—involving combinations of thinning, pruning, and pile burning or chipping—between the summers of 2021 and 2022. We used allometric equations to estimate differences in above-ground carbon stored on-site pre- and post-treatment and across treatment types while also accounting for the utilization of biomass removed off-site during treatment. We then combined field data with the First Order Fire Effects Model to quantify potential tree mortality and direct carbon emissions under three future wildfire scenarios in forest stands with and without fuel treatments. Results Fuel treatments reduced above-ground carbon storage across all treatment types, 1 year after treatment. High-intensity thinning treatments resulted in greater relative decreases to total above-ground carbon than low-intensity thinning treatments; however, high-intensity thinning improved carbon stability as represented by greater decreases to potential tree mortality from wildfire. High-intensity thinning treatments had greater biomass utilization than low-intensity thinning treatments due to the removal of merchantable timber, which has a longer-term carbon storage potential. Compared to pre-treatment conditions, fuel treatments had a minor impact on potential direct carbon emissions. Conclusions This work develops ecosystem-specific knowledge to critically evaluate the short-term effects of fuel treatments on forest carbon stocks in fire-prone landscapes of British Columbia and provides a foundation for future monitoring of carbon stocks over time.

title: A soil–feedstock greenhouse mesocosm matrix for screening carbon dioxide removal via enhanced rock weathering
summary: Enhanced rock weathering (ERW) is a carbon dioxide removal (CDR) strategy in which crushed silicate and carbonate rocks are applied to soils to accelerate mineral weathering, releasing base cations and converting CO 2 into dissolved bicarbo
content: Enhanced rock weathering (ERW) is a carbon dioxide removal (CDR) strategy in which crushed silicate and carbonate rocks are applied to soils to accelerate mineral weathering, releasing base cations and converting CO 2 into dissolved bicarbonate.The ocean is conservatively regarded as the final reservoir for this inorganic carbon.However, mineral dissolution alone does not necessarily translate into CDR.Alkalinity may be neutralised by existing soil acidity, and weathering-derived cations may be retained on soil exchange sites, taken up by plants, incorporated into secondary minerals or leached with non-carbonate anions rather than bicarbonate.Realised CDR is therefore strongly soil-dependent.In order to test this, here we present the design and methodology of GH2025, a greenhouse mesocosm experiment configured to systematically explore soil-feedstock interactions across a broad parameter space.It follows the multi-year Carbon Drawdown Initiative trial GH2023, which established that soil processes strongly influence alkalinity export and thus CDR, with weathering-derived cations largely retained in exchangeable, carbonate, oxide and clay-mineral pools and strong between-combination variability.These processes complicate the quantification of CDR and the development of robust measurement, reporting and verification (MRV) approaches.Identifying the soil-feedstock combinations that deliver efficient and verifiable CDR therefore remains a central challenge for ERW deployment.GH2025 comprises 450 lysimeter pots spanning 29 natural, agricultural and engineered technosol soils and 19 feedstocks representing seven mineralogical and dissolution-kinetic categories, including industrial by-products, carbonates, carbonate-silicate mixes and various types of silicates.The design prioritises breadth over replication, using one pot per soil-feedstock combination and three soil-only controls per soil to maximise parameter-space coverage.Leachate is sampled every six to eight weeks and analysed for total alkalinity, dissolved inorganic carbon, electrical conductivity, pH and dissolved oxygen.Following dismantling, soils will be analysed for pH, effective cation exchange capacity, soil inorganic and organic carbon and operationally defined solid-phase cation pools.The resulting dataset will support machine-learning approaches to identify the soil and feedstock properties governing alkalinity export and CDR, and to predict favourable combinations for scalable deployment.

title: Spartina anglica extract attenuates TNF-α/IFN-γ-induced inflammatory responses in HaCaT keratinocytes through suppression of the MAPK, NF-κB, and STAT1 signaling pathways
summary: This study investigated the anti-inflammatory effects of Spartina anglica extract (SAE) in a human keratinocyte model of inflammation. HaCaT cells were stimulated with tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and interferon-γ (IFN-γ) to induce infla
content: This study investigated the anti-inflammatory effects of Spartina anglica extract (SAE) in a human keratinocyte model of inflammation. HaCaT cells were stimulated with tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) and interferon-γ (IFN-γ) to induce inflammatory responses. Cell viability was assessed using the MTT assay to determine non-cytotoxic concentrations. The expression of the chemokines TARC/CCL17 and macrophage-derived chemokine MDC/CCL22 was quantified at both the mRNA and protein levels using quantitative real-time PCR and ELISA, respectively. In addition, the activation of key inflammatory signaling pathways was evaluated by Western blot analysis. SAE did not exhibit cytotoxic effects at concentrations up to 250 μg/mL. Under inflammatory conditions, SAE significantly reduced the expression of CCL17 and CCL22 in a dose-dependent manner. Mechanistically, this suppression was associated with decreased phosphorylation of MAPK signaling components, including ERK, JNK, and p38, as well as inhibition of NF-κB and STAT1 activation. High-performance liquid chromatography analysis revealed a major peak corresponding to the retention time of iso-orientin in SAE. These findings suggest that SAE may attenuate keratinocyte-mediated inflammatory responses through modulation of chemokine expression and key intracellular signaling pathways.

title: Canopy nutrient balance predicts autumn senescence across U.S. forests
summary: Terrestrial ecosystems are changing rapidly under global nutrient enrichment, yet how canopy nutrients balance shapes the seasonal end of photosynthesis, a critical control on ecosystem carbon cycling, remains unclear. Rising anthropogenic
content: Terrestrial ecosystems are changing rapidly under global nutrient enrichment, yet how canopy nutrients balance shapes the seasonal end of photosynthesis, a critical control on ecosystem carbon cycling, remains unclear. Rising anthropogenic nitrogen inputs are shifting many ecosystems towards relative phosphorus limitation, with uncertain consequences for autumn phenology. Here, we combined airborne imaging spectroscopy with remotely sensed phenology to test whether canopy nutrient ratios predict spatial variations in autumn senescence across National Ecological Observatory Network sites in the United States. Higher canopy N:P is consistently associated with earlier senescence in 20 out of 25 sites, whereas higher N:K has opposite effects in 19 sites after controlling for climate, elevation, dominant species, and canopy structure. Growing-season productivity is generally related to later senescence, but only modestly mediates the direct nutrient-phenology associations. These findings add a phenological dimension to the functional impacts of nutrient imbalance on terrestrial ecosystems and demonstrate that nutrients provide predictive power beyond climate alone. Continued nitrogen deposition is expected to increase relative phosphorus limitation, a shift that could be associated with earlier senescence and shorter growing season. Incorporating canopy nutrients into phenological models may therefore improve forecasts of canopy duration and carbon fluxes under ongoing nutrient enrichment.

title: Mineral Nutrition and Plant Energy Metabolism: A Hypothesis-Driven Review of Nutrient Function, Potential Energetic Leverage, and Crop Productivity
summary: Mineral nutrition is evaluated through nutrient supply, deficiency, tissue concentration, and yield response. These indicators help establish sufficiency but do not fully describe the metabolic costs or spatial and temporal constraints invo
content: Mineral nutrition is evaluated through nutrient supply, deficiency, tissue concentration, and yield response. These indicators help establish sufficiency but do not fully describe the metabolic costs or spatial and temporal constraints involved in correcting a nutrient-dependent limitation. This hypothesis-driven narrative review examines acquisition, assimilation, homeostasis, and respiration alongside photochemical energy conversion, ATP-dependent metabolism, carbon allocation, and crop productivity. It distinguishes basal fertilization from corrective functional mineral nutrition, which targets limitations arising from stress or disrupted acquisition and transport despite apparently adequate background supply. Three provisional, potentially overlapping profiles organize documented mechanisms and proposed energy–carbon connections: Group I (Ca, Fe, K, Mg, Mn, and P), Group II (Cl, Cu, N, S, and Zn), and Group III (B, Mo, and Ni). Their boundaries remain unvalidated and imply no fertilizer priority. Nitrogen is assigned provisionally to Group II because crop responses to additional N vary with nutritional status and sink demand. Correcting N limitation can substantially improve photosynthesis and harvested yield; beyond sufficiency, additional N may increase the costs of assimilation, protein turnover, and maintenance with limited productive benefit. The review distinguishes evidence for functional recovery, harvested yield, and measured energetic efficiency. Current evidence does not permit quantitative comparison of net energetic efficiency across all fourteen nutrients. Mineral correction and biostimulation may complement one another when they address different components of an active limitation.

title: High‐Energy Pulse Generation in a Passively Q‐Switched 2 μm Laser Based on a HfSe 2 /WSe 2 Heterojunction Saturable Absorber
summary: ABSTRACT In this work, a HfSe 2 /WSe 2 heterojunction saturable absorber prepared by liquid‐phase exfoliation combined with spin coating was employed in a passively Q‐switched Tm:YAP laser. At an incident pump power of 17.8 W, the maximum s
content: ABSTRACT In this work, a HfSe 2 /WSe 2 heterojunction saturable absorber prepared by liquid‐phase exfoliation combined with spin coating was employed in a passively Q‐switched Tm:YAP laser. At an incident pump power of 17.8 W, the maximum single‐pulse energy of 34.9 μJ, repetition rate of 73.1 kHz, pulse duration of 710.5 ns, and peak power of 49.1 W were obtained. The experimental results demonstrate that the HfSe 2 /WSe 2 heterostructure exhibits excellent nonlinear modulation capability in passively Q‐switched lasers operating at 2 μm.

title: Observation of Excess Benzene in Post-Fire Crude Oil and Risk Communication Implications
summary: Abstract This investigation examines whether benzene in heat-affected crude oil declines as a volatility-only model would predict after tank-fire extinguishment with fluorine-free foam (F3). Among BTEX compounds, benzene has the highest vap
content: Abstract This investigation examines whether benzene in heat-affected crude oil declines as a volatility-only model would predict after tank-fire extinguishment with fluorine-free foam (F3). Among BTEX compounds, benzene has the highest vapor pressure and the lowest molecular weight and boiling point; it should therefore be depleted from the surface layer at least as fast as toluene, ethylbenzene, and the xylenes (TEX), and faster if evaporative loss dominates. Liquid samples were collected from the top 12 in. (30 cm) of a 2.4 m diameter × 2.19 m high test tank before burning and after repeated F3-extinguished burns. Aliquots were aerated in a closed vapor chamber and the headspace was analyzed as whole air. That assay characterizes an enriched source profile; the reported concentrations are not outdoor or breathing-zone exposures. Absolute benzene in the chamber headspace declined (81 ppmv in the single fresh-oil sample versus a post-burn mean of 31 ppmv), but TEX declined far more (for example, toluene from 680 ppmv to a post-burn mean of 26.5 ppmv). Benzene’s share of ΣBTEX vapor therefore rose from about 5% before burning to about 43% after burning (about 60% in overnight mixed-oil samples). A volatility-only account does not explain that pattern. A source term is required: conversion of precursors in the hot zone (thermal or steam-related cracking) and/or resupply of benzene from the cooler bulk liquid. Distinguishing those mechanisms is outside the scope of this observational study. The practical implication is that post-fire crude oil in deep tanks should not be assumed to have been stripped of benzene the way thin-film in situ burns are, and risk communication for responders should treat the residual liquid as a continuing benzene source.
